en: *Jiatai Puding Lu*, Scroll One.
Compiled and recorded by the monk (Subject) Zhengshou of Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Temple in Pingjiang Prefecture.
Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Dengchuan said: "When the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he pre-emptively commanded Mahākāśyapa, saying:
'I now entrust to you the pure Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the true mark which is markless, and the subtle, sublime, and correct Dharma. You must protect and uphold them.'"
He further commanded Ānanda to assist in the propagation of the teachings so that they would not be interrupted. Guangdeng says:
Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda, "When the Bhagavat had not yet entered parinirvāṇa, he secretly entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to me before the Many-Sons Stūpa;
I now transmit it to you. These two [Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda] essentially embody the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Āgamas*.
The *Sūtra* refers to that which is received and transmitted. Thereafter, it was handed down from patriarch to patriarch for twenty-eight transmissions until Bodhidharma.
From Bodhidharma, it passed through five generations to Caoxi. After one transmission from Caoxi, it branched out into two pillars:
Qingyuan and Nanyue. Within less than ten transmissions from Qingyuan and Nanyue, the lineage of Nanyue further divided, resulting in what are known as Linji and—
They are called Cao-Dong, Yunmen, Guiyang, and Fayan.

Regarding the profound and esoteric principles of the Buddha-Dharma of India, both the detailed and abbreviated seasonal rites are fully contained herein, standing at the head of the three records of the *Chuan deng lu*. In this current compilation, there is no further redundancy;
rather, the record proceeds directly from Bodhidharma, the First Patriarch of this land, and below him, they are arranged in chronological order for posterity.

[The lineage] is inexhaustible. As for those such as the Fayan and the Guiyang [schools], which ceased after only a few transmissions, they cannot be recorded here (the circumstances regarding the current masters are not yet detailed;
these should be preserved to await future sages).
The sixth-generation patriarch, the First Patriarch Bodhidharma Mahāsattva, was of the Kṣatriya caste. He was the youngest son of King Gandhāra of South India.
This was because the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, had been traveling to convert that country, and the king [had previously] given three of his sons [to him].
They welcomed him and made offerings, presenting him with priceless jewels. Knowing that the time had come to transmit the Way, the Patriarch looked at the offered jewels and asked the three princes:
"This jewel is perfectly round and luminous; is there anything that can equal it? The two younger princes both replied, "Among the seven treasures, this jewel is the most honored;
it is worthy only of a Great Being, whose eloquence is clear and inspired, and whose discourse accords with the principle. The Patriarch sighed in admiration.

They regarded this with suspicion. When Xiangzhi passed away, the entire assembly wailed and fainted; only the Great Being remained resolute in his desire to leave the household life, sitting upright and unmoving.

He soon took leave of his two elder brothers and prostrated at the feet of the Patriarch, saying: "I have long had no regard for national rank or position, desiring instead to benefit all beings through the Dharma, yet I had not found a teacher.
I have waited for a long time, and now that I have met the Venerable One, my renunciation is certain. I pray you, [bestow upon me] your compassion and wisdom."
[Upagupta] granted him audience. The Patriarch [Dharmatrāta] shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*).

He then spoke a verse and entrusted to him the Eye-Treasury of the Dharma (*dharmākṣi-kośa*), further prophesying that he would go to China (*Cīna*), where there would be obstacles regarding time and season, and the rise and fall of the Buddha-dharma. Upagupta served diligently for over forty years; when the Patriarch passed away, he returned to his own country.
There he refuted the divergent interpretations of the six schools, whereby his fame spread throughout the Five Indias. More than fifty years having elapsed, he brought immeasurable beings across.

Later, he encountered King Vīradarśin, who held the Triple Gem in contempt. He dispatched Prajñātāra, the head of the Niṣphalavāda school, to visit the king’s presence, where he extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma.
The king attained realization and repented; he then asked, "Who is the teacher of your worthy self?"

He replied, "This is none other than Your Majesty’s uncle, the Great Being Dharmatrāta. The King was struck with awe for a long time and commanded his close attendants to invite him to the inner palace to perform repentance for his past transgressions.
The Great Being, however, reflected that the conditions in China were now ripe and the time had come to propagate the Dharma there;

he therefore took leave of the ancestral stupa, his fellow students, and King Harsa (Yijian), entrusting them with the protection of the teachings. The King prepared a large ship and personally led his ministers [to see him off].

[The relics] were entrusted [to him] and sent to the coastal borderlands. After three years had passed, on the twenty-first day of the ninth month of the first year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty (the gengzi year), they finally arrived at Nanhai.
Xiao Li, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, received them with full ceremonial honors.
He submitted a memorial to Emperor Wu. The Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial decree to welcome him back to the capital. On the first day of the tenth month, he arrived at Jinling;

the Emperor went out to the suburbs to receive him and invited him to reside in a separate palace. Thereupon, the Emperor inquired about the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), but their dialogue did not reach accord. This continued until the nineteenth day.

He traveled secretly to the north of the Yangtze River (*Chuanteng* states: "The Master arrived at Shaozhou in the eighth year of the Putong era, the Year of Dingwei [523]. At that time, the Regional Inspector Xiao Ang prepared ceremonial offerings to welcome him and submitted a memorial. However, according to the *Zhengzong ji* of Mingjiao Chan, it says:

"The Master arrived at Shaozhou in the first year of the Putong era, the Year of Gengzi [520], and the Regional Inspector Xiao Li welcomed him and submitted a memorial. This is because Xiao Ang never served as the inspector of Shaozhou; Li was actually the son of Ang. This can be verified by cross-referencing the *Nan shi* and *Bei shi*.)
Then one should take the *Zhengzong ji* as authoritative). Previously, when Master Zhigong was restoring Gaoseng Temple, he said to the temple master Lingguan:
"A Mahāyāna Bodhisattva shall come from the west to extensively transform this land. He then uttered this prophecy for me to hear: "Looking up, I behold two panels."
With a low-slung waist and a twisted hook, he shot down nine crows; only one remained, yet though it arrived, it did not truly arrive. It required the sword for its essential purpose;
meeting a dragon, it would stop; encountering water, it would flee. Having heard this, Lingguan silently took note of it. On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived in Luoyang.
At that time, it was the first year of the Zhengguang era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Later Wei (the *Chuanteng lu* states the tenth year of Taihe).
[He lived there for] nine years. He took up residence at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song, where he sat facing a wall and never spoke a word;
no one could fathom him. There was a monk named Shen Guang who had long resided in the region of Yi and Luo. Having extensively mastered both Buddhist and non-Buddhist texts, he once sighed, saying:

"The teachings of Confucius and Laozi merely provide a rough outline of the profound and subtle; the exegeses of the sutras and shastras have not yet exhausted the wondrous principles. Recently, I have heard of the Great Being Bodhidharma.
Dwelling at Shaolin, [Hui]guang realized that the Great Man was not far away; he was destined to enter the profound realm. Thus, throughout the nights, he attended upon the Great Being.

The Great Being sat solemnly and silently, and no instructions or exhortations were heard. Hui-guang thought to himself: "In the past, those who sought the Way would break their bones to extract the marrow and spread their hair to cover the mud.
If the ancients were already like this, what person am I? On the night of the ninth day of the twelfth month of that year, the sky grew dark..."
Snow and rain fell. Fotudeng stood firm and unmoving. At dawn, the accumulated snow reached his waist. The Bodhisattva saw him and asked, "You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?
Fotudeng wept and said, "I only pray that you will, out of compassion, open the gate of ambrosia and extensively deliver all classes of beings.

The Bodhisattva replied, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort through vast kalpas; one must be able to perform what is difficult to perform, and it is not for those lacking forbearance."
He remained patient. How could one with meager virtue and limited wisdom, harboring a frivolous or arrogant mind, hope to attain the True Vehicle without the toil of diligent practice?

Upon hearing this, Guang severed his left arm and placed it before the Great Being (Mahāsattva). The Great Being took him as a worthy vessel and said to him, "When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma.
That you now sever your arm before me in pursuit of it is likewise acceptable. Thereupon, he changed the man’s name.
Huike replied, "Huike. Huiguan asked, "May I hear about the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? Huike said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another person.
Huiguan said, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace. Huike said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will grant you peace.
Huiguan said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable. Huike said, "I have finished granting you peace of mind. At these words, Huiguan attained great realization. Thereafter—
Several people attained awakening together with him. When the Wei Emperor heard of his extraordinary qualities, he issued three edicts inviting him to court, but he did not come.

The Emperor then bestowed upon him a *kāṣāya*, a water jar, an alms bowl, silks, and other gifts. In the ninth year, wishing to return to India, he commanded his disciples to each speak of what they had attained.

After Dao Fu and the others had finished recounting their realizations, he finally turned to Huiguo, entrusting him with the protection of the Dharma. He then recited the verse on the transmission of the Dharma and spoke of prophetic words. This was transmitted.
Having finished his robes, he went with his disciples to Qiansheng Monastery at Yumen, where he stayed for three days to preach the Dharma for Yang Xuanzhi, the Governor of Qiqi.
He then returned to Shaolin Monastery, where he passed away while sitting upright on the fifth day of the tenth month of the Jiyou year, the second year of Yong’an in the Liang state.
The Emperor dispatched the Palace Attendant He Hongjian to carry a letter to the Liang court to announce his demise.
Emperor Wu was filled with deep sorrow for a long time. He issued an edict for the Crown Prince to compose a full eulogy, and together with the hundred officials, he went to present the offerings.
He bestowed sixteen precious articles to provide for the sacrifice, and granted one hundred bundles of ceremonial silk as a gift of condolence (the eulogy is found in the *Baolin zhuan*).
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month, an imperial edict from the Wei dynasty ordered that his entire body be enshrined in a stupa at Dinglin Temple on Mount Xionger.
Three years later, Emperor Wu heard that the Wei envoy Song Yun had seen him at the Pamir Mountains returning home, carrying a single sandal upon his hand.
He then compiled the master’s biography, from beginning to end, based on what he had heard along with the account of the opening of the tomb during the Wei dynasty.

During the Tang dynasty, Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Yuanjue (Perfect Enlightenment), and his stupa was named Kongguan (Contemplation of Emptiness). (*The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* states that the Patriarch passed away in the year of Bingyin, the nineteenth year of the Taihe era of Emperor Ming of the Later Wei.

Examining this against historical records, the Bingyin year of Taihe is seventeen years prior to the Renwu year of the first year of Tianjian. At that time, Emperor Wu of Liang had not yet ascended the throne; furthermore, Taihe was the reign title of Emperor Xiaowen, and the reign of Emperor Ming did not include the designation "Taihe. Only [Emperor] Ming...)

The chronological sequence of the *Jiaocan Shi Zhengzong Ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of Chan Masters) accords well with historical biographies; however, when compiling the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp), it frequently relied upon the *Baolin Zhuan* (Record of the Baolin Temple), which resulted in significant discrepancies.
The Second Patriarch, the Great Master Huike, was a native of Wulao. He was born into the Ji clan. Having inherited the entrusted mission, he succeeded in propagating the profound wind of the Dharma.

He sought widely for a dharma-heir until the second year of the Tianping era of the Northern Qi dynasty, when there appeared a lay practitioner over forty years of age who did not disclose his name or lineage.
He prostrated and said, "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a chronic wind-ailment; I pray that the Upādhyāya will grant me absolution for my transgressions. [Huike] said, "Bring forth..."
"Your transgression has arrived; I shall grant you repentance. After a long while, the layman said, "I have sought the nature of the transgression, but it is utterly unattainable.

[The Master] said, "I have finished granting you repentance for your transgression. You should dwell in reliance upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. The layman said, "Now that I see the Venerable Master, I already know what the Sangha is.

I do not yet understand what is meant by 'Buddha' and 'Dharma'. [The Master] said, "This very mind is the Buddha; this very mind is the Dharma. The Dharma and the Buddha are non-dual. The Jewel of the Sangha is likewise..."
The man said, "Today I have finally realized that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha-dharma; they are non-dual. The Patriarch agreed with him, shaved his hair, and said, "This is my treasure."

He was named Sengcan. He then received full ordination, whereupon [Huike] spoke a verse and transmitted the robe and the Dharma. For thirty-four years thereafter, he mingled his traces among the people.
On the sixteenth day of the third month of the *guichou* year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he passed away with serene composure due to an illness.

He was one hundred and seven years old at the time. His stupa was erected seventy li northeast of Fuyang in Cizhou. Emperor Dezong posthumously conferred upon him the title "Da... (The rest of the title is omitted).

As for Master Zu, the Third Patriarch, the Great Being Sengcan: his clan and native place are not clearly known. After he visited the First Patriarch, received ordination, and was transmitted the Dharma, he lived in seclusion on Mount Wangong in Shu.
During the period when Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty suppressed the Buddha-dharma, he traveled back and forth between Mount Sikong for more than ten years.
For many years, no one knew of him. In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era, there was a novice monk named Daoxin, fourteen years of age, who came forward, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"I pray that the Upādhyāya will, out of compassion, grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation. [The Master] asked: "Who has bound you? He replied: "No one."
Wurenbo asked, "Since there is nothing further to be bound, why seek liberation? At these words, he attained great enlightenment. He served as his attendant for nine years;

whenever [the Master] tested him with profound and subtle matters, he immediately transmitted to him the robe and the Dharma. He went to Mount Luofu and returned to his former residence after two autumns.

On the fifteenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Daye era, after receiving the offerings of laypeople and officials, he again extensively proclaimed the essentials of the mind to the fourfold assembly.
At the great tree beneath the Dharma assembly hall, he stood with palms joined until his death. His true-body stupa was enshrined at Sangok-ji Temple.
Later, Emperor Xuanzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Jianzhi and named his stupa Jueji.
The Fourth Patriarch, the Great Being Daoxin, was of the Sima clan. His ancestors had long resided in Henei, later migrating to Guangji in Qi. From birth, he was transcendent and extraordinary;
regarding the Dharma of liberation, his realization was as if from a former life. Since succeeding to the patriarchal seat, he had not laid his side upon a mat for nearly sixty years.
During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he led his disciples to Luling, where they encountered a band of rebels surrounding the city. Seven...
After ten days, he was released. In the Jiashen year of the Tang dynasty’s Wude era, he returned to reside at Mount Pòtóu, where his fellow practitioners gathered like clouds.

One day, while traveling to Huángméi, he encountered a young boy of extraordinary physical appearance. He asked, “What is your surname? The boy replied, “I have a surname, but it is not an ordinary one.
He asked, “What is this surname? The boy said, “It is Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). He asked, “Do you have no nature? The boy said, “Nature...”

Because he was [of such] empty nature, the Patriarch recognized him in silence. He sent an attendant monk to his home to entice him into the monastic life. His mother, also aware of their karmic affinity from past lives, showed no sign of reluctance.
The Patriarch then transmitted the robe and the Dharma to him. On the fourth day of the intercalary month in the *xinhai* year of the Yonghui era, he admonished his disciples, saying:
"All dharmas are entirely liberation. You each must protect and mind yourselves, spreading the transformation to those who have not yet been reached."
"Come," he said, and having finished speaking, he sat peacefully and passed away. He was seventy-two years of age. His true body was enshrined at his native mountain;

even to this day, the door of his stupa remains unopened, and his physical features remain as they were when alive. Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dàyī (Great Physician), and his stupa was named Ciyún (Cloud of Compassion).
The Great Master Wuzu Hongren was a native of Huangmei in Qi. He was born to a Zhou family maiden through the medium of the "Pine-Planting Wayfarer," who entered her womb in disguise;
thus, he followed his mother's surname. Having received the mandate of the Great Physician, he subsequently succeeded to the transformation [of the Dharma] at Mount Poutou.
During the Xianheng era, a layman named Huineng came to visit him. The Patriarch asked: "From where have you come?"

He came and said, "I am from Lingnan. The Master asked, "What do you seek? He replied, "I only wish to become a Buddha. The Master said, "As a person from Lingnan, you have no Buddha-nature; how can you possibly become a Buddha?
He replied, "People may come from the north or the south, but how could that be the case for Buddha-nature? The Patriarch inwardly marveled at this.
He had [Huike] stay in the granary for over eight months. Then, in secret, he took the *kṣaumaka* *kāṣāya* he had been wearing and, reciting a verse, entrusted it to him, saying:
"In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him; he transmitted the robe to demonstrate that he had attained the Dharma.

Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a source of contention. It shall remain with you; it will not be transmitted further. He also recorded the location where [the robe] was to be concealed. If one...
He performed the ritual of formal departure and, carrying his robes, traveled southward. None among the assembly were aware of this. From that time on, Huizang no longer ascended the Dharma hall.
After four years had passed, in the second year of the Shangyuan era, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying: "My work is now complete; it is time for me to go. He then entered his room.
He passed away while sitting peacefully. His lifespan was seventy-four years. He was interred in a stupa on East Mountain at Huangmei. His true body remains undecayed to this day.
Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Daman Fayu and the name of his stupa as Fayu-ta.
The Sixth Patriarch, the Great Being Huineng, was the son of the Lu family. His father was Xingtao, originally a native of Fanyang.

In the third year of the Wude era, he was demoted as an official to Xinzhou. He was born at the hour of the rat on the eighth day of the second month in the year of Wuxu, the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era.

A pure and auspicious light filled the room. When his father passed away at the age of three, his family was impoverished; his mother, Lady Li, moved their residence to Nanhai. Having grown up, he sold firewood to support them.

One day, while at a guesthouse, he heard someone reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until reaching the passage: "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere. He attained sudden and profound enlightenment.
Upon returning home, he informed his mother of his intention to seek a teacher for the Dharma and subsequently departed for Shaozhou.

She met the man of noble conduct Liu Zhilüe and formed a friendship with him. When she explained the wondrous principles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to the nun Wujinzang, he invited her to reside at Baolin Temple;
the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds, and it was soon transformed into a magnificent monastery. Suddenly, she thought to herself:
"I seek the Great Dharma; how could I stop halfway? She immediately traveled to a stone chamber in the Western Mountains, where she encountered Meditation Master Zhida.
He went to see Master Daman of Huangmei. Upon meeting him, Daman recognized his potential and ordered him to enter the workshop.

One night, he secretly bestowed upon him the robe and alms bowl, and they remained hidden between the regions of Huaiji and Sihui. On the eighth day of the first month in the first year of the Yifeng era, he arrived at Faxing Monastery in Nanhai.
Staying overnight in the corridors, he heard two monks debating whether it was the wind or the banner that moved. The Patriarch resolved their dispute for them.
There was a Dharma Master named Yin Zong who had frequently lectured on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and was highly esteemed by the assembly.

They marveled at his extraordinary speech and questioned him with great persistence. The Patriarch enlightened him through the principles of the Dharma. Startled, Yin Zong rose and asked, "By what means can this be verified?

The Patriarch directly recounted the beginning and end of how he had received the Dharma and produced the robe of faith, commanding that everyone pay homage to it. After Yin Zong and the others had prostrated themselves, [the Patriarch] further—
Question: When the Great Master transmitted his entrustment, how did he instruct [his disciples]? Answer: He spoke only of seeing one's nature;

he did not discuss meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimukti*), the untainted (*anāsrava*), or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Question again: For what reason did he not discuss meditative concentration and liberation? Answer: Because these two are merely dharmas.
"This is not the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha-dharma is the non-dual dharma. He asked again, "What is meant by the non-dual dharma?
[The Master] replied, "When the Dharma Master lectures on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he clarifies that the Buddha-nature is the non-dual dharma.

For instance, the Bodhisattva Gao-gui-de-wang addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, those who have committed the four grave prohibitions, committed the five heinous crimes, or are icchantikas—'"
"Is the Buddha-nature that severs the roots of goodness severed? The Buddha said, "Noble King of Virtue Bodhisattva, there are two kinds of roots of goodness:
first, the permanent; second, the impermanent. The Buddha-nature is neither permanent nor impermanent; therefore, it is not severed. This is called 'non-duality.
First, the wholesome; second, the unwholesome. The Buddha-nature is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; therefore, it is not severed. This is called..."
The non-duality of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the elements (*dhātu*). Ordinary people perceive them as two; the wise realize that their nature is non-dual.
This non-dual nature is the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, one knows that Buddha-nature is the dharma of non-duality.

Having heard this, Yinzong rose, joined his palms, and expressed his wish to serve him as his teacher. He then addressed the assembly, saying: "This layman is truly a *māṃsadhātu* (an incarnate body)."
"He is a Bodhisattva. My own preaching is like rubble and stones, while his discourse is like refined gold.
Did the people believe this? The entire assembly bowed their heads in refuge. On the fifteenth day, they gathered renowned virtuous masters to shave his hair.
On the eighth day of the second month, he received the full precepts from Vinaya Master Zhiguang. In the spring of the following year, he wished to return to his former [home].
Yin, together with over a thousand monastics and laypeople, escorted him back to Baolin Temple.
Wei Ju, the Prefectural Governor of Shaozhou, invited him to the Dafan Temple to expound the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for the fourfold assembly and to ordain various disciples.

On the first day of the seventh month in the second year of the Xiān Tiān era, he said to his disciples, "I wish to return to Xinzhou; prepare the boats and oars immediately. At that time, the great assembly...

Filled with grief and longing, he entreated the Master to remain for a short while. The Patriarch then expounded the essentials of the Dharma for him. He subsequently proceeded to Guoen Temple, where he again preached the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
A monk who had come from Youzhou arrived to pay his respects and said, "Great Being, the Buddha taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles."
He further said, "Regarding the 'Supreme Vehicle,' my disciples do not understand. I pray that you will grant us your compassion. The Patriarch told him: "You must see it within your own mind;

do not cling to external phenomena. There is no vehicle upon which to ride. It is the capacity of the human mind that creates distinctions. To merely hear, see, recite, and chant is the Small Vehicle.
To awaken to the Dharma and understand its meaning is the Middle Vehicle. To practice in accordance with the Dharma is the Great Vehicle. Upon these words—
Recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature.

When all phenomena are fully understood and all practices are complete, one remains unstained by anything, free from all views and appearances, dwelling nowhere moment to moment, yet establishing all phenomena. This is called the Supreme Vehicle.

As for the meaning of practicing this vehicle, it does not reside in verbal explanation; you must cultivate it yourself. Dharmas do not wait for one another; do not ask me about them. [The monk] then spoke these words:
The Emperor’s mind was greatly awakened. He further expounded the teachings for both the clergy and the laity, employing various parables and providing prophecies regarding future obstacles.
When he had finished reciting the verses, he sat cross-legged at midnight and passed away. A wondrous fragrance permeated the air, and a white rainbow descended to the ground.
It was the third day of the eighth month. Both Shaozhou and Xin’an venerated the Spirit Stupa and competed to invite the remains there.

The Prefectural Governors of the two commanderies burned incense to divine the matter; consequently, [the remains] were enshrined at Caoqi. On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, they entered the stupa. His worldly age was seventy-six.
The precious items bestowed by successive emperors were exceedingly numerous; these, along with his robe of faith, were stored within the stupa.
Emperor Xian posthumously conferred upon him the title Dàshèng (Great Sage). His stupa was named Yuánhé Língzhào (Enlightened Illumination of the Yuanhe Era).
(As recorded in detail in the *Zǔshī Shílù* [Record of the Patriarchs’ Realities] and the *Chuánguǎng Èr Dēng* [Two Lamps of Transmission and Expansion].

According to the *Chuánguǎng Èr Dēng Yílù* [Supplementary Record of the Two Lamps], there was the second-generation Chan Master Zhì (d.u., successor of Tóng'ān Pǐ) of Fèngqī Tóng'ān in Lóngxìng Prefecture, who served his predecessor, Tóng'ān.
After a long time, Baopai was about to pass away. He ascended the hall and said to the assembly, "Before the Many-Sons Stupa, the lineage son is outstanding;
before the Five Old Man Peaks, what is the matter? He raised this question three times. The Master stepped forward and replied, "Outside the curtain of the night-bright moon, they stand in ranks;
ten thousand miles of song and chant proclaim the Great Peace. Baopai said, "It must be this donkey-man indeed! He then entrusted the monastery to the Master.
He passed away with dignified composure. The Master succeeded him on the seat. Later, a monk asked: "All words and phrases fall into the realm of the present moment.
As a student who has come before you, I request the Master to point directly. The Master said: "Not manifest before the eyes; not deluded after the phrase. The monk asked:

"What about the matter beyond? The Master said: "Utterly unchanging; to aim for it is already to deviate. (Examining the lineage of the Hu-zhou school and the tenets of Cao-dong, one finds that Dong-shan Jia emerged from Yun-ju.)

Ying (膺). Ying was succeeded by Tong’an Pi (丕); Pi was succeeded by Tong’an Zhi (志). Current works such as the *Chuan deng lu* (Transmission of the Lamp) list Zhi under Tong’an Wei (威). However, according to the succession, Wei’s heir was Jiufeng Man (滿), and both Wei and Yunju Ying were successors of Dongshan.
Therefore, to list Zhi under Wei is an error.
Chan Master Huimin of Tong’an in Longxing Prefecture (he was a successor of Dongshan Yan). When he first arrived at Dongshan, he asked, “By what do all the sages take their life?

[Dongshan] replied, “Without interruption. Huimin asked, “Is there anything further beyond this? [Dongshan] said, “There is. Huimin asked, “What is this thing that is further beyond? [Dongshan] said, “It does not follow from interruption.
At these words, the Master attained realization. While residing at Tong’an, he once said: [The text continues with the Master’s teaching.]
The Master said: "If one is a true adept, one must raise [the matter] in this way. Nevertheless, even so, it is like a kitchen where the steamer is cold and the dust has accumulated.

"What is the mind of the ancient Buddhas? He replied: "Though the calendar of a thousand years may be of no use, should one offend it, the entire lineage is extinguished as before.
Question: "What is the realm of vast virtue? He replied: "The clear stream flows without interruption; the azure trees never wither. Question: [Continued]
"If you do not propagate the teachings of the Three Vehicles, how can you speak of the ancestors? He said: "The birth of the Prince was not through cultivation or progress;

Question: "The path beyond is not transmitted by the thousand sages; does the Master transmit it? Answer: "An iron ball stuffed into the mouth—hard to obtain."

Shanshan said, "So, you were making such a pretext! He then brushed his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "This old fellow thought I could not understand this koan.

Chan Master Yuanjing Yunhuo of Xifeng in Jizhou (a successor of Qingliang Minghe, who was in the lineage of Yunju Yong). He was the son of the Zeng family from Yonghe in the prefecture. Having abandoned Confucian studies in his youth, he became a bhikṣu and traveled abroad to pay homage to various masters, thereby clarifying his own fundamental matter. Later, he went to see Qingliang, where he stepped forward and asked: "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? Qingliang replied: "Clouds veil the trees at the gate of the sea. Yunhuo said: "After he appeared in the world? Qingliang replied: "The clouds have dispersed, revealing the golden mountain. Yunhuo then bowed. He subsequently received the Dharma seal from Qingliang and resided at Xifeng. His verse of realization reads: "The great function is not hidden; The true path is revealed. A single phrase strikes the heart; The three bodies are all present. He passed away on the twenty-third day of the second month in the second year of the Shaoxing era. He was seventy-six years old and had been a monk for fifty-two years. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Yuanjing. His stupa was named "Dongyue" (Eastern Peak). "What then? [Jingqing] asked. He replied, "I shall split open the Iron Ring Mountains. At these words, he attained great enlightenment and was finally granted formal certification (*in'ka*).
He returned to reside at Baolong on West Peak, where his companions gathered like clouds; this was in the second year of the Xiangfu era.

When Emperor Zhenzong heard of his reputation, he dispatched an attendant to summon him to court. The Emperor inquired about the essentials of his school and kept him at the Imperial Garden for some time.
There, he sat in meditation without food. The Emperor marveled at his extraordinary character and conferred upon him the title Yuanjing (Complete Purity).

Later, when he requested leave to return home, the Emperor could not dissuade him and finally granted his request. He declined all the lavish gifts bestowed upon him, yet the Emperor assigned him four attendants and presented him with ceremonial robes.
He ordained ten disciples and composed poems to honor their conduct. In the fourth year, he changed the name of Baolong to Xiangfu, thereby also commemorating the Master’s residence.
Once, when someone asked about the essential principles of the *Yi* (Book of Changes), the Master said:
"The spirit arises from the formless and is perfected through the formed; by proceeding from the existent to the non-existent, one can then accord with the wondrous, perfect, and correct."

The Way of Awakening. Thus, from the forty-nine hexagrams up to the eleven thousand five hundred and twenty, they exhaust the principles of the world and fully realize the nature of all things; this is no different from the teaching of our Sage.
On the night the Master entered nirvana, he struck the drum to announce it to the assembly and spoke this verse: "The sky is not high; the earth is not thick.
Thus, people of this age cannot see through it. Just look at the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month: As before, facing south, one gazes at the Northern Dipper."
He passed away peacefully. His body was cremated, and countless five-colored śarīras were obtained; his sacred bones were gathered together to form a stūpa.
He was seventy-seven years of age and fifty years since his ordination.
Chan Master Deyu of Yunding in Huai’an Army (who succeeded Huguoyuan) once asked Huguoyuan: "When it is said, 'Directly grasping the source is what the Buddhas have certified;
picking leaves and seeking branches is not for me,' what then? [Huguoyuan] replied: "Cease climbing the autumn trees for their fruit."
"Stop playing with the solitary moon-disc in the azure pool. Thereupon, the Master immediately resolved his doubts and returned to Yunjing. The assembly requested him to serve as abbot.

The Military Governor of Chengdu invited him to ascend the seat within the yamen. At that time, a military band commander rose from his prostrations and, looking back toward the horse-stand on the steps, said:
"Setting aside for a moment the saying 'sucking dry the waters of the West River in a single gulp,' I request the Master to swallow it instead."
At the horse-stand before the steps, the Master extended both hands and called out, "Wipe it clean and bring it here! The military officer was suddenly enlightened.
Chan Master Huai Gan of Beichen Monastery in Tanzhou (he succeeded Shimen Che): A monk asked, "What is the phrase by which all the sages benefit beings?
He replied, "The red sun illuminates ten thousand households; its light shines forth, yet it has no mind of its own. [The monk] asked, "Whose song does the Master sing?"
[The Master] said: "Shihu (Stone Door) does not dwell on the mind; he penetrates the profound mystery and the subtle essence. A monk asked: "What is the Buddha? [The Master] said:
"One foot is short, one inch is long.
Chan Master Shaoyuan of Shimen in Xiangyang Prefecture (he was a successor of Shimen Che). A monk asked: "When [the opponent] comes from the four directions and eight points..."
"How is it? he asked. [The Master] replied, "A barefooted Persian sniffs at the sky. He asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
[The Master] replied, "A stone ox blocks the ancient road; a wooden horse gallops atop the high tower."
Chan Master Qingfeng Yicheng of Fengxiang Prefecture (heir to Shimen Cheshan). A monk asked, "The non-arising of the three periods of time—of what person is this the realm?
He replied, "White snow joins the snowy peaks; the bright moon blends with the fisherman’s hook. The monk said, "I wonder, is there anything further beyond this?
He replied, "There is. The monk asked, "What is the matter beyond this? He replied, "The numinous light pierces through the lapis lazuli."
Form: When the light of the great earth comes, all traces and spots are severed. Question: "What is the house style of Qingfeng? He said:
"Facing the fire while eating sweet melons.
The Head Seat Yun (who succeeded Shimen Che) was a native of Taiyuan. He had been at Shimen for over thirty years. Within the monastic community...
He admired him. Once, while a monk was requesting tea, [the Master] asked, "What is the one stroke by which the Head Seat acts for others?
The monk said, "I still remember it from earlier. [The Master] said, "How about now? The monk replied, "Please serve some fine tea. One day...
Carrying a hoe, he entered the garden. A monk asked, "Among the three bodies, which one goes to perform manual labor? The Master stood holding the hoe.
The monk said, "Is it not that very one? The Master took the hoe and walked away.
Chan Master Chong of Shimen in Xiangyang Prefecture (heir to Dayang Jian). A monk asked, "Where has Dayang gone after his passing?
He replied, "Riding an ox without wearing a hat; sitting upright without walking crookedly."
Chan Master Hongyin of Shending in Tanzhou (a successor of Shoushan Nian) was of the Hu clan and a native of Xiangshui.

Having traveled to various regions, he spent his time clad in a single robe to weather both cold and heat. Once, while traveling with several senior monks through the region of Xiangmian, there was a monk who was quite erudite and quick-witted in discussing the vehicle of the school.
As they happened to eat at a roadside inn, their discourse continued unabated. The Master said to them, "The three realms..."
"Mind-only. All phenomena are consciousness-only. Consciousness-only is mind-only. "What kind of person speaks these words: 'The eye and sound, the ear and form'?
"It is a verse from the *Dharmākṣi* (Eye of Dharma). "What is its meaning? "Because it is mind-only, the sense organs and their objects do not reach one another.
Because it is consciousness-only, sounds and forms manifest in profusion. "Are the tongue and taste not also organ and object? "Yes. The Master took a chopstick and placed a vegetable on it.
With his mouth agape, he said in a mumble, "What is meant by 'mutual entry'? The entire assembly looked on in astonishment, none able to offer an answer.
The Master said, "The pleasures of the road do not mean one has reached home; to penetrate the subtleties of intellectual understanding is not called seeing the Way.
One must investigate with true investigation; one must awaken with true awakening. King Yama does not fear much talk. The monk bowed and withdrew, later returning.

Changsha [Zhaozhou] was living in seclusion at the Sengsheng Zang (Three Lives Treasury) on Mount Heng. A wealthy and nobleman from Xiangyin came to visit Fuyan Monastery and entered the Master’s quarters.
Seeing that his countenance was serene and tranquil, with only a single alms bowl hanging on the wall and no other possessions, the man was filled with admiration.

He then prostrated himself and requested, saying, "Shending is the place where my family has cultivated merit for a long time, yet it has lacked a true master. I pray that you, Master, will come with me."
"Go. How is it? The Master smiled and consented. He immediately loaded his own horse with the Master, and after ten years, he finally established a monastic community.
A single dilapidated bed served as his Dharma seat; his contentment with austerity was peerless. Furthermore, both his virtue and seniority were preeminent.
Venerated by all quarters like the ancient Zhaozhou, he ascended the hall and said, citing Dongshan: "Greed, anger, and delusion—how utterly ignorant they are!
Fortunately, today I have come to recognize them. When they walk, I strike; when they sit, I beat them. I entrust this to the Prince of Mind to investigate minutely.
For immeasurable kalpas they have remained unliberated; I ask you three, do you know? The Master said, "The ancients..."
Speaking thus, Shending would not have it so. Greed, anger, and ignorance—truly there is no one who knows them. Throughout the twelve hours of the day, let them be as they are:
when walking, they go; when sitting, they follow. Entrusted to the Mind-King, what could one possibly do? Since beginningless kalpas, they have been fundamentally liberated;
why need one further ask whether they are known or not? Ascending the hall, he cited an ancient verse by Longya (one source says Jinfeng): [Verse omitted] *Study.*
“The Way is like drilling for fire. When smoke appears, one must not stop. Only when the golden star manifests does one finally reach home.
The Master said, “Shending does not think so. Studying the Way is like drilling for fire: when smoke appears, one should stop immediately.

Do not wait for the golden star to manifest, lest you burn your feet and then your head. “Now tell me,” he continued, “when Shending speaks in this way, does he go against the ancients, or does he follow them?”
The ancients had their own way of doing things. You say that the person who goes away like that is good, or the person who comes back like that is good.
To reach this point, you must possess the eye of a patch-robed monk; do not let yourself be deceived by others. Be careful. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Let us set aside for now the fact that the wind does not whistle through the branches and the rain does not break the clods of earth. How would you strike a cartwheel somersault?"
[The Master] said, "Go to Mahābrahmā. If he is there, come out and perform a feat; is there anyone who can? Do not let Śakra become enraged.
Later, a monk entered the room and said, "At that time, I would have come out, turned once to the left, and returned to the assembly.
The Master said, "If you do not let Śakra become enraged, what then? The monk replied, "Those who recognize kindness are few; those who betray it are many."

[The Master] said, "It strikes right at the nostrils. A monk asked, "How is it before the fish-drum has been struck? He replied, "Look at the sky; look at the earth. The monk asked, "And after it has been struck?
He replied, "Holding the alms bowl, he ascends the hall. A monk asked, "As for those who transmigrate through the six realms, what is their ultimate state?
He replied, "They do not wish to become Buddhas. The monk asked, "Why do they not wish to become Buddhas? He replied, "Even the Buddha does not investigate them."
[The Master] finished speaking and said, “I ask for a word from the Master. [The Master] said, “Yesterday I still remembered; today there is no gate to the talk. A question was asked:
“What is it like when one is on a single horse with a lone spear? He said, “Shending strikes the drum of retreat. [The Master] said, “Ultimately, what is the matter?
He said, “I suspect you do not have such hands and feet. A question was asked: “When one brushes away the dust to see the Buddha, what then? He said, “The Buddha is also dust.”
Question: "What is the house style of the Master? He said: "When hungry, one does not choose among foods. Question: "If one kills father and mother, one repents before the Buddha.
But if one kills the Buddha and the Patriarchs, where does one repent? He said: "As the water rises, the boat rises higher. Question:
"The seven pure flowers are spread to bathe this stainless person. Since he is already a stainless person, why is he bathed? He said: "Purity."
Even purity is not established.
Regarding Zen Master Chongmi of Jianmen Ciyun (who succeeded Shoushan Nian), a monk asked: "What is the master’s house style?"
The Master held up his whisk. The monk asked, "What is it ultimately like? He replied, "Brewing tea and boiling water.

The monk said, "We share many fine days together. He replied, "Stop this endless prattling. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? He replied, "The red sun shines upon ten thousand households;
green waters wind around the blue mountains."
Chan Master Ruixin of Mount Jinshan in Zhenjiang Prefecture (a successor of Fuchang Shan), later resided at Tiansheng. He ascended the hall and said:
"Deshan’s single blow—what kind of hero is that? Jinshan values only his ability to steal the Chu banner and strike the Chu camp.
Linji’s single shout—what kind of ruffian is that? Jinshan values only his seizing the bandit’s sword to kill the bandit."
All the other old masters throughout the world are merely those who break through walls and tear down partitions in the marketplace;
as soon as they raise their hands, they reveal their flaws. Not even one among them has yet displayed the skillful means of a thief stealing a white fox-fur robe.

When Jinshan makes such a judgment, everyone in the various quarters hears it and does not fail to pucker their lips and flare their beaks. Why is this? It is because right now, it is Jueyuanhan [who speaks].
The spring breeze blows gently; upon the Bodhi tree, flowers cluster thickly. Who would have known that Kāśyapa possessed such a lineage style?
He took all things profound and subtle as his very eyes. Consequently, here at Mount Jinshan, the land is vast and the people are few;

those who meet him are rare. Yet, once a nature has been habituated, it is difficult to reform. Mount Jinshan would sooner freeze to death or starve to death than ever consent to don [the robes of the common].

He wears the stinking shirt of a falconer. Those whom he takes as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) have the golden chains split by him for the sick monkey, and the jewel in the garment crushed for the intoxicated guest;
yet they still cannot avoid dwelling in the shallows or nesting among the reeds.

One must not speak of mind or nature, nor speak of the profound or the subtle, within the society of tangled vines. Mount Jinshan will never indulge in idle leisure; when a single word accords with the Way, one dies.
He immediately ceased. The Great Peng spreads its wings, covering the Ten Continents; yet the things by the hedge fence chirp and squawk.
Entering the hall for instruction: That which the world prizes—the Beryl of He Shi and the Pearl of Lord Hou of Sui—Tiansheng calls donkey dung and horse manure.
That which is most esteemed in the supramundane realm—true suchness, liberation, bodhi, and nirvana—the celestial sage calls "the clanging of a hot bowl.
Now tell me, where does such talk land? It is not that the mind of grasping and rejecting is heavy.
To believe in heterodox and inverted views—do you all understand? A fierce tiger does not look back at the flesh upon its back;

how could a great furnace cast a needle already contained within its pouch? A monk asked: "I have a great affliction because I have this body. Before my parents were born, I do not know where this body was.
The Master said: "Throughout vast kalpas, it has had no location. If one discusses birth and extinction, they are both exhausted."

"No. "Then," [the questioner] said, "is it that the mind pervades the ten directions yet is not present in any single place? He replied, "Shaking a stake in the mud. Chan Master Shanxian Shixian (d.u.
of Kaishan on Mount Lu (a successor of Deshan Yuan) was a native of Linjiang. He traveled extensively among the seats of various masters, making enlightenment his sole ambition.
While he was staying with Deshan, one day he encountered the Master ascending the hall. Deshan looked out at the assembly and said, "A lion stretches its limbs."
The Elephant King looked back; Master [Xuedou] was suddenly awakened to the truth. He entered the room and related what he had seen. Xuefeng asked, "How do you ultimately understand this?

The Master looked back and said, "The donkey in the back garden is eating grass. Xuefeng approved. Later, when he arrived at Xuedou, Xuedou engaged him in dialogue with such sharp precision that he rejoiced in his transcendent mastery.
He bestowed upon him the title "The Monk Xian Who Roams Across the Sea" and subsequently appointed him to share the teaching seat.
The eminent monks from all directions revered him. One day, when he was appointed to head a monastery, the Master wrote two verses on the wall during the night and departed.
The verses read: "It is not that I lack the intent to continue the ancestral lamp; I am ashamed that my Way has not yet equaled that of Neng of Lingnan.
At the third watch, beneath the moon, I leave Xuedou; With lingering affection, I gaze silently upon the green peaks. For over twenty years, I have wandered through the four seas."
