Compiled by the Monk (Subject) Zhengshou of Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Temple in Pingjiang Prefecture.
The Eleventh Generation of Nanyue (the Seventh Generation of Linji).
Chan Master Huanglong Pujue Hainan of Longxing Prefecture was a dharma heir of Chan Master Nanyuan Ciming Chuyuan.
His secular surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Yushan. From childhood, he was profound and serious;
at the age of eleven, he left home and served Master Zhilan of Dingshui as his teacher. Once, while attending Zhilan on a journey, he saw...

Whenever he visited shrines and temples, he would go there wielding his staff to strike them. At nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination. He traveled far to Mount Lu, where he relied upon and returned to Zongbao of Qixian;
he stayed there for more than three autumns. Crossing the Huai River, he went to pay respects to Cheng of Sanjiao. After a long time, he was invited to share the teaching seat.
Master Yunfeng Yue urged him to proceed to Shishuang, but on the way, hearing that Shishuang did not attend to formal affairs, he instead stayed at Foyan.
At that time, Master Xian was appointed as the Director of Records (Di Jishi). When Xian passed away, Ciming succeeded him in the abbacy. The Master went out to welcome him and was struck with awe.

Upon hearing his preaching of the Dharma, he found that [Ciming] had stripped away all the various interpretations of other quarters as being heterodox—interpretations which were precisely those the Master himself had previously realized through his own extensive travels and study.
Thereupon, the Master turned over in realization and said: "How can a great man harbor doubts within the very core of his own heart?"

Ai went to his residence to request the transmission of the Dharma. Ming invited him to sit; the Master firmly declined with earnest sincerity. Ming said, "You have studied with Yunmen as a secretary;
you must surely be well-versed in his essential meaning. As for the three blows of the staff at Dongshan—were they deserved or not? Yun said: [He was deserving].
[Changqing] said, "You may eat together with him. [Xuefeng] said, "I initially suspected that your master was not up to the task; now, however, you may pay him homage.
He added, "Setting aside Dongshan’s three blows of the staff for a moment, where exactly did Zhaozhou see through the old woman? As Xuefeng was about to respond, Changqing struck his mouth.
Xuefeng attained great enlightenment and composed a verse to present to him. He remained for over a month before taking his leave; at that time, he was thirty-five years old.
He first resided at Tong’an, and subsequently served at Guizong, Huangbo, and Huanglong.

There were seventy-nine people who attained the Great Dharma under him, yet most of those he received were at Jicui Hermitage. Monks flocked to his reputation and vied with one another to exhaust themselves in the pursuit of the Way.
On the day he first accepted his invitation, Sanjiao sent a monk to examine the Master’s proclamations; among them was the statement: "Wisdom..."

The ocean has no inherent nature. By awakening to delusion, one becomes an ordinary person; by realizing that delusion is fundamentally empty, one perceives the Buddha within the very mind of an ordinary person.
Then, simply let it rest. One might think that Tongan had no resolution, yet he followed whatever you desired, even in your confusion: "Seven for the Southern Dipper, eight for the Northern Dipper.
When the monk returned and related this to Cheng, Cheng was displeased. Shortly thereafter, he heard that [Tongan] had opened the hall and become a successor to Ciming. Cheng then made a vow.
Consequently, more than half of the members of the Sangha of Sanjiao abandoned him and departed. He ascended the hall; after the questions and answers were finished, he said:
"Before I ascended this seat, there was not a single thing at all. As soon as I ascended this seat, there have been so many questions and answers.
I dare ask the assembly: Is even a single question and a single answer truly the Dharma of our School? If you say it is, then [the entire] Tripitaka..."
How could the teachings lack questions and answers? Why then do you say that the Way is transmitted outside the teachings and handed down only to those of superior faculties?

If you say this is incorrect, then what was the purpose of all those many questions and answers just now? You who travel as pilgrims should open your own eyes; do not allow yourselves to regret it later.
As for this matter, it is not something that can be reached through supernatural powers or cultivation and realization, nor is it something attained by extensive learning or wisdom.
Discourse: The Buddhas of the three periods have said nothing more than that one must know for oneself; even the entire Great Canon of teachings cannot fully explain or annotate this.
Therefore, among the hundreds of thousands of myriads of followers on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, only Kāśyapa was granted the privilege of hearing it directly.

When the seven hundred eminent monks at Huangmei were entrusted with the robe and bowl, it was not because you—given over to greed, lust, folly, and attachment, and preoccupied with victory and defeat—were capable of such things. Truly, those who have left the household life must...
One must possess the resolute will of a man of integrity, severing both ends to return home and sit securely.
Only then may one open wide the gates of the house, bring forth the family’s own wealth, receive those who come and go, and provide relief to the orphaned and destitute;

only then can there be even a small measure of repayment for the Buddha’s profound kindness. Were it otherwise, such a thing would be impossible. With his whisk, he struck the meditation seat once, and then—
[He] offered thanks (as detailed). He ascended the hall and spoke of the wondrous and discussed the profound; these are the treacherous thieves of a great peace.
To administer blows and shouts is the way of heroes in a chaotic age. Heroes, treacherous thieves, blows, shouts, the profound, and the wondrous—all are but superfluous things.
Under Huangbo’s gate, none of these are of any use at all. But tell me, what does Huangbo’s gate usually employ? [He] shouted.
A shout. Ascending the hall, he said: "Where people dwell, I do not dwell; where people walk, I do not walk.
Regarding this principle that is thus clear and bright, you must understand it as being to cast one's entire body into a fire pit. He drew a line with his whisk and said:
Foul smoke billows and swirls; red flames blaze intensely. Those whose eyes are not yet clear are all within this place.
Since antiquity, no sage has failed to enter the pit of birth and death, drawing sentient beings out from within the fire of ignorance.
How, then, do you all enter? If one can enter, it may be said that they are not burned by fire and not drowned by water. If one enters...
"It is not permitted. Not only can you not benefit yourself, but you also cannot benefit others.

Since you can neither benefit yourself nor others, there is no benefit at all in this shaven head and square-cut robe. After a long silence, he summoned the assembly. When the assembly raised their heads, the Master said:
"The ox-head goes out; the horse-head returns. He ascended the hall. After the assembly had gathered for some time, the Master said: "The fine fish dwells in the deep; it is hidden."

The bird perched for a long time and then descended from its seat. He ascended the hall; the bell was struck and rang out, the drum was beaten and resounded, and the assembly respectfully offered their greetings.
Tong’an remained composed with palms joined. "Which of these is worldly dharma? Which is Buddha-dharma?"

"Ha! [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "There is one person who studies the *Avataṃsaka* in the morning and contemplates the *Prajñāpāramitā* in the evening, diligent day and night without a moment's lapse.
There is another person who does not engage in Chan meditation nor discuss doctrine, but simply drags along a tattered mat and sleeps in the sun.
When these two people arrive together at Huanglong—one with effort and one without effort—which one will you settle?"
[He] was silent for a long while, then said: "The Goddess of Merit and the Lady of Darkness—no wise host accepts either.
He ascended the hall and said: "The mind-king does not move falsely; the six realms are simultaneously penetrated. I have laid aside the three-foot sword; I shall no longer handle the single bow.
He struck the meditation seat and descended from the hall. Ascending the hall again, he said: "The World-Honored One, the Great Awakened One, said: 'I now protect you...'"
"Entrust this matter to you; it shall never be in vain. You all should apply yourselves with diligent vigor and practice this samādhi.
The Master said, "As for diligent vigor, everyone here certainly possesses it. But what is this samādhi? He then said, "Kāśyapa’s rag-robe is worth hundreds of thousands of millions;
the jewel from the crest of a Wheel-Turning King is not worth half a penny. With a single strike of his whisk, he descended.
[The Master] was seated. A monk asked, "One does not go; two do not stay. Please, Master, speak. He said, "Before the Hall of the High Ancestor, Fan Kuai was enraged.
[The monk] said, "In that case, today I have met the Master. He said, "Looking up at the sky, one does not see the sky."
Question: "Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout have remained until this day with few people able to take them up. I ask the Master to take them up. The Master said:
"A crossbow of a thousand *jin* does not discharge its trigger for the sake of a field mouse. The monk said: "To act as a master of the lineage—there is one today!

The Master then shouted. The monk bowed. The Master said: "Monks from the Five Lakes, practitioners with their single staff—before you have even arrived, you are already the same [as those who have]."

"Peaceful. Do not let it remain as a matter of doubt. Question: "The old year has passed and the new year has arrived. Without falling into either of these two paths, I beg the Master for instruction.
He said: "In the east, Jia and Yi are wood. Question: "What is the realm of Huanglong?
He said: "I only arrived here yesterday; I have not yet looked at it in detail. Question: "Who is the person within the realm? He said: "The tall are tall; the short are short."
[The Master’s] words were brief. While the Master was sitting in meditation, a monk stood in attendance.

The Master gazed at him for a long time and said, "I shall explain to you in a single phrase the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and the immeasurable wondrous gates. Do you believe me? The monk replied, "I believe the Honored One’s sincere words."
"How would I dare not believe you? The Master pointed to his left and said, "Come over this way.

As the monk was about to move, the Master shouted, "Chasing after sounds and pursuing forms—what end will there ever be? Get out! Another monk heard this; as the Master approached him, he repeated the previous words and questioned him.
The monk also said, "How would I dare not believe you? The Master again pointed to his left and said, "Come over this way. The monk remained firm.
As he stood there, Linji did not approach him. The Master shouted, "You have come to draw near me, yet you refuse to listen to my words! Get out!
In the room, Linji raised his hand and asked the monks, "How does my hand compare to the Buddha’s hand? He then lowered his foot and said, "How does my foot compare to a donkey’s foot?"
"Every person has their place of birth. Where is the Elder’s place of birth? No student was able to grasp its meaning.
The monastic communities came to call this the "Three Barriers of Huanglong. Whenever someone offered a response, the Master never accepted or rejected it;

no one could fathom his intention. When asked the reason for this, the Master said: "One who has already passed through the barrier walks straight on with arms swinging; how would they know there is a barrier?"
The customs official questioned his attendants as to whether he might pass through; this was because he had not yet penetrated the barrier.
On the sixteenth day of the third month in the second year of the Xining era, he ascended the hall to take leave of the assembly and spoke a verse (the words of which appear in the *Xu deng lu*).

On the seventeenth day, after having provided meals for the two special envoys from the Fourth Patriarch’s monastery, Huiri, he sat cross-legged before his quarters. The great assembly gathered around him in a circle, and after a long while, he passed away. Seven days later, his body was cremated.
He obtained five-colored śarīra relics, which were enshrined on a ridge before the Thousand Mountains. He lived for sixty-eight years and sat in meditation for fifty summer retreats.
In the spring of the fourth year of the Daguan era, he was posthumously granted the title Pujue (Universal Enlightenment).

Chan Master Yangqi Fanghui of Yuanzhou was a native of Yichun in the commandery. (The *Xu deng lu* states he was from Hengyang, not [Yichun]). His clan name was Leng. From his youth, he was alert and quick-witted.

Upon reaching adulthood, he did not concern himself with writing or study. He served as a tax collector for the government, achieving the highest records in revenue collection. However, being dismissed for dereliction of duty, he fled by night to Mount Jiufeng.

There, he felt as if he were visiting a familiar place; filled with affection, he could not bear to leave and subsequently shaved his head. (The *Xu deng lu* states he relied upon Chan Master Jinqiu of Jiufeng, or alternatively, [relied upon] Daowu.)
Whenever the Master read the sutras, his mind would merge with them and his spirit attain realization. He was able to humble himself to seek instruction from veteran masters.

When Ciming moved from Nanyuan to Daowu and then to Shishuang, the Master served as his assistant, overseeing all affairs of the monastery. Although he relied upon him for a long time, he had not yet attained awakening.
Whenever he went to consult him, Ciming would say, "The administrative affairs of the storehouse are too numerous; go now. On another day, when the Master asked again, Ciming spoke as before.
Someone said to him, "In time, the descendants of the Abbot will spread throughout the world; why be so anxious?
There was an old woman living near the monastery whom no one could fathom—she was known as Cimingpo. Whenever there was an opportunity, Ming would surely go to her place.
One day, it began to rain, and knowing that Ming was about to visit, the Master (Zhaozhou) scouted for him on a narrow path. Upon seeing him, he grabbed him and said:
"This old fellow must speak with me today; if he does not, I shall beat you. The next day, Mingzhe said, "Abbot, if you know such matters, then let it be.
Before he had finished speaking, the Master attained great enlightenment. He immediately prostrated himself in the mud before him, then rose and asked, "What is it like when we meet on a narrow path?
Mingzhe said, "You should step aside for now; I have somewhere I must go. The Master then returned.
One day, [Zhaozhou] prepared his formal robes and visited the Abbot’s quarters to offer thanks. Baizhang Ming rebuked him, saying, "Not yet. You must attend the formal inquiry session tomorrow.
After the morning gruel was finished, a long time passed without the sound of the drum being struck. The Master asked the attendant, "Today is the day for the formal inquiry;

why has the drum not been beaten? The attendant replied, "The Abbot has gone out and has not yet returned. The Master went straight to the kitchen. Seeing Ming tending the fire and the nun boiling the gruel, the Master said, "Abbot..."

"Today we are to attend the assembly. The great multitude has been waiting for a long time; why have you not returned? Ming said, "If you can utter a turning word, you may return at once. If you cannot, let us go our separate ways.
The Master covered his head with his straw raincoat and walked several paces. Ming was greatly pleased and subsequently returned with him.
From that time on, whenever Ming went out for a walk in the mountains, the Master would invariably wait for him to emerge; even if it was late, he would certainly do so.
The drum was beaten to assemble the community, and Ming hurried back, saying angrily, "It is late in the day for a forest monastery to take the seat;
where did you get such a rule? The Master said, "This is the evening *san* (private instruction) of Fenyang. Why do you say it is not a rule?

Today, the reason why practitioners still attend the *san* after the recitation on the eighth and thirteenth days is rooted in this. On another day, when Ming ascended the hall, the Master came forward and asked:
The hidden birds warble in soft tones. Leaving the clouds, they enter the peaks in confusion. At that time, how was it? [The guest] said: "I walk amidst the wild weeds;
you, again, have entered a deep village. [The guest] said: "An official does not permit even a needle; may I ask one more question? Ming then shouted. The Master said: "A fine shout!"
Ming shouted again; the Master also shouted. Ming shouted twice in succession, and the Master prostrated. Ming said, "This matter can only be shouldered by one who is a true person.
The Master shook his sleeves and departed. When Ming moved to Xinghua, the Master took his leave to return to Jiufeng, where he lived in obscurity among the granaries.

However, the clergy and laity of Pingbin welcomed him to reside at Yangqi, after which he successively moved to Yun’gai (the words of his acceptance of these invitations are found in the *Xu deng lu*).
Ascending the hall, he said: "Mist shrouds the vast sky; wind rises across the great fields. The hundred grasses and withered trees let out the lion’s roar, expounding the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time turn the Great Dharma Wheel beneath the feet of you all.
If you can understand this, your efforts will not have been in vain. If you cannot understand it, do not say that the terrain of Yangqi Mountain is treacherous."
Beyond this, there is yet a supreme peak. Entering the hall: The scenery has just cleared; all things are at ease and flourishing.
In every step, there is a thousand-fold Maitreya; in every movement and function, there is a Śākyamuni everywhere. Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are both right here.
In the assembly, there was one who would not tolerate being mocked, who said: "Yangqi buys flour mixed with bran. Although this is so, it is like putting an awl in a cloth bag.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The phrase exists; the phrase does not exist. Like a vine leaning against a tree. Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti—letting go, they return home.
Yangqi speaking thus is merely looking at a rusted iron lock. There is yet another subsequent statement, which is not [to be found here].
[The Master] gave a discourse on an error. He ascended the hall and said: "This very mind, mind, mind is Buddha; it is the most wondrous thing in the worlds of the ten directions.
Śākyamuni the Old Man spoke a dream; the Buddhas of the three periods speak dreams. Now I ask you all: have you ever dreamed?
If you have dreamed, bring forth a single phrase from the midst of the dead of night. After a long silence, he said: "Though humans may..."
There is a true message. Steal a glance at Yangqi’s dream-telling. *Chan.* Ascending the hall: "Living at Yangqi with meager merit, my strength has declined over the years.
The cold wind withers the fallen leaves; yet I still rejoice that an old friend has returned.
*Lālala!* Taking up this head of dead firewood, let us for now go where there is no smoke or flame. Ascending the hall: "When the Old Śākyamuni was first born, he took seven steps."
After taking seven steps, he looked around in the four directions, pointing one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth.
Nowadays, all Zen monks merely imitate these gestures, saying, "In heaven above and on earth below, I alone am honored. Yun-gai cannot bear to spare his life [in commenting on this].
He also provided a model for all people, saying: "When the Yang energy arises, there is no solid ground. In the evening *can*, he addressed the assembly:
"The wisdom of all things penetrates without obstruction. He raised his staff and said, "I am displaying my spiritual powers right before you all.
He then threw it down and asked, "Do you understand? It is enough to cause heaven and earth to shatter and the mountains and peaks to tremble."

[Yangqi] did not see the Way. [When asked about] the purity of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), he struck his meditation seat and said, "Thirty years from now, do not say that Yangqi has the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake.
A monk asked, "When one parts through the clouds to see the sun, what then? He replied, "Those who come from the east sit in the east.
The monk asked, "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral style does your lineage follow? He replied, "Beating the drum across the river."
[The Master] did not respond to the sound. [The monk] said, "A son of Xinghua, a direct grandson of Linji. [The Master] said, "Today, because of the communal celebration, I ask:
What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? [The Master] said, "The eaves do not fail to carry the books. [The monk] asked, "What was the intent behind the wall-gazing at Shaolin?

[The Master] said, "The man from the Western Heaven does not understand the language of Tang. [The monk] asked, "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear. [The Master] said, "The man from the Western Heaven does not understand the language of Tang."
"The earth attains tranquility by obtaining the One. A patch-robed monk obtains the One—what can he do with it? [The Master] said, "The mouth of the alms bowl points toward the sky.
In his room, he asked a monk: "How will you swallow the thorny chestnut? How will you leap over the diamond circle?"
One day, three [monks] arrived briefly to pay their respects. The Master asked, "When three people travel together, there must be one who possesses wisdom.
He then held up his sitting mat (*zuoju*) and said, "Head monk, what do you call this? The monk replied, "A sitting mat. The Master said, "Is it truly so? The monk replied, "Yes."
The Master said, "What do you call this? He replied, "A sitting mat. The Master looked around at those present and said, "The head of the assembly indeed has eyes.
He then questioned the second monk: "If one wishes to travel a thousand li, the first step is the beginning. What is that very first phrase?
He replied, "When I come before you, Master, how would I dare to reach out my hand? The Master made a sweeping gesture with his hand. The monk said, "Finished."
The Master extended both hands. The monk hesitated. The Master said, "Understood. He asked the third monk, "Where have you recently come from? [The monk] replied, "Nanyuan.
[The Master] said, "Today Yangqi has been exposed by you, Senior Monk. Sit and drink tea. He asked another monk, "The clouds are deep and the path is remote;
from where have you come on such a grand carriage? [The monk] replied, "The sky has no four walls. [The Master] said, "How many straw sandals have you worn out? The monk then—
"Ho! The Master said, "After one shout and two shouts, what then? The monk replied, "Look at this old monk, he is in a hurry.
The Master said, "The staff is not here; sit and drink tea for now. He asked another monk, "Amidst the piled-up clouds of withered leaves, where did you depart this morning? The monk replied, "..."
Guanyin said, "Regarding the one phrase beneath Guanyin’s heels, how do you speak it? The monk replied, "We have already met just now.
Guanyin said, "How is it that you have met? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Let the second seat act as the head of the assembly and speak for him.
He too was speechless. Guanyin said, "Both of you have failed each other. At the memorial service for the anniversary of Ciming’s death, the assembly... [text ends]

The assembly gathered. The Master went before the True Image, clenched both hands into fists and placed them upon his head; with his sitting mat, he drew a line and struck a circle, then burned incense.
Stepping back three paces, he performed a woman’s bow. The Head Seat said, "Stop making such a fuss. The Master asked, "How about you, Head Seat?
He replied, "Preceptor, stop making such a fuss. The Master said, "A rabbit eating cow’s milk—this is the second [instance]."
The Master approached the seat. He drew a circle in the air, then burned incense. Stepping back three paces, he performed a woman’s bow.
The Master stepped forward and made a gesture as if listening. As the Seat-Holder hesitated, the Master struck him with his palm and said, "This lacquer bucket is acting recklessly!"

Chan Master Xinghua Zi (Zi was a successor of Shending Yin) passed away. When a monk arrived, he left behind a written testament. The Master asked, "When the World-Honored One entered nirvana, he revealed a single foot from within his coffin.
Now that you, Reverend, have returned to the truth, what sign do you leave behind? The monk was speechless. The Master struck his chest once and cried out, "Heaven! Heaven!
He passed into stillness in the first year of the Huangyou era (1049). His life span was fifty-eight years. (His specific deeds are not detailed.)
Chan Master Daoning Daoquan of Longxing Prefecture ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he said:

"The life-force of the Buddhas of the past and the administrative framework of the Buddhas of the future are both contained right here. Now it is put to use: becoming clouds and rain, becoming auspicious omens and blessings;
benefiting humans and gods, and traversing birth and death. In other worlds, it appears and disappears, rolls up and unfurls. If you can penetrate this..."

The entire body is the mouth; words cannot exhaust its expression. The entire body is the eye; illumination cannot reach its limit. When a single thought accords with reality, a single instant is ten thousand kalpas. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The matter that has come down from of old is not obtained from the Buddha, nor is it sought from the Patriarchs.

The nature of a man of integrity is inherently natural from the beginning. His movements and stillness accord with propriety; his coming and going are free from attachment. He is like a fish in water, acting according to his own nature."
Floating and sinking, like a bird flying through the sky, both are without obstruction. Regarding such talk, who is the one who knows? After a long silence, he said:
"The single breath speaks not, yet it contains all forms; where do the myriad spirits go to express their gratitude for its impartiality? A monk asked:

"Since it is the One True Dharma-realm, why are there nevertheless thousands of differences and ten thousand distinctions? He replied: "The roots are deep, so the leaves flourish. [The monk] said: "Not yet."
[The Master] examined him closely and asked, "Can you still produce this? He replied, "To strive for cleverness is to become clumsy. A question was asked:

"In the teachings, 'acting,' 'stopping,' 'relying,' and 'extinguishing' are called the four illnesses. How should those of later generations direct their practice? He replied, "When a skilled craftsman wields his axe, he cuts the wood without using a measuring line.
A question was asked: "When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, why did the temple steward’s eyebrows and beard fall off? He replied, "A thief."
"He does not strike at the poor man's house. A monk asked, "When the Venerable Kāśyapa saw the World-Honored One holding up the flower, why did he smile?
The Master said, "He could not restrain his impatience for excellence. A monk entered the Master’s quarters and asked, "What is the white ox on the open ground?
The Master stuck a pair of fire tongs into the brazier and asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Its head is not lacking; its tail—"
"Not a single one remains. When the Master was at Tong’an, a monk once asked: "Since it is Tong’an, why is there still a sick monk passing away?
He replied: "Giving alms is not as good as paying back one's debts."

Chan Master Cuiyan Zhenke of Longxing Prefecture (whose native village is unknown) prided himself on having traveled extensively to study under various masters; the monastic community called him "Zhen the Open-hearted.
Later, he arrived at the presence of Ciming. Upon seeing him, Ciming asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?

Zhen replied, "Cloudless peaks arise above; the moon descends into the heart of the waves. Ciming rebuked him, saying, "With hair white as snow and teeth yellowed by age, you still harbor such a notion!"
[Zhaozhou] saw Mingjue and was struck with awe, seeking his instruction. Mingjue said, "Ask me. Zhaozhou repeated his previous words and questioned him.
Mingjue shouted, "No clouds arise upon the mountain peaks; the moon descends into the heart of the waves! At these words, the Great Dharma was suddenly clarified within him.
He resided at Cuoyan, which at that time was regarded as the foremost Dharma cave in all under heaven. Entering the hall, he said: "Not seeing a single dharma..."
A great calamity! The mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the sun, moon, and stars; form, emptiness, light, and darkness—none of these are a single dharma.
Raising his staff, he said: "When an ordinary person sees this staff, they call it a staff.

When a Śrāvaka sees this staff, they recognize it as inert emptiness and dismiss the staff as non-existent. When a Bodhisattva sees this staff, how has it ever hung from their teeth? When hunger comes..."
When hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps; when cold, one turns toward the fire; when hot, one seeks coolness. Has it not been said:
"The wisdom of all wisdom is pure"? To speak in such a manner is to laugh until the nostrils of the local deity burst. Ascending the hall, he said: "To feel for emptiness, there are no tracks."
The echoes have faded and can no longer be heard; Śākyamuni and Dharmatrāta have been banished to other realms, while Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra have been relegated to the status of minor messengers.
Where, then, do you all establish yourselves and find your livelihood? Therefore it is said: there is the provisional and there is the real;
there is the luminous and there is the dark; there is the illuminating and there is the functional; there is the guest and there is the host. Let go...
He stepped over one [step]. Why did he not speak? He then gave a shout and struck his staff once, then descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he raised an example: A monk asked Baling, "What is the Way? Baling said, "A person with clear eyes falls into a well.
Again, he asked Baoying, "What is the Way? Baoying said, "Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion. Again, he asked Shoushan, "What is..."
Regarding the Way, Shoushan said: "The mud beneath one's feet is three feet deep. These are the three turning words: one phrase stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high;
one phrase is a boat traveling on dry land; one phrase is the mutual penetration of host and guest. Is there anyone among you who can discern them?

"Come forward and speak! If you have nothing to say, then practice the compassion of an Arhat, for it shatters the thieves of the fetters; practice the compassion of a Bodhisattva, for it brings peace to sentient beings;
practice the compassion of a Tathāgata, for it realizes the mark of suchness. He ascended the hall and said: "Sound does not mingle with sound;
form does not mingle with form. Why is this? The sound of a bell contains no resonance of a drum; the sound of a drum contains no resonance of a bell. He raised his staff and said: "This..."
Is this not form? Where is sound? Sound does not reach the ear; how can form come to the eye?
Eye, form, ear, and sound—all phenomena are naturally distinguished. Last night, the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta discussed their respective merits.
Upon arriving at Cuoyan’s place, he immediately delivered a judgment for him; thirty years later, [the master] acted in accordance with it.
He ascended the hall and cited Longya’s verse, which says: "Studying the Way is like drilling wood for fire: when smoke appears, one must not yet stop; one must wait until the golden star manifests."
"Returning home, one finally reaches the destination. Shending said, "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire: when you encounter smoke, you should stop at once.
Do not wait for the appearance of the star; it might burn your feet and then your head. The Master said, "If we speak of the Sudden, Longya is still only halfway there."
If we discuss gradualism, even the Divine Cauldron still has a slight awakening remaining. Regarding this, how would you proceed? O worthy ones, this year there are many fallen leaves;
at how many places will they be swept back home? Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Above, it is not in heaven; below, it is not on earth."
"It is not within, nor does it abide in people. He raised his staff and said, "Right now, it is acting as the Bodhisattva Anantagātra in the hands of Cuoyan.
Do you all see it? If you see it, you truly do not see the Tathāgata’s crown-mark.
If you do not see it, today we shall go on rounds to pay our respects in the various quarters. A monk asked, "What is the phrase for a student's exertion? He replied, "A thousand days."
[He said,] "The firewood is cut once and burned for a day. [The monk asked,] "What is the point of intimacy for a student? [He replied,] "The whole family boards the boat at the river crossing.
[The monk] asked, "What is the Way? [He replied,] "As soon as you step out the door, you see it. [The monk asked,] "What is one who is on the Way?"

[The Master] said: "Carrying a cangue and confessing one's crimes. [The student] asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? [The Master] said: "Deep plowing and shallow sowing. [The student] asked:
"What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? [The Master] said: "The five supernormal powers of the worthy sages. [The student] said: "I do not understand. [The Master] said: [Silence].
His tongue reached up to the Brahma Heaven. Question: "What is the place where a student turns over their body? He replied: "One wall; a hundred walls are harmonized. In the hall, he asked the monks:
"When Lu Zu saw a monk coming to pay his respects on that day, for what reason did he simply face the wall?

The assembly offered various responses, but none were in accord with the truth. The Master then composed a verse, saying: "Severing the ten thousand mountains and myriad peaks, I urge people to cast away right and wrong."
Difficult. There has been no news from Chiyang for some time. Indeed, Zhongdang did not witness it with his own eyes (the remaining words are found in the *Xùdēng*).

In the first year of the Zhìpíng era, as the Master was about to enter extinction, he manifested illness that was exceedingly arduous. He spread straw mats upon the ground and rolled about, finding no rest.

Attendant Zhe wept and said, "Throughout your life you reviled the Buddhas and scolded the Patriarchs; why now are you acting like this? The Master gazed at him intently and rebuked him, saying, "Do you also hold such a view?
He then rose and sat in the full lotus posture, calling for the attendant to burn incense. As the smoke rose, he passed away.
He then entered nirvana.
Zen Master Dao Wu Zhen of Tanzhou ascended the hall and said: "If the scales and weights are broken, by what means will you determine weight?
If the bowl, spoon, and chopsticks are cast aside, with what will you eat your porridge and rice? It would be better to go toward a village of three households."
Divining east, divining west; suddenly he struck it and pulled out his nostrils. Ascending the hall, [he said]: "The lion cub roars; the dragon-horse colt leaps.
The mirror of the ancient Buddha is bright; the solitary moon over the three peaks is clear. He then performed a dance and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, [he said]:
"If one relies on the Patriarchal Command, everyone here must be utterly bewildered. Grant this old monk a single thread of leniency."
Furthermore, look east and west within the eyebrows. Ascending the hall: Puhua’s strikes—both manifest and hidden;布袋 (Pudai) scattering [the bag] horizontally and vertically;
the Stone Chamber Attendant treading the pestle—why has he forgotten to set foot down? Ascending the hall: The sun and moon of ancient and today;
the mountains and rivers remain as they were. If you can understand this, then the *Bhagavāns* of the ten directions are on one path to *nirvāṇa*.

Section. If one does not understand this clearly, one slanders this sutra; for such reasons, the retribution incurred is as described above. Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case:
Dongshan said, “On the summit of Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; before the steps of the Buddha Hall, it is a ‘dog-urine sky’; atop the head of the pagoda pole, a *jizizi* is being fried;
three monkeys toss coins at night. The Old Monk says it is not so: “The three-faced *lilu* treads upon the moon.”
Two white oxen with smoke in their mouths; a crowned green hare standing on a courtyard cypress; a shell-shedding turtle flying up into the sky.
Old Master Dongshan’s entanglements have all been seen through by you all.
Although he was truly extraordinary, even so, he could only manage three or four steps, and did not go beyond seven or eight leaps.
Furthermore, tell me: where does the error lie? Today, this old monk will not spare his eyebrows; he shall give it all away at once. After a long silence, he said:
"Caution and entreaty damage one's virtue; silence truly possesses merit. Let the blue seas change as they may, I shall never explain it for you. A monk asked:
"When one understands immediately upon encountering stillness, what then? He replied: "A mouse carries a grindstone on its tail."
The Mallet. Question: What is the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*)? He said: "When the yakṣa bends his knee, his eyes are black.
Question: What is the function of True Suchness? He said: "The vajra strikes and the iron mountain crumbles. Question: What is constant illumination? He said: [The Mallet.]
"Mount Sumeru upon the point of a needle. [The monk] asked, "What is 'tranquil illumination'? He replied, "The seawater within the eyebrows. [The monk] asked, "What is 'original illumination'?
He replied, "Treading and leaping within the straw sandals. The monk withdrew. The Master said, "Tranquil illumination is constant illumination; original illumination is constant illumination.
Beneath the straw sandals, one is constantly treading and leaping. Furthermore, understand that Mount Sumeru is upon the point of a needle, and the water is always within the eyebrows."
Miaomiao. Chan Master Weizheng of Jingde Monastery in Longxing Prefecture later resided at Baiyang. He ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma drum is struck;
the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust stand arrayed before you. I wonder, do you all see them or not? If you say you see them,"
"Flowers blooming in the eye. If you say you do not see them, there is a film over your pupils. Apart from these two paths, bring me a single phrase.
If you hesitate or deliberate, *tut*! This is the obstructing Māra-king. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:
"Master Yantou used three copper coins to obtain a wife; she only knew how to dredge for shrimp and clams, yet she could never give birth to a son."
She raised a daughter, yet even until this very day, the family lineage has been severed. Do you, the great assembly, wish to recognize the wife of Master Huo?

Today at Jingde, I shall not begrudge my lips and teeth as I explain it for all of you: "Tangled hair and thorn-leaf hairpins are rare in this world; her cloth skirt is still the dress she wore on her wedding day.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The communal labor (pǔqǐng) of Tiantai is known by everyone; [the communal labor] of Nanyue is..."
"Mountain. Again, how do you understand this? If you understand, the lantern will laugh at you; if you do not understand, you have eyes but are like the blind.
A monk asked, "When Niutou had not yet seen the Fourth Patriarch, why did the hundred birds carry flowers to offer him? The Master said, "With money, one can travel a thousand miles.
The monk said, "After he saw him, why did they no longer carry flowers? The Master said, "Without money, one is deaf even next door. [The monk] asked, "Dara..."
[The Master] asked, "What is it like when grinding in the future? He replied, "Six times six is thirty-six. [The Master] asked, "What is it like after coming?
He replied, "Nine times nine is eighty-one. A question was asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? He replied, "Mushrooms grow on the tips of trees."
Question: "All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. What is the meaning of this? Answer: "Under one mountain range, there is another person.
Question: "When it is thus and as it is, how is it? Answer: "A withered tree does not encounter spring. Question: "When it is thus and not thus, how is it?
Answer: "Walking on water wearing boots. Question: "What is the aspect of not coming while coming? Answer: "Clouds."
Shenglingshang said, "How is it that one sees while not seeing forms? He replied, "Water flows from a high source.
A monk asked, "To act above and have those below imitate is not yet the work of a master; to turn one's back on Chu and flee to Wu is what makes one a man of realization.

Is this not the Master’s own words? He replied, "It is. The monk said, "This is like a father’s wealth being used by his son. He replied, "Try using it then. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
A monk asked Chan Master Yue of Ruiguang in Pingjiang Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Daoyu Shouzhi: "What is the meaning of 'Juzhi’s single finger'? He replied: "..."
The moon sets at the third watch as he passes through the marketplace.
Chan Master Shizi Jingduan of Xiyu, Huzhou, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Qiyue Longhua.
He was a native of his own prefecture; his clan name has been lost. (Some accounts state he appeared under the moon over Lake Dongting.)
When he first saw Nong Shizi, he clarified the essentials of the enlightened mind. Later, upon visiting Longhua, he received formal certification (in'ke).
He then returned to his hometown, where he fashioned a lion skin from dyed silk and occasionally wore it; consequently, he was known as Duan Shizi. Chancellor Zhang Gong admired his Way.

He personally requested [the Master] to open the Dharma at Wushan, where his transformative influence spread widely. On the day he accepted the invitation, after the question-and-answer session had concluded, he said:
"Maitreya is truly Maitreya; he manifests a thousand billion emanations. From time to time he reveals himself to those of this age, yet the people of this age do not recognize him.
Is there anyone among this assembly who recognizes him? Come forth and deliver a message. If there is no such person, I shall go on to draw legs upon a snake."

[It is so. Why do the great assembly not recognize it? It is simply because it is too near. Sentient beings have long wandered through birth and death precisely because they are unaware of it in their daily lives.
Having not yet attained true awakening, they constantly dwell in the realm of dreams. An ancient said: "Last night I had a dream; in the dream I saw a sphere of emptiness.
This morning, intending to speak of the dream, I looked up and again saw emptiness. I, this mountain monk, am likewise...

I had a dream that was unlike those of the ancients. Last night, I dreamed that the local deity said to me, "Tomorrow, Master Yeweng and others will enter the mountain to invite the Abbot to preside over Shousheng Chan Monastery.
Furthermore, since you have never traveled on pilgrimage throughout your life, how can you possibly preside? To which I, the mountain monk, replied to the deity: "Chan has attained it."
"It is within the mind. Why trouble yourself with such wide-ranging pursuits? If one is a true lion cub, they are able to roar as soon as they are born.
The local deity then asked, "What is a true lion cub? Is it not seen in Yongjia’s words: "The lion cub follows the herd;
at three years old, it can already let out a great roar. If a jackal pursues the Dharma King, its hundred-year-old monstrosity is in vain."
Opening his mouth—how truly marvelous! How truly marvelous! This lion cub on the mountain of study has lain deep within the dense forest for many years.
This morning, he slowly steps forth from the mountain cave. He bares his fangs and claws, spreads his shaggy mane, and his twin eyes flash with brilliant radiance.
Even the blue-eyed barbarian monks do not recognize him; how could the local spirits or mountain demons know? While dreaming, he was struck by the mountain...
The monk struck him once with his staff, and suddenly he was gone. "The assembly need not stand for long; I pray you all take care.
On the day of the opening of the hall, while the Vinaya Master was reciting the formal proclamation, [the Master] reached the lines: "Pushing over and turning back, kicking over and not leaning.
Before the seven volumes of the Lotus Sūtra had been recited, the sound of the "Fisherman's Song" was heard first. The Master stopped him and then ascended the seat to offer incense.

After the ritual for the Emperor’s longevity was concluded, he chanted with a drawn-out tone: "Originally a fisherman of Xiao and Xiang, wandering west, east, south, and north. The assembly acclaimed this in unison.
The Master looked at them and laughed, saying, "Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma King;

such is the Dharma of the Dharma King. He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "The second day of the second month—what does the Zen elder have to say? The spring breeze touches everything before one's eyes."

A hundred flowers bloom; the young nobles and sons of kings are drunk and tipsy day after day. Only the cypress trees from the Chen dynasty before the palace do not conform to the tastes of the fashionable.
To those who follow the Zen school, this is all there is: do not engage in discursive thought. After a meal, there is simply a cup of tea, served with ease and composure.
"Stretching out one's legs and sleeping on a long couch—shame! Upon arriving at Huating, the assembly requested that he ascend the hall. 'The lion of Vulture Peak roars amidst the clouds;
the Buddha-dharma is beyond discussion. It would be better to perform a somersault,' and with these words, he descended from his seat."

A monk asked, "What is it like when the wild goat has not yet hung its horns? The Master said, "I am afraid. The monk said, "Since you are a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), why are you afraid?
The Master said, "I have never seen such a strange beast. The Master suffered from a painful tooth that did not heal for a long time.
One day, he suddenly said to the assembly, "Tomorrow I am going to perform a somersault. The assembly took this to be a joke. He wrote: "The Master Duan is too lazy;

before he dies, his teeth will already have rotted away. At the two formal sessions, he accompanies the assembly to the hall, yet he cannot even distinguish between the morning gruel and the midday meal.
Now that he has attained death, it is a blessing; he shall sleep forever, unconcerned with any of the hundred affairs. This is the foremost priority."
Do not look at the official. Second, do not eat gruel or rice. At the fifth watch of the night, he indeed entered nirvana.
He was seventy-two years of age.
[He was] a Dharma successor of Chan Master Langya Guangzhao Huijue.
Chan Master Fang of Mount Jiang in Shaoxing Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "Passing through clouds but not crossing waters; crossing waters but not passing through clouds.
Holding fast to heaven and earth yet not holding them fast; letting emptiness pass yet not letting it pass. Transverse, threefold; vertical, fourfold."

Parting and joining for a moment; using the long to compensate for the short—this I do not ask of you all. "The meal is made from rice"—a single phrase that is difficult to speak of. After a long silence, he said:
"Private matters cannot be rewarded by official means. Ascending the hall, he said: "It is not a matter of being able to speak or unable to speak;
everywhere people take this to be something extraordinary. Hanshan burns fire, his head full of ashes; laughing and scolding, he is abundant."
"Kill this old thief! A monk asked, "What is 'one mote of dust entering right concentration'? He replied, "A snake biting the tail of a rat.
The monk said, "What is 'all motes of dust arising from samādhi'? He replied, "A turtle biting a fishing rod.
The monk said, "If that is so, then east and west are not distinguished, and north and south are not discerned. He replied, "A bowl of luminous lamp before the hall; outside the curtain—"
Several stalks of green, slender bamboo. [The student] asked: "How is it before all Buddhas have appeared in the world? He replied: "One does not recognize the wine-scoop.
[The student] said: "How is it after they have appeared in the world? He replied: "Bestowing three blows upon a fishing boat. [The student] asked: "What is the Venerable Immovable One? He replied:
"Wearing only a single cotton shirt, he passes through the marketplace. [The student] said: "I do not yet understand. He replied: "Riding a donkey, he steps on [it]."

[The Master] says: "Breaking through the waves of Dongting Lake. [The Student] asks: "Having penetrated the three-tiered waves, one listens intently for a single clap of thunder. [The Master] says: "Stretching out one's hand, one does not see one's own palm.

[The Student] asks: "Do you permit the student to advance further? [The Master] says: "Treading upon the ground, one addresses the void. [The Student] says: "Beneath the Gate of Thunder, a cloth drum is difficult to sound. [The Master] says:
"Upon the eight-petaled flower ball, there is no need to embroider a red banner. [The Student] says: "Thirty years..."
Later, this story became widely circulated. The Master then struck him. [The monk] asked: "How is it when the lotus flower has not yet emerged from the water? He said:

"One who tries to thread a needle complains that the eye is too small. [The monk] said: "And how is it after it has emerged from the water? He said: "Throughout the day, one spreads a frown of sorrow.
[The monk] asked: "A rushing torrent crossing a blade; a swift flame passing through wind. I wonder, under the gate of Jiangshan, is it permitted to borrow [these things] or not? He said: "Heaven."
"Cold days are short, but the night grows longer. [The Master] said: "An embroidered phoenix couple in a brocade curtain; travelers find it difficult to see. [The monk] said:

"The breath from within a skull shoots toward the heavens. The Master called out, "Monk! The monk responded, "Venerable Sir. The Master said: "The head of a rooster and the tail of a phoenix. [The Master] said: "Everywhere else they wash in the mud;
Jiangshan has brought it forth in a painting. [The monk] said: "Today Jiangshan acts as the guest; I hope you, Dharma brother, will transmit this well."
Nevertheless, even though it was so, he did not let him off; he struck him.
Chan Master Xian-duan of Bailing in Fuzhou was asked by a monk: "What is the formless Buddha? He replied:
"A stone lion at the riverbank. The monk asked: "What is the meaning of this? He said: "With mind dwelling upon the river, one need not fear the waves washing away the sand."
Question: "What is it like when one is stilled and profoundly tranquil? He said: "That is not where you, the disciple, should establish yourself or find your livelihood. The questioner asked:

"Then what is the place where this student may establish himself and find his livelihood? He replied: "The clouds have the air of leaving the mountains; the water has no sound of plunging into the ravine."
Chan Master Xingjiao Tan of Ningguo Prefecture was the son of the Niu family of Yongjia. He worked as a silversmith;

while sharpening and polishing vessels, he attained a realization and immediately left the household life to don the monastic robes. He visited Guangzhao at Langya, where his words and spirit were suddenly in accord.
Later, he relied upon Chan Master Tianyi Huai, who was then residing at Xingjiao. Huai promoted him to the position of First Seat. When Huai received an invitation from elsewhere, [he departed].
Upon hearing of the vacancy at the monastery, he requested that the Master succeed him. On the day he accepted the invitation, Xuedou Huashan Shengzong came forward and asked:
"Before the Buddhas appeared in the world, everyone’s nostrils reached the heavens; after they appeared in the world, why is there no news at all? The Master replied: "..."
"Within Mount Jizu, Feng is majestic," he said. "Not yet," [the Master] replied. "Speak further. [Feng] said, "Thirty blows are sent to be struck at Xuedou.
The monk bowed. The Master said, "The New Teaching has lost ground today," and then descended from his seat (there are versions with slight variations).
Chan Master Guizong Ke Xuan of Jiangzhou was a native of Hanzhou. In his youth, he became a monk and immediately crossed the gorges to rely upon Guangzhao.
A single word suddenly struck home, and his many doubts were instantly extinguished; Guangzhao approved of him. Before long, he was ordered to share the teaching seat.

When the layman Jingkong Guo Gongfu visited his door to inquire about the Way, they became close friends. Later, when the Master took charge of Guizong, at that time Gongfu was serving as the Prefect of Nan...
Changwei. Shortly thereafter, the district magistrate resented that the Master did not pay him due respect and began to persecute him severely.

He then wrote a letter to Gongfu, saying: "I have six years remaining of my worldly karmic ties; however, the local governor oppresses me so much that I must cast off this final breath to take rebirth in your household.
I pray you do not obstruct me. When Gongfu read the letter, he was both surprised and delighted, and he nodded his head in agreement. In the middle of the night, his wife saw the Master in a dream.
They entered her chamber. [Xuedou] cried out in distress, "This is not the place from which the Master came! Gongfu shook her and questioned her; his wife related the matter in detail.
He called for a lamp, took the letter, and showed it to her; they laughed together without ceasing. Consequently, she became pregnant. When the child was born, he was named Xuānlǎo.
At one year of age, his memory and questioning were as they had been before. When he reached three years old, Chan Master Băizhūn Duān arrived at their home, where he first met him.
[The Master] said, "My nephew has come. Duan asked, "How many years have passed since you parted from the Monk?

Xuan counted back on his fingers and said, "Four years" (in fact, he had been dead for only one year since they parted). [Duan] asked, "Where did you part? He replied, "At Bailian Village. [Duan] asked, "What is the proof?
He said, "Father, Mother, invite the Monk for a meal tomorrow. Suddenly, the sound of a cart being pushed was heard. Duan asked, "The gate—"
"What sound is that outside? Xuande made a gesture with his hand as if pushing a cart. Duan asked, "What about after it has passed?
He replied, "Two ruts on level ground. Guo died at the age of six without illness; other words [of his] have not been seen to appear elsewhere.
The lecturer Zixuan of Changshui in Jiaxing Prefecture was a native of Jiaxing in the commandery. Since his tonsure, he had recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* without ceasing.
While listening to Master Hongmin lecture on the passage concerning the two aspects of motion and stillness—where it says they "are clearly seen not to arise"—he attained a profound realization.

He said to Huimin, "Striking the air or hitting wood (one version says 'hitting bamboo') still falls within the realm of the trap and the snare; raising an eye or lifting a brow has already become a matter of deliberation.
Only by departing from these verbal roots can one accord with this principle. Huimin patted him in confirmation. However, wishing to explore the source of Chan, he knew not where to turn.
Hearing that Langya’s Way was esteemed in his time, he immediately went to his seat. Happening upon the occasion when the Master was ascending the hall, he stepped forward and asked:
"It is pure and inherently so. How is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Layun replied, "It is pure and inherently so.
How is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? The Master attained awakening and, bowing in gratitude, said, "I wish to serve you with the water jar and towel."

He said, "Your school has long been without vigor; you ought to rouse your resolve to support it and repay the Buddha’s benevolence and virtue, without making distinctions based on differing lineages.

[Zhiyuan] then followed these instructions and took his leave with a double prostration. Later, while residing at Changshui and receiving instruction daily, he looked toward the fourfold assembly and said, "The Way is not attained through words or images;
Chan is not known through conjecture or deliberation. To realize the meaning and penetrate the source, there is never anything else to be found."
Both schools held him in high esteem. He once composed commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and other scriptures, which became widely circulated throughout the world.
He was the dharma successor of Chan Master Tianyi Zenzong Yihuai (the fifth generation of Yunmen, the eleventh generation of Qingyuan).
Chan Master Yuanzhao Zongben of Hui-lin Temple in Tokyo was originally from Wuxi. His clan name was Guan. He possessed a robust and imposing physique and was naturally sincere and earnest.

At the age of nineteen, he went to Chengtian Temple in Gusu and relied upon Chan Master Daosheng of Yong’an. There, he performed his duties in the kitchen—grinding grain and cooking rice—without ever growing weary.
Whenever he encountered Daosheng entering the inner quarters for private instruction, he would join the assembly in seeking guidance. Daosheng said: "The Way..."
"Is it not a slight hardship to exert oneself in this way? The Master said, "If one were to abandon even a single dharma, it could not be called fulfillment.
I truly wish to realize Bodhi with this very body; what hardship could there be? Shenying marveled at this.

Ten years later, he shaved his head, received the full precepts, and served the Master for another three years before requesting leave to travel. He arrived at Chiyang and visited Tianyi at Jingde Temple.
[The Master] raised his robe. As Vasubandhu descended from Maitreya’s inner palace, Asaṅga asked him:

"Four hundred years among humans constitute a single day and night for those devas. In a single session, Maitreya brings five billion devaputras to realization in the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
I wonder what dharma he teaches? Vasubandhu replied: "He teaches only this very dharma. It is as follows:
"What is this Dharma? he asked. After a long time, he attained enlightenment. One day, while in his quarters, he questioned the Master: "What is it like when 'this very mind is Buddha'?
The Master replied, "What difficulty is there in killing people and setting fires? Thereupon, his fame spread throughout the world.

The Canal Commissioner, Lord Li Fugui, commissioned the Master to open the Dharma at Rui Guang Monastery, where the assembly grew increasingly prosperous. Lord Chen Xiang, the Governor of Wulin, [invited him as well].
The Emperor appointed the Master to reside at either Chengtian or Xingjiao Monasteries. However, the people of Suzhou crowded the roads to block his departure and entreat him to stay.

Furthermore, because Jingci Monastery made a firm request, he issued a formal letter to both the clergy and the laity, stating: "I shall borrow the Master for three years to plant the seeds of merit for this region;
I dare not occupy him for long. Only then did the clergy and the laity comply. In the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, Emperor Shenzong issued an imperial edict to expand the Xiangguosi Monastery.
The sixty-four monasteries were divided into eight groups: two for Chan and two for Vinaya. The Emperor summoned the Master to be the first patriarch of Hui-lin Monastery.

Upon his arrival, the Emperor dispatched an envoy to inquire after his well-being. After three days had passed, an imperial edict was proclaimed for him to expound the Dharma at the three gates of the monastery for the sake of the officials and the common people.
On the following day, he was summoned for an audience at the Yanhe Hall, where he was granted a seat; the Master then sat with his legs crossed.

He fell and was about to collapse. The Emperor immediately ordered his close attendants to provide him with two additional brocade seats (the details of which appear in the *Shixing shi* [Record of the Master’s Travels] and the *True Eulogy of Layman Yang Jie* of Wuwéi).

When Emperor Shenzong passed away, he was commanded to enter the Funing Hall to preach the Dharma. Requesting to retire to the forests and valleys due to his old age, he received an imperial decree allowing him to wander freely as he pleased;
no prefectures or commanderies were permitted to compel him to serve as an abbot. He then struck the drum to bid farewell to the assembly.
He spoke in verse: "Originally a guest with no home, how can one afford to wander at will? With a favorable wind, the oars and paddles are added; the boatman descends to Yangzhou.
Having departed the capital, the carriages and horsemen of kings, dukes, and nobles who came to see him off followed one after another. As he was about to part, the Master instructed them, saying:
"The passage of years and months cannot be toyed with; old age and sickness do not wait for anyone's appointment. Strive only in diligent cultivation and do not be indolent."

This was a true manifestation of the Dharma; those who heard it could not help but shed tears of emotion. In his later years, he resided at Lingyan, where more than a hundred people succeeded him in the Dharma and transmitted the Way.

Entering the hall for formal discourse, he said: "When the great sound is once split open, heaven and earth are shaken. When the Dharma-commands are put into practice, the myriad functions are suddenly pared away.
The paths of sage and ordinary are cut off; the sentiments of Buddhas and patriarchs are forgotten. At this moment, east and west cannot be distinguished, nor south..."
No distinction between north and south. Following the teaching, for a thousand ages, ten thousand ages, all is pitch-black. To fill the ditches and block the ravines—no one understands.
(He plants his staff upright. He descends from the seat. Ascending the hall: Nothing is more precipitous than the Peak of Chicken Foot. When travelers reach this place, the path is difficult to pass.
Only fearing that those who are guests under the Patriarch’s gate will not move even a hair’s breadth to enter within. *Chan.* Ascending the hall. A question was asked.
It is no hindrance. The answer is likewise without fault. Why? Because gaining it does not make one first, and losing it does not make one last.
If one penetrates this principle, how can one discuss emptiness or existence? Since time immemorial, the thousand sages have simply remained at ease. Let the birds and hares race for the head prize;
formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness pass in the snap of a finger. Gain and loss, right and wrong, are but a single mouth. *Tut!* Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "For now..."
At the side of the Su Terrace, one does not speak of spring and autumn. Before the eyes of a patch-robed monk, how could one discuss the profound and the subtle?
One can only wear clothes and eat food, enjoy the water and gaze at the mountains; see the stars at night and the sun by day. With both hands grasping the plow, the water rises above the knees.

The prediction bestowed at Vulture Peak was just like this: throughout kalpas, how has it ever been different from today? Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Within the tip of a single hair, manifest..."
In the Jewel King lands, he sits within a mote of dust and turns the Great Dharma Wheel. Holding up his staff, he said: "This is the dust.
How can one speak of the principle of turning the Dharma Wheel? Today, this mountain monk will not spare his eyebrows to explain it through for you all.
He held it up: "When he lifts it, the waters of the ocean surge into waves and Mount Sumeru trembles. When he lets it down, the four [continents]..."
The seas are calm and clear; heaven and earth are solemn and still. I dare ask you all: tell me, is it when he picks up [the whisk] that it is so?

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "My late teacher first served Xi-xian Yi and Le-tan Cheng for twenty years.

There was nothing among the wondrous subtleties of the ancestral gate or the profound essentials of the sutras and treatises that he did not master. Yet, when Yun-feng pointed him toward Ci-ming, then—"
Not a single word was of use; he thus established three "gateless barriers" (guānyǔ) to test practitioners. Yet, the Chan followers were like Yegong painting a dragon:
when the dragon appeared, they were struck with terror. On the fifth day of the eighth month in the third year of the Jiànyán era, he passed away at Zhāngjiāng in Fúzhōu.
He was ninety-eight years old and had been a monk for seventy-eight years.

The Abbot Zhizhi of Guizong on Mount Lu was a native of Linjiang. Having become a bhikṣu in his prime, he relied upon Huanglong at Guizong and thereby attained the profound meaning [of the teachings].
He composed a verse which says: "If you have not yet arrived, you must arrive; once arrived, it makes people laugh. [His] eyebrows...
The "Mao" edition is useless; it lacks the "bottom-wave" refinement. Before long, the Dragon led his followers away, and Zhixu sank into the mud along with his thousand followers.
One day, after the communal labor was finished, he wrote: "The tea buds, rustling, have just left the roasting kiln; The bamboo shoots, in their haste, are already bursting from the mud."
"In my mountain hut, the affairs of spring are settled for the year; having found leisure, who cares that the headboard is low?

Because of this, the monastics flocked to him, which made Master Zhi displeased. He retired to a thatched cottage on a mountain peak and composed a verse: "A single room atop a thousand peaks: The old monk occupies half, the clouds the other half.
Last night the clouds followed the wind and rain away; In the end, they are not as free as the old monk. (Some versions differ slightly.)
He passed away at this mountain.
Chan Master Shouzhen Baoyun of Shuzhou, a successor of Chan Master Fange Yangqi, was a native of Hengyang.
His clan was Ge (the *Xudeng* states it was Zhou, which is incorrect). In his youth, he served as a scribe.
Mo was weary of worldly affairs. He received the tonsure under Chan Master Yu of Chaling. He went to study with Chan Master Yong of Yungai;
after Yong passed away, Yangqi succeeded him. When Yangqi saw Mo, he spoke with him all night. One day, he suddenly asked, "Who is your preceptor? Mo replied, "Venerable Yu of Chaling.
Yangqi said, "I have heard that he had an awakening upon crossing the stream and composed a remarkably wondrous verse."
"Can you recite it? The Master recited: "I have a bright pearl; for a long time it has been locked away by the dust of worldly toil.

Today the dust is cleared and its light shines forth, piercing through the myriad peaks of mountains and rivers. Qí laughed and hurried away. The Master stared at him in astonishment and could not sleep.
At dawn, he consulted [the Master]. It happened to be the end of the year. Qí asked, "Did you see those who were performing the *dǒu nán* (exorcism) yesterday?

He replied, "I saw them. Qí said, "In this one matter, you fall short of them. The Master was again startled and asked, "What is the meaning of this? Qí said, "They loved being laughed at; you feared being laughed at.
The Master attained great enlightenment. He served as an attendant for a long time. In the fourth year of the Jiàyòu era, he took his leave to travel to Mount Lú.
Upon seeing him, Chan Master Yuntong Ne declared that he himself was inferior. He was appointed to reside at Chengtian Temple, where his reputation became exceedingly great;
subsequently, he yielded the position at Yuntong to others and moved in turn to Fahua, Longmen, Xinghua, and Haihui. At every location he visited, the assembly gathered like clouds.

On the day of opening the hall, after the question-and-answer session had concluded, he said: "In the past, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One held up a flower, and Kāśyapa smiled.
The World-Honored One said: 'I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye; I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa.
Let it be transmitted in succession so that it never be severed. Up until this very day, O Great Assembly—if this is indeed the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye of Śākyamuni..."
Laozi himself had no portion [to bestow]. With what could he have entrusted it? With what could he have transmitted it? Why is this so?
Furthermore, within the sphere of each and every person, there is already the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.

From the moment they rise each day, whether they judge right and wrong, distinguish north and south, or engage in all manner of activities—all of these are but the radiance and reflections of the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. This...

When the eyes are opened, the heavens and earth, the sun, moon, and stars, and the myriad phenomena of the universe are all right before one’s face, yet not even a hair’s breadth of form is seen. When these eyes were not yet open, all of this was already within everyone’s own eyes;
those for whom they have now been opened are not subject to this limitation. For those whose eyes are still unopened, this mountain monk will not begrudge his hand in opening them for you all.
Looking at this treasury of the Dharma-eye, [the Master] raised his hand and held up two fingers, saying: "Look! Look! If you can see it, then matters are as one family.
If you have not yet attained this, I, this mountain monk, cannot help but speak another verse for you: 'The Dharma-eye treasury of all people—none of the thousand sages can equal it.
For your sake, I open a single thread; its radiance fills the Great Tang. Sumeru enters the sea; in the sixth month...'"
A severe frost descends. Although the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks thus, there is no phrase to be deliberated upon.
"Great Assembly," since it has already been spoken from his full mouth, why is there no phrase to be deliberated upon? He lets out a shout and says, "Look at the body divided into two places."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Within the realm of heaven and earth, amidst the expanse of the universe, there is a single treasure, hidden within the mountain of form.
Great assembly, your eyes are above your nose and your feet are below your belly; tell me, where does this treasure reside? He then said:
"One knows not where the human face has gone; the peach blossoms still smile upon the spring breeze. Ascending the hall, he raised his staff and said: "The edge..."
He leaped upon the blade. Holding it crosswise, he said: "A horse gallops within a mote of dust; toiling on, it goes and returns again. This is the one who is truly alert.
He threw down his staff and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "There has never been delusion; do not seek enlightenment.
Why is it that from the beginning there have nevertheless been lineages of teachers and patriarchs? If you understand this, enter the local customs as they are. If you do not understand this—"
He starved to death on Mount Shouyang. Nevertheless, even so, one sees a tall man upon entering the water. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Today is the first day of the season;
Yang (the principle of growth) is born on this very day. He raised his staff and called to the assembly, saying: "Tell me, what is this?
If you can see it, then you may thus receive blessings in accordance with the time. If you wait until the New Year arrives..."
There is still snow on his head. This is why Chengtian usually stops nine times out of ten when he speaks.
Why is this so? One should not plant thorny brambles at the gate; otherwise, future descendants will get their clothes caught upon them. Even so, it remains as it is.
Thirty years later, Grand Duke Tai fished. (Pause. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said:

'To offer this profound mind to every dust mote and land is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness. Yuan Tong does not do it this way: at times he gathers wild vegetables and boils them with their roots;
he chops fresh firewood and burns it with its leaves. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. Arriving here—"
"Are there any who have escaped the net? After a long silence, he said: "The August Heaven has no partiality. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The Elder Śākyamuni had four great vows, which state: 'Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them all. Afflictions are inexhaustible; I vow to sever them all.'"
"I vow to study the immeasurable Dharma-gates; I vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way. The *Lotus Sūtra* also possesses these four great vows:
when hunger comes, one must eat; when cold arrives, one adds clothing; when weary, one stretches out the legs and sleeps;

in the heat, one longs for a breeze. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Even if one could spend ten thousand taels of gold daily, it would not suffice at the gate of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Even if one were to..."
"Half a penny straight through. One has just entered the gate of the Lotus Sutra, but has not yet ascended to the hall of the Lotus Sutra, nor entered the chamber of the Lotus Sutra.
But tell me, what kind of person can ascend to the hall of the Lotus Sutra and enter its chamber?
He then said: "His eyes have three corners; his head is as sharp as the Five Peaks. Ascending the hall, he said: "Today it is this very thing; tomorrow it is also this very thing."
"This one—how about that one? A lacquer bucket! Go to the hall for study. When the layman Guo Gongfu of Jingkong visited the Master, he ascended the hall and said:

"Last night on my pillow, I composed a mountain verse to thank the great scholar Guo Gongfu. I truly wish to strip off the flesh-bound sweatshirt from every monk with nostrils throughout the world; do not say I did not speak of it. He then [recited]: The verse says: A single phrase of the Buddha’s teaching, Like a bright pearl in the palm of the hand.
If you can see it clearly, You will immediately transcend the three realms. He then added: "I have already spoken; do not say I did not say it. He then descended from the seat.
It says: "The Superior Man; Qiu Yi Ji; transformed three thousand; seventy scholars; you, little students; eight or nine children; well-cultivated benevolence;
one may know propriety thereby. Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "The ancients left behind a word or a phrase; as long as it has not been penetrated,"
"It is like bumping into an iron wall. Once you suddenly see through it one day, you will finally realize that the iron wall was yourself all along.
Now, how do you penetrate it? He said again, "An iron wall! An iron wall! A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? He replied, "In the boiling cauldron, there is no place that is cold.
The monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? He replied, "Pressing down a gourd underwater."
Lu said, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? He replied, "The crow flies; the hare runs.
A monk asked, "Not seeking after the sages and not esteeming one's own spiritual nature is still not the business of a patch-robed monk. What, then, is the business of a patch-robed monk?"
He said, "A stagnant pond does not harbor dragons. Yun asked, "What is it like when one proceeds in this very manner? He replied, "It will ruin you!
In the fifth year of the Xining era, he passed away at the age of forty-eight.

Chan Master Baoning Renyong of Jiankang Prefecture was a native of Siming. His clan name was Zhu. His appearance and demeanor were profound and elegant; he became a monk at the age of seven and mastered the Tiantai teachings.
Shortly thereafter, he donned dark robes and relied upon Chan Master Mingjue Xian of Xuedou.

Xian perceived that Renyong was capable of bearing the burden of the Dharma, yet one day he rebuked him. Renyong, feeling both indignant and resolute, immediately went to rely upon [Chan Master Dahui] Letan. More than a decade passed, yet his doubts remained unresolved.

Hearing that Yangqi had moved to Yun’gai and was able to act as a strict gatekeeper for students, he went directly to the master’s quarters. Before a single word had been exchanged, he suddenly realized the Mind-Seal.
He left to reside at Baoning, where he remained for over twenty years, greatly propagating the Way of the Patriarchs.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Dust upon dust, world upon world; mountains are mountains, waters are waters. Maitreya does not enter the pavilion, and Sudhana does not [enter the garden]."
Snap your fingers and draw a single line with your hand, saying: "The worlds as numerous as motes of dust melt like ice and crumble like tiles.
Now tell me, where are Maitreya and Sudhana? If you can penetrate this point here, you will naturally be honored wherever you go;
if you do not see it, the traveler's road is as vast as heaven and the nobleman's gate is as deep as the sea. Ascending the hall on the day of the Start of Spring, he struck [the board].
The Spring Ox: One blow, two blows; a thousand heads, ten thousand heads. Amidst the deep snowflakes, they cannot be distinguished; yet the eye atop its head gazes vacantly into the void.
Clapping his hands, he says: "Loro liri! The spring wind continues to cause such turmoil, never ceasing. Ascending the hall, he said:
The autumn wind is cool; the pine tones are long. The traveler who has not yet returned yearns for his native land. But tell me, who is this traveler who has not yet returned?
Where is that native land? After a long silence, he said: "On the long couch, there is porridge and rice. Ascending the hall, he raised [the following]:
San-sheng said, "Whenever I meet someone, I come forth; but when I come forth, I do not act for others. Xing-hua said, "Whenever I meet someone, I do not..."
He stepped out. Having stepped out, he immediately became a man. The Master said, "These two venerable elders acting in such a manner for the sake of others are still only halfway there.
Baoning, seeing this injustice today, took up his staff and descended from his seat; the assembly all scattered at once. He threw it down and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
