Should it not yet be so, immeasurable afflictions and all worldly defilements will stand like mountains before one’s face, chilling the ancient path. Ascending the hall, he spoke of the Mysterious Way.
It cannot be attained through forceful effort. Wondrous wisdom cannot be known with a conceptual mind. Ultimate truth cannot be grasped through a self-centered understanding.
The supreme principle cannot be realized through worldly activity. If you can penetrate this, Kāśyapa’s rag robe from the dustheap is worth hundreds of thousands of millions;
if you cannot penetrate it, the jewel in the crown of a universal monarch is not worth half a penny. *Can*.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The ancients said: 'Following the limbs, casting out the faculties of hearing and intelligence; leaving behind form and discarding wisdom, one becomes one with the Great Way.
At such a time as this, tell me: who is it that edits the *Shi* and *Shu*, and establishes ritual and music? Do you understand?"
"The Book of Rites says, 'The rites, the rites! Are they merely jade and silk? The Book of Music says, 'The music, the music! Is it merely bells and drums?
A monk asked, "Within the realm of True Suchness, there is fundamentally no cause for delusion or enlightenment. Within the gate of expedient means, I pray you will reveal the melody of non-arising.
The Master said, "Six times six is thirty-six; the clear breeze stirs the tall bamboos. The monk said, "A single burst of this great sound startles heaven and earth!"
"There are insentient beings who all receive this grace. He said: "One song, two songs—no one understands;
after the rain, the autumn pond’s waters run deep. Question: "I have heard your words, Master: 'Where the clouds are dark, Mount Duxiu towers forth;
within the hazy moonlight, the light of Lake Letan arises. Is this not the realm of Baofeng? He replied: "If it is the realm of Baofeng, rely on you [to realize it]."
"Look closely," [the Master] said. The monk asked, "What is it like to be a person within the realm? He replied, "Observe when the command is being executed.
The monk asked, "As for the saying, 'One must understand the source when receiving the words; do not establish your own rules,' what is the Master’s source?

He replied, "You must know that beyond the clouds, atop a thousand peaks, there is a distinct numinous pine, cold with dew. While it was snowing, a monk asked, "The Patriarchal intent came from the West..."
He did not ask what the circumstances of the time were. [The Master] said: "One fragment, two fragments, three or four fragments—falling into the eye, one still does not realize it.

On the *xinchou* day of the first month in the second year of the Jianyan era, during the evening assembly, he raised the fact that the fundamental tenets of the Cao-Dong school had become as thin as a single thread.
He then sighed, lamenting those in the present age who continue the lineage of wisdom. The following morning, he closed his door and claimed to be ill.

He observed the summer retreat as usual. Suddenly, he wrote a farewell letter to his senior disciples. In the middle of the night, he instructed the attendants not to handle the funeral according to worldly customs.
When an attendant requested a final verse, the Master replied with a colloquial remark and passed away.
Seven days later, his body was cremated, and śarīra relics like pearls and beads were obtained; his tongue and teeth remained unchanged. Director Feng Wenshu was deeply amazed by these events.
On the *gengshen* day of the second month, he was interred on the western peak of the monastery. He was forty-five years of age and twenty-five years of *dharma*-years.
On the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday, the National Teacher Nanchan of Jianshang Army’s Zaiseng Monastery ascended the hall and, looking around at those present, said:

"Do you all understand? The Lord outside the curtain of night-brightness remains unchanged through ten thousand transformations; the Honored One atop the crystal palace [remains constant] throughout the four seasons..."

Your servant is not ignorant of this: he governs with dignified composure; his commands are carried out without being issued. His lifespan exceeds that of ten billion Mount Sumerus, and his transformative governance extends throughout the sands of the great trichiliocosm.
But tell me, at such a time as this, how does he conduct himself? "The rustic elder knows nothing of the nobility of the imperial yellow palace."
"I am too weary to listen to the sound of the quiet-whip in the six streets.
Chan Master Wei of Dongshan in Yunzhou ascended the hall and said: "The sun is warm and the wind is gentle; the willow eyes are green. The ice melts and the fish leap;
ripples form upon the waves. Skillfully grasping the Seal of the Empty King at the front line, At midnight, Kunlun walks bearing snow upon his head."
A monk asked, "What is the matter of silent resonance? He replied, "A mute man eating bitter melon.
Chan Master Shousui Jingyan of Dahuang in Suizhou was a successor of Chan Master Dahong En.
He was a native of Pengxi in Suining and belonged to the Zhang clan. Before he had reached the age of twenty (the *guan* ceremony), [he became a monk].
Liyun took refuge with Zizheng as his teacher at the age of twenty-seven. He shaved his head and received full ordination, then traveled far to knock at the master’s door.
Later, he received secret certification at Mount Hong and went forth to reside at Shuinan, subsequently moving to Dahong. Ascending the hall, he called to the assembly, saying:
"With one punch, I topple Huangge Lou; with one kick, I overturn Yingwu Zhou. I am accustomed to galloping my royal steed across high towers."
Once, in swift waters, one struck a golden ball; yet even though it was thus, how could one avoid having five-colored silk cords binding the hands and feet, and three gold locks fastening the throat?
Even if you were to smash the gold locks and sever the silk cords, you must know that there is still another layer obstructing you. Tell me, what is this one layer? Do you understand? Subhūti!
Vimalakīrti’s discourse was beyond reach; Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra looked on like the blind. Ascending the hall, he raised this case:
"In the past, an official asked Mount Medicine (Yaoshan), 'What is your surname, Master? Yaoshan replied, 'It is precisely now. The official was at a loss.
Later, he went to the administrative officers and asked, 'Just now I asked the Elder what his surname was, and he answered, "It is precisely now. Is this indeed correct?'"

"What is your surname? The administrator replied, "It is simply Han. When Yaoshan heard this, he said, "If one says 'it is precisely the season' in the sixth month, one cannot say 'I am hot by nature.
Furthermore, Yantou asked a lecture-monk, "I have heard it said that you, Venerable Sir, understand the teachings;
is this true? He replied, "I dare not say so. Yantou raised his fist and asked, "What teaching is this? The monk replied, "It is the provisional teaching."
Yantou said, "How bitter! Had I asked you with my legs extended, you could not have said it was taught by the feet. The Master said, "How extraordinary!
These two elders possessed the sword that kills and the sword that gives life. One turn of phrase was like planting flowers upon a rock;
another turn of phrase was like hanging a sword in mid-air. Had there not been the subsequent words at that time, the entire school of Bodhidharma would have been swept away."
The earth is exhausted. Do you people wish to see these two old masters? It would be better to cut out one's tongue than to violate the national taboo.

Chan Master Wuxin Wuxin of Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture was a native of Qujiang, Shaoyang.

He was born into the Huang family on the twenty-ninth day of the second month in the third year of the Qingli era. A purple fleshy protuberance covered his left shoulder, appearing like a *saṃghāṭī* robe when he bared his right side;
white light illuminated his room. From infancy, he never cried. As he grew older, he became exceptionally gifted, and by the time he reached adulthood...
Having received the tonsure and full ordination under the virtue of [Master] Foyuan, he said to his old friends: "As a monk, one should aspire to both mundane and supramundane dharmas;
how can one remain mired in the common affairs of one's hometown? Thereupon, he traveled to various regions with staff and alms bowl. In the eighth year of the Xining era,
He went to Huanglong to pay his respects to Huitang. Huitang held up his fist and asked, "To call it a 'fist' is to commit the fault of *touch*;
not to call it a 'fist' is to commit the fault of *aversion*. What do you call it? The Master was at a loss for words. It took two years before he finally attained realization;

yet, he still engaged in debate without contradiction. Huitang was concerned about this. Once, while conversing with him, as the Master reached the height of his sharpness, Huitang suddenly said, "Stop! Stop!"
"How can merely talking about food satisfy a person's hunger? The Master was cornered and said, "I have reached this point with my bow broken and my arrows exhausted.

I pray that the Master will show compassion and point out a place of peace and happiness for me. The Hall Master replied, "A single speck of dust flies up and obscures the heavens; a single mustard seed falls and obscures the earth.

As for a place of peace and happiness, we strictly forbid you, Venerable Sir, from possessing such a multitude of worldly attachments. You must simply die [to them]—all that has come down through immeasurable kalpas."

"Only when you have devoted your whole heart can it be so. The Master hurried out. One day, while sitting silently on the edge of the meditation platform, he heard the administrative official, the *fuxingzhe*, speaking;
suddenly, a clap of thunder struck, and he attained great enlightenment. He hurried to see Huìtáng, forgetting to remove his shoes, and immediately proclaimed his realization, saying:

"The people of the world all merely 'attain' through Zen; I am one who has 'awakened. " The Abbot laughed and said, "To have attained the first rank in the selection for Buddhahood—how could anyone surpass you?
Consequently, he was given the title "Old Man of the Dead Heart" (Sīxīn Sǒu). He attended and assisted [the Abbot] for a total of eighteen autumns.
He never grew weary or discouraged. At first, he was invited to share the teaching seat; later, he visited the doors of all the elders. His spiritual responses and discourse were transcendent.
In the seventh year of the Yuanyou era, he went to reside at Yunyan. In the fourth year of the Shaosheng era, he moved to Cuoyan. At the beginning of the Zhenghe era, he dwelt at Huanglong.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Profound, firm, remote, and far-reaching—no one can reach it. Did Śākyamuni Buddha reach it or not? If he reached it, why is it that no one can?
If he did not reach it, who says it is profound and remote? Ascending the hall, he said: "The Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs."
It resembles the mechanism of the iron ox: when it departs, it seals; when it abides, it breaks. As for neither departing nor abiding—is it the seal? Is it not the seal?
"The golden fruit was plucked by the monkey at early dawn; the jade flower was carried back by the phoenix at late evening. Ascending the hall, [he said]:
"Deshan’s staff as soon as one enters the gate, Linji’s shout as soon as one enters the gate—these too are merely acts of a thief."

The human mind is empty. When Yunyan entered the gate, [the Master] neither struck him with a staff nor shouted at him. Tell me, what did he use? Time and again he knocked on the door, but no one came out to welcome him;
so he turned his body and went straight inside to look. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "High-ranking travelers on the pilgrimage path..."
Untie the cloth bag. Set down the alms-bowl pouch. Cast aside the medicinal prohibitions. One must reach where there is one person;
one must reach where there is half a person; one must personally reach even where there is no one. Ascending the hall, he snapped his staff in two:
"With what will you climb mountains and cross waters? He set aside the bowl, spoon, and chopsticks: "With what will you eat gruel and rice? No.
It is like casting lots east and west at a crossroads; if you suddenly cast the lot and hit it, then you all have won the prize.
If you do not hit it, then it cannot be blamed on Yunyan. Ascending the hall, he said: "Mañjuśrī rides a lion;
Samantabhadra rides an elephant king; Śākyamuni the Old Man treads upon red lotuses. But tell me, what does Huanglong ride? Liang [replied].
[The Master] said, "Lately, being old in years, every step is a true step. He ascended the hall and said, "Sometimes I break two into three;
sometimes I bring three back to one; sometimes the three and the one are merged as one; and sometimes I do not fall into any numerical measure.
Now tell me, where is Huanglong’s place for benefiting people? After a long silence, he said, "Take care. He ascended the hall and said, "Coarse words..."

[The Master] spoke in a low voice: "All things return to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). You lot, you bed-wetting ghosts—though you have passed through sixty kalpas over three lifetimes, you have not even dreamed of the primary meaning.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "An ancient said: 'Conceal the person, do not conceal the illumination; conceal the illumination, do not conceal the person;
conceal both person and illumination; conceal neither person nor illumination. Later generations have raised this many times; those who understand it are few."
Those who [attain this] are extremely few. Today, Huanglong, not sparing a single hair on his eyebrows, shall explain it through for all of you:

"The person conceals but does not conceal the illumination; the egret standing in the snow is not the same color as it. "The illumination conceals but does not conceal the person; the bright moon among the reeds and flowers is not like that.

When both person and illumination are concealed, when everything is thoroughly understood, there is nothing further to be understood. When neither person nor illumination is concealed—*xuan, xuan, xuan*.

Even while dwelling [in the world], one must still reprove [delusion]. He spoke again: "Do you understand? With earnest devotion I sing this song of the profound mystery: can one grasp the moonlight within the void? Ascending the hall, he said:
"When a pure pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot help but become clear.

When mindfulness of the Buddha is directed toward a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot help but become the Buddha. Since the Buddha is not distracted, the turbid water naturally becomes clear. Once the turbid water has become clear..."
"Clear. "Where does the merit reside? After a long silence, he said: "How many times have black winds overturned the great ocean?

Yet I have never heard of a fishing boat capsizing. A monk asked: "What are the four great poisonous snakes? He replied: "Earth, water, fire, and wind. The monk said: "What are earth, water, fire, and wind?
He replied: "The four great poisonous snakes. The monk said: "I do not yet understand; I beg the Master for a skillful means. He replied: [Silence].
If one great element is thus, the four great elements are the same. Question: "The bow and arrow are in hand; the blade of wisdom faces the front line.
The dragon and tiger formations are complete; I request that you, Master, meet me. He said: "A defeated general is not executed. [The questioner] said:

"If that is so, then the bronze pillar stands near the marker by the Xiushui River, and the iron gate is high-locked at Fenghuang Peak. He said: "One does not stop until reaching the Wujiang River. [The questioner] said: "If that is the case..."
"Seven times captured, seven times released; the true command is fully upheld. He said, "Staring with eyes wide open inside a coffin.
A monk bowed, and the Master said, "Suffering! Suffering! A monk asked, "I have heard your words, Master:

'This old monk this summer cast three hundred and sixty fishing rods into the Yellow Dragon Pool, yet never encountered a single scaled fish with a crimson tail. Is it because the hook is not skillful?"
[The Master] asked, "Is it that the fragrant bait is difficult to find? [The monk] said, "After the rain, the bamboo wind is clear; when the clouds part, the mountain peaks are revealed.
[The Master] said, "If so, you have already received the good news of the True Man; there shall be no further doubt between the human realm and the heavens.

[The monk] said, "The hook-head is not subtle; the fragrant bait is difficult to find. [The Master] said, "To leave the body may still be easy, but to speak from the standpoint of total detachment is surely difficult. [The monk] said, "Chaos!"
"Zen practitioners are as numerous as hemp and millet. A question was asked: "What is Huanglong’s phrase for receiving people?
He replied: "Opening one's mouth to scold someone. The questioner said: "That which scolds is the phrase for receiving people; what about the phrase for testing people?

He replied: "Simply recognize the one who scolds. A question was asked: "What is 'first illuminating, then acting'? He replied: "The clear breeze brushes against the bright moon. The questioner said: "..."
"What is 'first action, then illumination'? He replied, "The bright moon brushes against the clear breeze. He asked, "What is 'illumination and action simultaneous'?
He replied, "The clear breeze and the bright moon. He asked, "What is 'illumination and action not simultaneous'? He replied, "Without the clear breeze, there is no bright moon.
He said, "If that is so, then the clear breeze of Longxiu cannot be hidden, yet the bright moon of Xian'an..."
Yong said: "The poor have no eminent man with gold to provide relief; the sick have only idle people to speak of medicinal prescriptions. In his room, he asked the monks:

"On the dark night of the last day of the month, if one were to apply five colors within the gloom and have hundreds of thousands of people look at those colors in the night, would any of them be able to distinguish blue, yellow, or white?
The monks were speechless. The Master spoke on their behalf, saying: "Every single one of them [sees it]."
He was blind. Again he asked the monk, "How do you understand the fundamental tenet of the Mahāyāna? The monk had no reply.

The Master said, "Suppose a dead man were to take a sharp blade in his hand, cut off the head of another dead man, and present it to me; I would immediately grant my approval to you. Such is this man.
As for his conduct, he went to the shrines of the Guanghua spirits and destroyed the sacrificial offerings of oxen and grain; he smashed the revolving sutra repository at Yunyan.

On the reverse side of the stele, it is recorded that Master Chen’s wife and children were cast down; the account of Jiyin’s hardships was brought about entirely by the Master’s effortless power (*anabhisamskāra*).
Consequently, the site of practice became solemn and pure, and the minds of Māras and heretics were transformed, such that they did not dare to even look upon its boundaries.
In the spring of the fifth year of the Zhenghe era, he happened to say to his attendant: "This year there is a matter of great significance that no one knows."

The multitude could not fathom this. On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month of that year, he went to the Zhaomo Hall to prepare a vegetarian feast for his Dharma-brother, Chan Master Linyuan Qing.

He then replied to letters from old friends, appending them with verses. That day, he conducted a tour of the quarters and gave a small *can* (sermon) at dusk, offering earnest exhortations to his disciples with words of profound depth.
He further spoke a gāthā, saying: "When speaking, it is all topsy-turvy; when silent, it is perfectly clear."
While remaining silent, he uttered "two" and "three. To report this to the Chan travelers of the Five Lakes: the Heart-King is sovereign; cease your inquiry.
On the fourteenth day, he went down to the Shí-bái (White Stone) manor. He personally inscribed his own name upon the pavilion, saying "An-xīn" (Peace of Mind), and wrote a record for the ridge.

He ate *harā* rice as usual. Having finished eating, he lay down to rest. At the hour of *bǔ* (noon), his attendants requested that he return. The Master said: "The great chiliocosm is my home; what [need is there to go]?"
Because he had returned [to his room], the assembly was clamorous with discussion, saying, "The Master lies there and does not rise; is he perhaps ill?

They summoned the physician-monk Huachong, who arrived intending to examine him. The Master rebuked him. Zanghui Xuan said, "When the Abbot reaches this point, you should instead exercise caution and self-reflection."

The Master said, "The marshy weeds of the river—do not confuse the Way. Having finished speaking, he sat in the lotus position and passed away. When his body was carried back to the Dharma Hall, it remained dignified and serene as if alive.

Three days later, he was placed in the coffin; nobles and commoners from near and far gazed upon him with choked voices and weeping. Reaching into his breast with their hands, they found his flesh and limbs still warm.
On the twenty-second day, his body was cremated, and the assembly obtained five-colored *śarīra*. After the snow had fallen, there were those who passed by [his remains].
The area where he was buried is particularly prominent. A stupa was erected to the north of Huìtáng’s meditation hall.
His secular age was seventy-two, and his years since ordination were forty-six.
Chan Master Lingyuan Weiqing of Huanglong Fushou in Longxing Prefecture was a native of Wuning in Nanzhou. His clan name was Chen.

When he was just a young child, he entered school and could recite a thousand words daily; his spirit was so clear and translucent that when he chanted, monks who heard him were struck by his extraordinary character.

Gazing at him intently, [Fengxue] said, "This child is a Dharma-boat for the ocean of suffering. He informed his parents of his intention to leave the household life, and they granted their permission.
He went to rely upon Master Jie; at the age of seventeen, he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*). He went to visit Chan Master An of Yanyen, who directed him to consult with Baojue.
When the Master arrived at Huanglong, although he lived and worked in harmony with the assembly, he was utterly at a loss when it came to answering questions. One day, while casually perusing...
Xuansha said, "When weary, one should practice walking meditation (caṅkrama). As he walked with short steps, he left his sandals behind; as he bent down to pick them up, he attained great awakening.

He informed Baojue of this, and Baojue said, "One who enters through conditions will never again fall back or lose what they have gained. Thereupon, eminent officials and veteran monks came to regard him as their teacher and friend.

He was repeatedly invited to visit famous mountains, but he resolutely refused. Only when Lord Zhu Jing, the Commissioner of Grain Transport for Huainan, earnestly requested him from Taiping in Shu, did he deign to accept.
Monastics and laypeople vied with one another to welcome him. He subsequently moved to Huanglong, where he ascended the hall and said:
"As soon as the drum sounds, the great assembly gathers like clouds; infinite celestial mechanisms are all at once revealed. To not fail the True Eye is precisely what one ought to do."
Return to the hall. To further indulge in verbose rhetoric would bury the essential principle. Even if one were to say that Śākyamuni did not appear in this world, yet preached for forty-nine years;

or that Bodhidharma did not come from the West, yet the Shaolin Monastery possesses a wondrous secret—Master Xiu’s situation is like looking toward one's hometown from ten thousand miles away. It is also said:
"If a person recognizes the Patriarchs and Buddhas, they transcend at that very spot. Even if you were to attain such an awakening...
"Go with kindness! There is yet another path for turning back. 'Having examined him, strike him! [With this, he struck the meditation seat once with his whisk and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. Through the eternal night and the clear evening, who else is there?
Mist, dew, clouds, and mists cannot conceal it. Within this, one still says, 'It is better to return. But to what would one return? The lotus leaves are round and full."
The ball is like a mirror; its rhombus corners are as sharp as awls. Entering the hall: The Buddhas of the three periods do not know existence—no gratitude for such profound kindness.
The cat and the white dog, however, do know existence—their merit is not bestowed in vain. They manifest great function and understand the great mechanism;
they leave no trace, inconceivable. It is good to go back; no one knows. He breaks through the azure void, where pines reach a thousand feet.
Severing the stream of the red dust world. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination.
Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and all will be transparently clear. The Patriarch speaking thus has blinded the eyes of people throughout the world.
How can a monk who recognizes right from wrong and distinguishes the black from the white discern the truth when he reaches this point? He has not yet been able to walk until the water runs out.

"Abiding in the place where it is difficult to understand, sit and watch as the clouds arise. Since the Master feigned illness to announce his retirement, he resided in the Jomok Hall for fifteen years.
He sat slumped in a single room, yet no one in the world could surpass his lofty character.
However, mindful that his followers had fallen into mere views and hearsay, he once said: "The reason why those who study today cannot transcend birth and death lies in their fundamental ailment..."
Where is it? It lies in the fact that the thieving mind has not yet died. However, this is not the fault of the student; rather, it is the fault of the teacher.
It is like the Han Emperor Gaozu, who deceived and killed Han Xin. Although it is said that Xin died, was his mind truly dead?

Where does the efficacy of the ancient students lie in attaining liberation from birth and death beneath a word? It lies in the fact that the thieving mind has already died. However, this is not due to the student’s own...

It is so. Truly, the master’s forge and hammer are subtle and profound. It is like Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, who, upon seeing Hou Jing in the imperial hall, did not move a muscle or utter a word;
yet the heart of Jing was already withered and drained of all vitality. Nevertheless, what has been said by various masters is not without its beauty.
One must understand that it is like the flowers painted by Zhao Chang—though they are lifelike, they are not real flowers. The ninth month of the seventh year of Zhenghe.
On the eighteenth day, after his meal, he closed the door of his quarters and summoned the head seat Yixi to speak of their parting.
He then rose for a bath, changed his robes, and touched the crown of his head with his finger. His attendant monk shaved his hair, and he sat upright, passing into stillness.

Ten days prior, he had composed the "Epitaph on True Return as Unborn and Ever-Abiding" and several hundred words of final instructions, admonishing that his remains be enshrined at Haihui Temple to manifest his birth.
"Even in death, one must not be separated from the community. His disciples dared not disobey this admonition and have faithfully upheld it. Thus says the Record.
Chan Master Shànqīng of Cǎotáng at Lètán in Lóngxìng Prefecture was a native of Bǎochāng in Nánxióng. His clan name was Hé. In his youth, he relied upon Fǎsī of Xiāngyún Monastery.
In the fourth year of the Yuánfēng era, he passed the scriptural examination and received full ordination. Initially, he visited Chán Master Zhé of Dàyuè.
The Master next went to Huítáng’s seat. Huítáng asked, “It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. What is it?
The Master stood there lost in thought. Huítáng struck him out. After a short while, he went again to request guidance. At that time, a cat was crouching nearby;

because of this, Huítáng said to the Master, “Do you see how that cat intends to pounce on a mouse? Its two eyes do not blink, its four paws are planted on the ground, and its head and tail are in a straight line.”
"Wherever you aim, there will be no miss. If you can truly be thus, with a mind free from distracting conditions, then the six sense faculties will naturally become still.

Investigate this in silent contemplation, and you will fail not once in ten thousand attempts. Thereupon, the Master completely swept away all his former scholastic learning. The Abbot of the Hall (Dongshan Liangjie) approved of him.
In the year Yiwu of the Zhenghe era (1115), he went forth to reside at Huanglong. Later, he dwelt at Mount Cao and Mount Shu, and subsequently moved to Letan.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Form and mind are not different; self and other are without distinction. Raising his whisk, he said:
"If you call this a whisk, you will enter hell like an arrow. If you do not call it a whisk, you have eyes but are as if blind.
Even if you manage to slip through both ends, you are still a black ox lying in stagnant water. Ascending the hall, he cited: Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, "The World-Honored One transmitted..."
Apart from the golden robe, what dharma was transmitted separately? Kāśyapa called out, “Ānanda! Ānanda responded, “Yes?

Kāśyapa said, “Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate. The Master said: “Before the banner-pole has even been thrown down, it pierces through the skulls of all people and replaces their eyes.
After the banner-pole has been thrown down, where will you see the Old Śākyamuni? Investigate! (End of scroll)
The Hall. Fayan said, "Recognizing the bench, it is more than sufficient all around. Yunmen said, "Recognizing the bench, heaven and earth are vastly different.
Xuedou said, "A vast marsh conceals the mountain; a wildcat can subdue a leopard. The Master said, "These three fellows all rely on external interpretations;
they have two divergent paths of clarity and obscurity and have not escaped the realm of seeing and hearing. They are like the moon in the water. Huanglong...
Not so. It fills the expanse of heaven and earth; it unfolds the sun and moon anew. Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "The profound waters are without waves; bubbles arise stirred by the wind.
When the wind ceases, the bubbles vanish; when the water is still, it reflects the void.

At this very moment, even if there were gold from Yan to fill the seas and mosquitoes to shake the mountains, the crimson-tailed golden-scaled fish would glide about in their own ease. Now, is there anyone who can discern the floating?"
"Sink! Gauge the depth of consciousness! Is this one who casts the line and hurls the hook? If such a person exists, come forth and meet me.
If not, then return for now to the base of the cliff and together watch when the moon is full. Ascending the hall, he raised the case:

Master Fushan Yuan said, "If you wish to obtain a true hero, you must first have the four requirements fully prepared; only then will the path of a patriarch be revealed. What are they? The first is..."

A man asked Master Nanquan, "In my home there is a piece of stone. I have sat upon it and I have lain upon it. I intend to carve it into a Buddha; would that be permissible?
Nanquan said, "It would be permissible. The man said, "Would it not also be impermissible? Nanquan said, "It would be impermissible.

The Master called to the assembly, saying, "One who acts as a good spiritual friend must possess clear discernment. Why is it that when another says 'it is permissible,' you say it is permissible, yet when he says 'it is impermissible,' you say it is impermissible?"
"Others cannot say it; they truly cannot say it. But do you know where Nanquan lands?
Baiyun will not spare his eyebrows to explain this through for you. Who is it that says 'it can be attained'? And who is it that says 'it cannot be attained'?
If you still do not understand, I, the old monk, shall provide you with a model. He then raised his hand and said, "Take the three realms and the two..."
The eighteen heavens form the Buddha’s crown; the golden wheel at the edge of the waters forms his feet;
the four great continents form his body. Although he has thus become a Buddha, where do you all establish yourselves and find your livelihood?
Has the assembly understood yet? The old monk shall now provide a second illustration. Take Pūrvavideha...
In the east, he becomes a Buddha; in Jambudvīpa, he becomes a Buddha; in Aparagoyānī, he becomes a Buddha; in Uttarakuru, he becomes a Buddha.
Grasses, trees, thickets, and forests are Buddhas; all wriggling and moving sentient beings are Buddhas.
Since this is so, what then do you call "sentient beings"? Do you understand yet? It is not as good as being bound and folded.
He returned those from Pūrvavideha to Pūrvavideha; he returned those from Jambudvīpa to Jambudvīpa;
he returned those from Aparagoyānī to Aparagoyānī; he returned those from Uttarakuru to Uttarakuru;
he returned grasses, trees, and forests to grasses, trees, and forests; and he transformed sentient beings and living creatures back into sentient beings and living creatures. This was because...
The Way. This is the abiding of phenomena in their place; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Since it is thus, what do you call "Buddha"? Do you understand?
Suddenly, if a man were to come forth and say, "White Cloud, cease your drowsy talk," everyone in the assembly should take note of this turning word.
A monk asked, "I have heard the Master’s words: 'Before the mountain lies a stretch of vacant land. Just as..."

"Before King Majestic Sound (Vaiśravaṇarāja), I do not know who was the master. [The Master] said, "Ask the person who wrote the contract. [The monk] said, "Why does the Master trouble someone else to answer for you?
[The Master] said, "It is precisely because you have instructed another to ask. [The monk] said, "I am leaving on equal terms with the Master.
[The Master] said, "That is a long way off. [The monk] asked, "What is the Buddha? [The Master] said, "The mouth is the gateway to calamity. Furthermore—
[The Master] said, "Fat enters through the mouth. [The student] asked, "The temporal teachings of a single lifetime are a 'cutting foot' (a homophonous pun).
I do not know which character it cuts. [The Master] said, "Pralāpa. [The student] said, "I only asked about one character; why did you answer with so much? [The Master] said, "..."
Seven characters, eight characters. [The monk] asked: "What is the matter of Linji? He replied: "The five heinous crimes hearing thunder.
[The monk] said: "What is the matter of Yunmen? He replied: "Red banners flashing. [The monk] said: "What is the matter of Caodong? He replied:
"A letter sent does not reach home. [The monk] said: "What is the matter of Guiyang? He replied: "A broken stele lies across the ancient road. The monk bowed.

He paid his respects. The Master said, "Why do you not ask about the affairs of the Fayan lineage? The monk said, "I shall leave that for the Master. The Master said, "A patrolman violating the curfew.
[The monk] asked, "What is the Master’s house style? He replied, "Iron banners and iron drums. [The monk] said, "Is there only this, or is there something else?
He replied, "Look at the stone-gathering ferry crossing. [The monk] said, "If a guest were to arrive suddenly, with what would you receive them? He replied, "With the same."
[The Master] said, "Dragon liver and phoenix marrow—wait for another time. [The Guest] said, "The guest is the host’s teacher. [The Master] said, "Thank you for your offering.
[The Guest] asked, "What is 'first illumination, then function'? [The Master] said, "The King’s words are like a fine thread.

[The Guest] asked, "What is 'first function, then illumination'? [The Master] said, "Their manifestation is like a thick cord. [The Guest] asked, "What is 'illumination and function simultaneous'? [The Master] said, "Lifting up [the mirror of] Xuanyuan."
Jian [said]: "Chiyou has suddenly lost his majesty. [The Master] asked: "What is 'illumination and function not occurring at the same time'?

He replied: "Gold is tested by fire. [The Master] asked: "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? He replied: "The great fool is not as good as the small fool. [The Master] said: "After he appeared in the world, how was it? He replied:
"The small fool is not as good as the great fool. [The Master] asked: "How was it when Niutou had not yet seen the Fourth Patriarch?"

[The Master] said, "On his head he wears a dangling ornament. [The monk] asked, "After seeing it, what then? [The Master] said, "A blue cloth covers his front. [The monk] asked, "Before he had seen it, why did the hundred birds bring flowers to offer him? [The Master] said, "Wealth and honor are what all people desire. [The monk] asked, "After he had seen it, why do they no longer bring flowers to offer him? [The Master] said, "Poverty and low status are what all people detest. [The monk] asked, "How is it? [The Master] said, "It is like a man who has lost his way. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has not yet lost their way? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has found the right path. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither lost nor found the way? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never set out on a journey. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has already returned from the journey? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has reached home. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has never left home? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never been away. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both left and returned? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has traveled back and forth. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither left nor returned? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never moved. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both moved and remained still? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both walked and stayed. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither moved nor remained still? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never acted. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both acted and refrained from acting? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both done and not done. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither acted nor refrained from acting? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never made a choice. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both chosen and not chosen? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both decided and not decided. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither chosen nor not chosen? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never made a resolution. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both resolved and not resolved? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both committed and not committed. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither resolved nor not resolved? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never made a vow. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both vowed and not vowed? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both pledged and not pledged. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither vowed nor not vowed? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never made a promise. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both promised and not promised? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both given his word and not given his word. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither promised nor not promised? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never spoken. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both spoken and remained silent? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both uttered words and kept them unspoken. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither spoken nor remained silent? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never uttered a sound. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both sounded and remained mute? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both made a noise and kept quiet. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither sounded nor remained mute? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never made a sound. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both made a sound and not made a sound? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both produced a tone and not produced a tone. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither made a sound nor not made a sound? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never produced a resonance. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both resonated and not resonated? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both vibrated and not vibrated. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither resonated nor not resonated? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never vibrated. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both vibrated and not vibrated? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both quivered and not quivered. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither vibrated nor not vibrated? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never stirred. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both stirred and not stirred? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both moved and remained unmoved. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither stirred nor not stirred? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never been agitated. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both been agitated and not been agitated? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both been disturbed and not been disturbed. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither been agitated nor not been agitated? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never been perturbed. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both been perturbed and not been perturbed? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both been shaken and not been shaken. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither been perturbed nor not been perturbed? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never been tossed about. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both been tossed about and not been tossed about? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both been whirled and not been whirled. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither been tossed about nor not been tossed about? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never been turned. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both turned and not turned? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both rotated and not rotated. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither turned nor not turned? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never revolved. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both revolved and not revolved? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both spun and not spun. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither revolved nor not revolved? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never whirled. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both whirled and not whirled? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both circled and not circled. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither whirled nor not whirled? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never turned in a circle. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both turned in a circle and not turned in a circle? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both completed a circuit and not completed a circuit. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither turned in a circle nor not turned in a circle? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never gone around. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both gone around and not gone around? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both traversed a path and not traversed a path. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither gone around nor not gone around? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never traveled. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has both traveled and not traveled? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has both journeyed and not journeyed. [The monk] asked, "What about one who has neither traveled nor not traveled? [The Master] said, "He is like a man who has never set
[The Master] said, "This is the Buddha. [The monk] asked, "What is the Dharma? He replied, "A general amnesty, with no one spared. [The monk] asked, "What is the Sangha?
He replied, "Saying thanks to Third Uncle on the fishing boat. [The monk] asked, "With no gates on any side and the mountain peaks so majestic, how can the seasons be distinguished within this?
He replied, "The Lord of Spring knows the details; sprouts and buds break forth everywhere. [The monk] said, "Spring has passed."
"The affairs of autumn have arrived just as they were before. [The Master] said, "As soon as you have finished rolling the ball, you must immediately grasp the Vajra.
One day, he asked his disciples, "How will you all carry on my school in the future? Fogian replied, "A variegated phoenix dances in the crimson heavens.
Foyan replied, "An iron snake lies across the ancient road. Foguo raised his foot and said, "Look at the kick! The Master said, "Excellent!"

He said, "The one who will extinguish my lineage is Keqin. On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month in the third year of the Chongning era, he ascended the hall to take leave of the assembly, saying:
"Venerable Master Zhaozhou had a final phrase. How do you understand it? Come forward and speak.
If you can understand it, you will be free and at ease; if not, how can you handle this fine matter?"
After a long silence, he said, "I have already finished speaking. It is simply that you do not understand. Do you wish to comprehend?

The wealthy lament that a thousand mouths are too few; the poor resent that a single body is too many. Take care. At that time, there was construction work involving earth and wood at the mountain gate.
He went in person to supervise it, saying, "Exert yourselves; I shall not come again. Upon returning to his quarters, he shaved his hair and bathed his body.
At dawn, he passed away with auspicious signs. That same evening, mountains collapsed and stones fell; for forty li within, the cliffs and valleys roared and shook.
Upon cremation, śarīras fell like rain. A stupa was erected to the south of Mount Dongshan. He was over eighty years of age.

The thirteenth-generation successor of Mount Nanyue (the ninth generation of Linji and second generation of Cuiyan), Chan Master Muduo Zhenru Muzhe of Daming Mountain, was succeeded by Chan Master Zhikai Puyong Daoping of Dongjing.
He was a native of Xiandu and belonged to the Xu clan. He had previously served as a disciple under Master Quan.
He possessed ten thousand scrolls. When Lord Jing invited him to reside at Jiangshan, the Master went with him and was appointed to oversee correspondence.
He then took his leave to visit Zhenru at Daming Mountain. Upon hearing the story of washing the alms bowl, he attained sudden enlightenment and composed a verse, saying:
"Seven topsy-turvy, eight upside-down, The karmic consciousness is in a frantic rush. When I turn my head toward Luojiang, I laugh until I kill Xie Sanlang. Zhao Bi and... [text continues]
The gold from Yan, the precious rings, and the jade pendants—lifting up the rabbit-horn hammer, he shattered them all at once.
As his interrogation was without flaw, his reputation thereafter spread in all directions. Later, he entered the monastic hall six times and received imperial edicts on four occasions.
He ascended the hall and said: "This mountain monk does not understand the Buddha-dharma; there is no basis for my acting on behalf of others. At times, I leave things half-open and half-closed."
At times, there is total release and total gathering. It is like dropping a cold stone from amidst a crowd of ten thousand people;
only when it suddenly strikes one does one realize that it flows everywhere. Ascending the hall, he said: "Zhaozhou has four gates, and gate after gate leads to the Great Road.
Yuyuan has four paths, and path after path leads to Chang’an. Gate after gate leads to the Great Road—after all..."
"Who has personally arrived? The road leads through Chang'an; look clearly as you take a step forward. [He] pats his knee once and says:
"The traveler who has not yet returned at year's end finds the cold outside the West Phoenix Gate. [He] ascends the hall and cites: "Panshan addressed the assembly, saying:
'Like the earth supporting a mountain, one does not know the mountain’s towering loftiness; like a stone containing jade, one does not know the jade’s flawlessness. The ancients were thus..."
"What kind of talk is this? It is very much like embracing a thief and crying out for injustice. Under Puyong’s gate, every person is resolute and spirited;
they capture tigers and oxen alive and seize fierce dragons in their hands. They can accommodate Mount Sumeru in their eyes and the great ocean waters in their ears.
He then took up his staff and said, "This is not to boast of one's own skills to others; the bearing of a true man of spirit ought to be thus. He struck the ground with the staff.
He took up his staff and descended from his seat. At the beginning of the Jingkang era, he retired from his duties and returned to Bazi Mountain in Huangzhou.
On the second day of the tenth month of the first year of the Jianyan era, he manifested his passing.
Chan Master Letan Jixiang of Longxing Prefecture was a native of Nancheng, Jianchang. His clan name was Fu;

his father, Yu, served as the Magistrate of Yongfeng, and his mother was Lady Shangguan. Her dream was of crimson banners and black streamers surrounding a magnificent man who called himself the General of the Frontier.
When he was subsequently born, she named him Segong (The Frontier Lord) accordingly. Upon reaching adulthood, he was alert and quick-witted, possessing a powerful memory.
He was widely learned. He often dreamed at night that he was stabbing a person with a knife. One day, while asleep, a divine being bestowed a verse upon him; thereafter, he no longer had such dreams.
When Yongfeng passed away, he remembered him with boundless grief, feeling that nothing short of the supramundane Dharma could repay his debt.

Hearing that Chan Master Qi was preaching the Dharma at Lingjiu, he went to listen. Upon hearing it, he suddenly attained realization and enlightenment. He followed Qi to shave his head and receive the precepts.
He traveled to distant regions and reached Dayue (Daguang). After a long time, he attained enlightenment and remained there daily to serve [the master], exhausting his skillful means.
Once Dayue had passed into nirvana, he returned to live in seclusion at Linchuan. Ten years later, various monasteries invited him to reside there, but he generally did not accept.

In the fourth year of the Daguan era, as the seat at Letan happened to be vacant, the provincial governor extended three invitations with letters and gifts; having no choice, he finally accepted the summons.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an example: "Master Jingqing addressed the assembly, saying: 'If one acts according to the current order, the old barbarian with blue eyes cannot escape fault.
If one were to carry out the order to its ultimate conclusion, it would be necessary to close the gates of the monks' hall and hire someone else to guard the monastery.
At that time, a monk asked: 'What is it like when the order is carried out to its ultimate conclusion? He replied: 'Do you wish to disperse the assembly? The Master said: [The Master then spoke].
Today Bao Feng brings up this story; do not touch it. Leave it for the various quarters to examine. On the Festival Day, he ascended the hall and said:
"The world says that the Way of the superior man flourishes while the Way of the petty man wanes. Where does that which wanes go? From where does that which flourishes come? Therefore it is said:
if one says it exists, there is no thing to be maintained; if one says it does not exist, it is touched upon [by all]."
It accords with the myriad paths. If one says it is new, it is an ancient cause from time immemorial; if one says it is old, no thing can defile it.

Therefore, when among birds, it joins the birds’ song; when among beasts, it joins the beasts’ cry; in heaven, it is one with heaven; among humans, it is one with humanity. Then, picking up his staff, he said:
"Tell me, what is it that you share here? After a long silence, he said: "The Patriarchal Hall transmits the practice of rectitude."
The edict: "Let the sprouts of reeds be pulled up, covering the ground in spring. Ascending the hall on the Mid-Autumn Festival:

The talk at Vulture Peak, the pointing at Caoxi—letting pass the one who chops his forehead upon first birth. Before even asking the old, ancient spike of Longmen: Last night at the third watch, he turned toward the west.
At such a time as this, if someone were to ask, "What is the moon when brightness and darkness have not yet been distinguished?
if you can utter a single phrase, you will join hands with the ancients. If you have not yet reached this state, Bao Feng cannot help but follow the model and provide a response for the occasion.
He then drew a circle and said: "Its pure radiance endures through ten thousand ages, and again through ten thousand ages."
How could it be seen for but a single night among men? A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
He replied, "Of ten fingers, eight are missing. [The monk] asked, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? He said, "It is difficult to distinguish gold from brass. [The monk] said, "..."
[The Master] asked, "How are my feet like a donkey's feet? [The monk] said, "The road of Huanglong is perilous. [The Master] said, "Every person has their own karmic affinity (*jìngyuán*).
What is the Master’s karmic affinity? [The Master] said, "I firmly guard the critical pass; neither ordinary people nor sages are permitted passage. In his private quarters, he questioned a monk:
"When Bodhidharma returned to the West, he carried a single sandal in his hand. Why did he not take both at that time? [The monk] said, "This land [also has its own]."
He intended to leave behind a message, saying: "One foot is in the Western Heaven; one foot is on this Eastern soil.
For what reason? The monk was speechless. The Master asked a monk: "The single, solid, and dense body manifests within all dust. What is the body that manifests within the dust?
The monk pointed to the incense burner and said, "This is the incense burner. The Master said, "You have brought trouble upon yourself."

"The Buddhas of the three periods of time have all fallen into hell. The monk was at a loss for what to do, and the Master struck him. He then asked another monk, "The cloth bag is opened wide in the midst of the marketplace;
how do you understand this? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "If it is an iron cauldron, just call it an iron cauldron. If it is wooden sandals, just call them wooden sandals.
You have let the opportunity pass right before your eyes—the celestial palace of Maitreya. What kind of filth are you looking for? Thereupon, he pushed the monk out.
The Master did not feel well while traveling. A monk asked, "How is the Master’s health these days? He replied, "I have burned two sheets of paper before the local deity.

The Master often sat in meditation at night with his hands crossed, as if facing a great guest. When he first sat down, his hands were joined at his knees; by the fifth watch, they would invariably reach his chest.
Consequently, he was called "Xiang Chashou" (Auspicious Crossed-Hands). His solemnity was such as this. At the beginning of the Jianyan era...
Carrying his staff, he traveled to Mount Tiantai. The Prefectural Governor reported this to the Imperial Court, and by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Fushan.

On the seventh day of the tenth month in the second year of the Shaoxing era, he gathered the assembly to bid them farewell. When an attendant monk requested a verse, the Master said, "Fortunately, there is neither coming nor going;
what need is there for a verse? He then sat cross-legged and passed away. After the cremation, his eyes, teeth, and tongue remained unburnt, and five-colored *śarīra* were recovered.
His disciples divided the stupa between Fushan and Letan.

On the day when Chan Master Renxian of Dongming in Tanzhou opened the hall for formal discourse, a monk asked, "When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, Brahma King led the way in front and Indra followed behind;
when you, Master, appear in the world, what auspicious signs are there? He replied, "Even were there hundreds of thousands of..."
The Buddha once drove [the ox] toward the water-buffalo pen and asked, "What auspicious signs are there? [The ox] replied, "This mountain monk’s eyes have not grown dim.
Master Zhengjue Zizun of Donglin on Mount Lu ascended the hall and said: "Before the fifteenth day, let it loose..."
"One move has passed. After the fifteenth day, it cannot yet be discussed. It is precisely on the fifteenth day; try and speak a single phrase. After a long silence, he said:
"The mountain colors are lush and verdant as the spring rain ceases; fragrant clouds gather in the cypress courtyard as the *mulan* blossoms open."
Chan Master Wuxiao Qin of Sizhou Puzhao Temple ascended the hall and said: "Reaching out a hand to grasp at emptiness—turning back and forth, one can never catch up.
Flipping over to cast off one's shadow—is this merely to weary one's own body? When something is brought forward right before one's face, it is nonetheless missed. After all, how is it?
He struck the meditation seat and said, "In the end, it was a mistake to deliberate upon it. A monk asked: "Whose song does the Master sing? What is the lineage?"
"Whose successor is the Wind? He replied, "Even closer to the east than the east. [The Master] said, "He is the son of Guishan and the direct grandson of Zhihai.
[The Master] added, "He laughs at bystanders who hold fishing rods."
Chan Master Huilan of Kuangxiao Temple in Hezhou was a man of unknown origins. He styled himself the "Man of the Azure Void" (Biluo Daoren).
He once wrote the names of the Seven Buddhas upon his undergarments; thus, the monastic community referred to him as "Lan the Undergarment-Wearer.

One day, he composed the "Song of the Thatched Hut" to instruct the assembly, its lyrics as follows: "I have built this hut, yet it is not a worldly treasure; My entire being is but grass of non-arising."
The original foundation is level and even; in the four quarters and above and below, there is no boundary or limit. The person within this hermitage neither undergoes birth nor old age;

their wondrous function extends in all directions without effort or fabrication. It is neither a village nor a city, nor is it a deep mountain; the passing of summer and the arrival of winter do not reach it.
If you ask where this hermitage is located, grasp it well before your parents were born. If the mechanism of a flashing bolt has not yet been seized—

Divided! Piercing through clouds and ascending ridges, you have instead brought about mutual delusion. What face do you have, you who dwell in mountain huts? When the primordial chaos first divided, it was capable of such intricate detail;
at that moment, a single stroke was too distinct. Unable to understand, you continue as before to strike the tiles for divination.

Some say it is great: it is casually gathered within the realm of a needle’s point. Some say it is small: the myriad phenomena are universally stamped upon the tip of a single hair. Some say it is noble: it is encountered face-to-face.
When pointing it out, there is nothing to show. Some say it is base; yet ten-thousand-bushel pearls of the black dragon can never be exchanged for it.

Some say it is manifest; even the *śakrāloka* eye finds it difficult to behold. Some say it is hidden; yet it fills the void, its light blazing brightly. If you wish to know the person who was formerly within the hermitage, the entire trichiliocosm of dust-motes has utterly perished.
At the end of the Jianyan era, when the rebel invaders breached the Huai River, they captured the Master and presented him before their chieftain.
The official Chang said, "Do you hear my name? The Master replied, "All I hear is the name of the Great Song Emperor.

Chang became enraged and ordered his attendants to strike him with a hammer; yet every time the hammer reached him, it broke into pieces. Chang was struck with wonder and invited him under his command to serve him with reverence.
After ten days had passed, the Master sought firewood to immolate himself, but no one dared to provide it. He personally gathered the wood and constructed a niche for his own cremation.

He sat upright with a serene expression. As smoke and flames rose together, radiant light surged forth in all directions. The barbarian knelt and prostrated himself; many had their skin scorched by the fire.

When the blaze subsided, he obtained five-colored *śarīra* relics, which he took along with the bones and returned north. All the monks and nuns he had been holding were then allowed to go their own way.
People have been chanting this to this day.
A monk asked Chan Master Huixiao of Guangxiao Temple in Jizhou, "If one can turn things around, one is equal to the Tathāgata.
The pillar is a thing; please, Master, turn it. He replied, "I will not let the falling flowers drift away with the water. The monk asked, "Why is it like this?"
This [is said]: "I fear that it might cause ordinary guests to enter the mountains.
Chan Master Fuyan Zhi of Tanzhou ascended the hall and said: "The clouds upon Mount Chanyan unfurl and roll up at will with the coming and going of dawn and dusk.
Suddenly they fall onto level ground; when a guest arrives, it is difficult to find the gate. He then ascended the hall and cited: Zhaozhou asked a monk, "Recently..."

Chan Master Haiyin Zhizue of Xiangyan in Dengzhou was a man of unknown origins. Having long studied under masters and attained realization, he profoundly understood the source of the Dharma.
He left the capital to reside at Jianfu Monastery in Yingzhou, and in the third year of the Shaosheng era, he moved to Xiangyan.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The Minister of Personnel, Prefectural Governor, has this day commanded this mountain monk to open the hall to offer prayers for the Emperor and to continue the ancestral lamp.
But how is the ancestral lamp to be continued? Have you not seen what the ancients said: 'In the six streets, the bells and drums resound with a deep thud;
this very place is a world spread in gold. The ponds grow lotuses, the courtyards grow cypresses—what further dharma could there be? "
To expound the True School in such a manner is also because there is no other way.
Should someone who cannot tolerate this come forward, pull the mountain monk down from his meditation seat, and give him a severe beating, only then may he be recognized as a monk of true standing.
If you have not yet attained such mastery, do not act with haste or superficiality; you must examine the very foundation of your own feet.
"You have not truly gone where you were heading; you must instead turn around and eat the handle of the spade from Jianfu’s own hand. Do not say I did not tell you.

A monk asked, "The Dharma-thunder has already resounded and the field for selecting Buddhas has opened. Since you are not ignorant of the fundamental vehicle, I pray that the Master will point directly. He replied:

the immortal flowers of the Awakened Garden bloom overnight. He said: "Be careful not to follow after them."
Chan Master Baoyue Jueren of Ba’en Monastery in Changzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jinshan Zhijue Fahui.
He was the son of the Zheng family from Sheng County in Yue. Once, he ascended the hall and said:
"Students who engage in empty talk without substance must seek wondrous awakening. To abandon wondrous awakening for empty talk is like..."
This is merely a case of chasing after stench. Nevertheless, although it is so, those who have their ears pierced are rarely encountered, while those who mark the boat are frequently met.

On the first day of the fifth month in the sixth year of the Xiangxing era, he exhorted his disciples, saying: "Worldly conditions are easily stained; the work of the Way is difficult to accomplish. You must all exert yourselves."
Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Chan Master Chongxin Changlu Jingzhao was the dharma successor of Chan Master Cishou Huishen of Huiyin Monastery in Dongjing. He was a native of Li'an in Shouchun. His clan was Xia. From birth...
Auspicious light appeared over the dwelling. When Chan Master Wen-shu Xing-jian saw it from afar, he suspected it was a fire; upon closer inspection, he learned that the Master had just been born.
Jian sighed and said, "This is no ordinary child. He went to visit him, but as soon as the Master saw Jian, he laughed. The mother, Lady Zhang, consented to his renunciation of the world.
At fourteen, he severed his attachments, donned the crown, and shaved his head. Four years later, he went abroad to seek the Way. At the beginning of the Chongning era, he went to Jia...
Heo. Relying on Jingzhao at Zifeng Temple, he was appointed as the head of the assembly. Jingzhao raised the kōan concerning the encounter between Liangsui and Magu, asking:
"What is the place where Liangsui knows? The Master immediately understood it with complete clarity. When Jingzhao moved to Changlu, he summoned the Master to lead the community.
In the early Zhenghe era, Ji Gongfu, the Governor of Yizhen from the Ministry of Personnel, invited the Master to Zifu Temple south of the city; his shoes were piled outside the door. At Jiangshan...
When Chan Master Fojian Qin was traveling along the river to propagate the Dharma, he encountered him. After the tea ceremony concluded, the Master led him on a tour of the quarters.
Upon reaching the section for the thousand-monk community, Fojian asked, "Since this is the section for the thousand-monk community, why is there only one person here?

The Master replied, "Much emptiness is not as good as little reality. Fojian said, "Is that so? The Master was abashed. It happened that the Imperial Court [had recently] appointed [him] to Zifu Temple.

He served at the Shenxiao Palace and subsequently went to Mount Jiang, where he stayed at Xianan. Chen requested further instruction, and Yanjian said, "Zifu, when you understand such matters, you should simply let them be.

Chen replied, "I am truly not yet at ease; I hope the Master will not reject me. Yanjian brought up the story of the "Clever Woman’s Separated Souls" and examined it with him repeatedly until his doubts and obstacles were completely cleared away.
Chen presented a verse, saying: "It is merely the place where one travels with one's old belongings."
"Carelessly mentioning it, one immediately distorts it. Last night a gale arose, blowing down how many peach blossoms?
As he spoke, Xuedou struck the table. "Is this not the living meaning of the Patriarch? Not long after, by imperial decree he resided at Mount Jiao for four years;
then, by imperial edict, he was appointed to head Huilin Temple. When the Jingkang era began, he requested to return home, but his request was not granted. In the autumn, [he was summoned] again.
He declined the offer, but eventually accepted. He went directly to the Stone Bridge on Mount Tiantai, and later moved to Lingyan.

After some time, by imperial decree, he was appointed to Jiangshan. Within a few months, he retired to Baoshan on Lake Dongting. Subsequently, responding to the invitation of the Wang family, he became the first patriarch of the *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuánjué) school.
Entering the hall, he said: "It is neither the environment, nor is it the mind; even when called 'Buddha,' it remains submerged in the mud. This one—
The Middle Way is inherently without gradations; one must strictly avoid seeking within that which is without gradations. To seek at all is an even deeper error.
Only by shattering Yunmen’s "rice-bag" can one realize that red earth is gold. Ascending the hall, he said: "The ancients said, 'Endurance.'"
"Endure! The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have all emerged from this. Abound! Abound! Myriad calamities and a thousand misfortunes are all extinguished from this.
Be silent! Be silent! Unsurpassed Bodhi is attained from this. The Master said: "Once you have understood these three kinds of words, you will be a truly lively fellow.
This mountain monk simply takes an ox from one person and gives a horse back to another; he splashes water and spits in return, and thrusts his snout to meet the other's."
He scolded them. Holding up his staff, he said, "Come forth! Come forth! He ascended the hall and said, "From which mountain does the cloud arise?
From what ravine does the wind spring? What a fine point of entry! Yet on the royal road, few people travel.

He ascended the hall and said, "In the past, there was a man who obtained a piece of iron and cast it into a set of sounding blocks. When people heard them, they immediately felt a sense of pleasure; this is what is called 'joy'."
A musical instrument. Later, he had a *fangxiang* (square-sounding gong) melted down to cast a single *qing* (stone chime). When people heard it, they immediately gave rise to wholesome thoughts.
After that, because someone was going off to war, he had the *qing* recast into a single sword. When people saw it, they were struck with terror. At a later time...
Furthermore, he once cast a sword into the form of a Buddha statue. When people saw it, they immediately felt a sense of devotion and turned toward it with faith.
O virtuous ones, fundamentally it was merely a single piece of iron; for what reason did it give rise to such a multitude of thoughts—of wonder, joy, goodness, and evil?
Consider this carefully. A monk asked, "What kind of person is not swallowed by impermanence? The Master replied, "I only fear that he has no place for the jaws to enter."
[The student] said, "If so, then with a single thought one penetrates the profound mystery, and the three *śi* demons lose their guile.

[Dongshan] said, "You have a 'single thought'; you will surely be swallowed up by it. [The student] asked, "What is it like when there is no single thought? [Dongshan] said, "I have caught you, Master.

[The student] asked, "When one knows the Way but cannot express it, what then? [Dongshan] said, "A mute person eating honey. [The student] asked, "When one can express it but does not know it, what then? [Dongshan] said, "A deaf person listening to music."
"What? [The monk] said, "A parrot calling out to people. The monk bowed. The Master rebuked him, saying, "You messenger of words!
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? He replied, "A yellow face is not true gold-plating. The monk asked, "What is that which is above the Buddha?
He replied, "One arrow, one lotus. The monk bowed. The Master snapped his fingers three times. On the full moon of the fourth month in the second year of the Xiangshu era, for...
In a general informal discourse (*sō-sam*), a monk asked about the "final phrase. The Master remained silent for a long while and said, "Look after five days.

On the twentieth day, he indeed manifested a slight illness and finally passed away. He was fifty-six years of age and thirty-six years since his ordination. His remains were cremated according to the precepts.

The light was divided into five colors, and countless śarīra were obtained. At the places where the smoke reached—among the bamboo, stones, grasses, and trees—they appeared in clusters like strung pearls.
Even when digging pits into the earth with a spade, they were found there as well. The relic bone stūpas were distributed to Xianqing on Mount Bao and Yuanjue on Mount Sichui.
Chan Master Zhengwu Rugui of Guangxiao Temple in Pingjiang Prefecture was the son of the Wei family of Jianning.

On the day he ascended the hall, a monk asked, "What is the scenery of the Suzhou Terrace? He replied, "The mountains stand tall and majestic like lions; the waters connect with the clarity of Lake Tai. Thus it is said.
"What is it like to be a person within the realm? He replied, "After the imperial robes of the Great Song, before the rites and music of the Great Zhou.
Whenever the Master saw a monk, he would invariably ask, "How have you been lately? When the monk was about to respond, the Master would pat him on the back and say, "Inconceivable!"
When he was about to pass away, the assembly gathered, and he spoke again: "Inconceivable. He then joined his palms and passed away.
Regarding Chan Master Tianyi Ruzhe of Shaoxing Prefecture, his clan and origins are unknown. After retiring from his monastic seat, he resided at Wanshou Monastery in Pingjiang.
He ate and drank without discrimination, and many people mocked him. Someone asked him about the saying of Ruiyan: "Call out the Host."
The Master replied with a verse: "Ruian constantly calls out to the Host; / He stands out prominently atop the highest peak of Mount Sumeru.
/ The great earth is overturned and nowhere can he be found; / A single melody of flute and song resounds within the painted tower. One day, he said, "I am going."
He ordered his bamboo sedan chair to be wiped clean, then wrote a verse to address the assembly, saying: "The Way lies in the place of action;
the Way is applied in the face of death. People of this age merely crave pleasure and delight, refusing to study non-action.
Having recounted his past inquiries and exhorting the assembly to advance in their cultivation, he suddenly raised his fist and asked, "Tell me, everyone, where does this fall? The assembly—
Wu-dui. The Master struck the desk once and said, "I entrust everything all at once to the autumn wind. He then entered his sedan chair, sat upright, and passed away.
This was the twenty-third day of the eighth month of the Gengchen year of the Shaoxing era. On the day of the cremation, the entire prefecture brought incense and firewood;
those who escorted him crowded the roads. As the Master’s body began to move, everyone claimed he had returned to life.
Chan Master Zhizhe Fhuan of Wuzhou ascended the hall and said: "To strike the profound pivot, one must possess integrity and be utterly resolute;

The Master replied, "Sitting for too long becomes weary. The monk asked, "And what was it like after he saw him? The Master said, "It does not hinder me from walking east or west."
Chan Master Weishang of Guangfu Temple in Yanguan, Lin’an Prefecture, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jueyin Ziying of Baoning.

[Zhimen] said, "It must be Nanquan who can do it. Yinzhi then cross-examined him with the previous words, but the Master was unable to respond.
Upon returning to the Sangha Hall, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and said, "The ancients said, 'From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks of the world.
Now I truly believe this. He presented a verse to Yinzhi, saying: "It must be Nanquan’s foremost pivot; I did not know..."
"Unawares, a spike pierces the head. If you do not have the 'blue and white eyes' [discernment] when facing him directly, it will be like a *gàn-niǎo* bird guarding an empty pond.

If not, it shall remain leaning idly by the side of the meditation seat, leaving it for descendants to point out the way.

Lun said: "A thousand rivers share one moon; ten thousand households all encounter spring. Yun said: "Where the Wheel of Dharma turns, those who attain it all know;
when sandalwood is burned, the fragrant breeze pervades the earth. Lun said: "Hanshan claps his hands; Shide laughs 'he-he'."

Twisting the nostrils upward and pressing down the clouds, Heyuan knew how to beat the drum of Yanguan, and Wu Daozi did not paint the oxen of Dai Song. Mount Lu..."
Lingmi’s rice; Touzi’s oil; Xuefeng continues as before to roll his twin balls. Last night the wind brought news from Hengyang:

Linji suddenly took up his staff, called to the assembly, and said, "Now tell me, what excellence does Daowei have over Linji?

He struck the ground once with the staff and let out a shout, saying: "Having experienced the great ocean, one need not boast of its waters; were it not for Mount Sumeru, there would be no mountains. He ascended the hall and said:
To cast aside delusion in search of enlightenment is to fail to realize that delusion is the very hammer and tongs of enlightenment. To love the holy and hate the ordinary...

Not knowing that this is the forge of both the holy and the ordinary—when the holy and the ordinary are both extinguished and delusion and enlightenment are both forgotten—how do you speak this one phrase?
"At midnight, colored clouds enshroud the jade image; at daybreak, five-colored clouds veil the mountain peak.

He replied, "If you have a horse, ride it; if you have no horse, walk. [The monk] said, "What about the matter on the road? He replied, "It is humble."
Avoiding the Noble.

Chan Master Shishuang Fachong of Tanzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Xueling Jiashan.
