The Emperor summoned him and asked, "In the past, the [scriptures brought by] Kāśyapa-Matanga were not burned; why are they burned now? The monk had no reply. (Mingjue would have replied on his behalf: "Your Majesty has not forgotten the entrustment.")
The Emperor once dreamed that a divine being informed him, "I request Your Majesty to give rise to the bodhicitta.

Consequently, at the early court audience, he inquired of his attendants, "How does one give rise to the bodhicitta? None of the attendants could respond. (On behalf of Mingjue, I would have replied: "Truly, it is something rarely heard of in antiquity or today."
National Teacher Zhiji presented a diagram of the Three Realms to the Emperor. The Emperor asked, "In which realm do I reside? Zhiji had no reply.
(Chan Master Renyong of Baoning once offered a reply on his behalf, saying: "Your Majesty, where is there that you are not honored as the Sovereign?

One day, after the court session had ended, he held up his alms bowl and asked Prime Minister Wang Sui, "Since it cannot be lifted at the head of Dayu Ridge, why is it now in Your Majesty's hand? Wang Sui had no answer.

When asked this, Chan Master Ciming Chuyuan later replied on behalf of the Emperor, "Your Majesty possesses great strength. Chan Master Baiyun then commented, "Tell me, does he have strength in his wrists, or does he have strength to rule the world? Please try to decide for me."
Since the True Sect Emperor ascended the throne, he has perused the scriptures of the Buddha and explored the profound mysteries of the Patriarchal Teachings.
He attained clear realization of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and once composed a verse, which says: "Silent and still is the great void, Profoundly deep like autumn waters.

Wiped clean, it is originally without dust; It belongs to none—Zhang, Wang, or Li. Consequently, he established the Zhikai Monastery (Zhizhai), which stands magnificent as the preeminent temple in the capital.

The Emperor issued a decree to widely summon Chan practitioners. He dispatched an imperial edict to invite Chan Master Benyi of Zhengjue Temple to preside over the event. When Benyi arrived and was summoned for an audience, his responses accorded with the Imperial will.

The Emperor granted him the previous verse to be composed in response. After Benyi had expressed his gratitude for the favor, he divided it into four chapters. The first says: In the profound stillness of the great void, Who can penetrate this principle?
Originally there is not a single thing; Buddhas and patriarchs have forever left their traces hidden. The second says: [omitted] The third says: [omitted] The fourth says: [omitted]
The first said: "Profoundly still like autumn waters—whom can this mind be entrusted to? Only those who have realized emptiness; when they meet, they merely snap their fingers. The second said:
"Wiped clean, it is originally free of dust—a single wheel of the moon in the blue sky. Majestic and without obstruction, the body of the Dharma King is fully revealed.
The third said: "It does not belong to the Zhangs, Wangs, or Lis; from the beginning, it has been one's own ground. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—"
"Throughout his entire being, there is nothing that is not [the Buddha-nature]. The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him the title "Zhengjue" (Right Enlightenment).
Emperor Renzong governed the world with a Buddha-mind; as the kings of the four quarters came to court, he desired to promote the Buddhist teachings.

Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued for the monk Huailian to enter the private audience hall. He was commanded to ascend the seat and, having pleased the Emperor, was granted the title Chan Master Dajue.
The Emperor composed twenty additional poems and two pieces of instructional discourse in praise of him.
Lian once presented a verse containing a "perfect circle" (yuanxiang). The Emperor consequently composed two stanzas in praise and bestowed them upon Lian, saying:
"I now behold that the Elder of Jingyin has depicted a perfect circle within his Chan verse. This [circle] is possessed by every person;
save for those of dull faculties and inferior intellect who do not understand the place within where there is no arrangement and no nostrils. Hehe! Yet there is another layer."
I, An Di, with my meager learning and shallow understanding, venture to compose this one verse. First: "The means of guidance is originally beyond words;

appearing and disappearing, it comes and goes as it pleases. There is fundamentally no place of increase or decrease; it is simply like the full autumn moon. Second: "In my ignorance and delusion, I understand nothing at all."
The supreme sages are ultimately difficult to know. Thirty years later, another layer was added, and I ordered Yuanlian to provide a commentary.
Once Yuanlian had finished his notes, he presented three verses and requested to retire to the forest. The Emperor annotated one of Yuanlian’s verses and further issued a decree, saying:
"The mountain is the very substance of suchness; where could he go? Order him to reside once more in the capital and promote the Buddha-dharma."

Falin offered this verse: "Thousand clusters of cloud-covered mountains, ten thousand valleys of flowing streams; I turn my heart toward the Buddha-dharma to spend my final years upon this mountain peak. The Emperor said: "The Buddha-dharma is vast and great; it is not merely these valleys and peaks.
Return your heart to it to grow old upon this mountain peak. The Emperor said: "Not only upon the mountain peak—be even more discerning and meticulous."
"Do not err. Morning and evening, simply pray that Yao may have long life. The Emperor said, "But all living beings share the same longevity as Heaven.
"A single incense stick of sandalwood smoke fills the stone tower. The Emperor said, "Throughout the entire Dharma realm, the white smoke and ashes have subsided."

Lian further presented two verses in expression of gratitude, one of which said: The Imperial Messenger transmits the decree from the inner palace, Commanding me once more to dwell here within these Zen gates.
The green mountains refuse to conceal my thousand follies; With white hair, what can I offer to assist in the myriad affairs of state?
The grace of the imperial favor is as deep and vast as the dew upon the heavens; My affection for the forest streams is bitter and lingering. O, the benevolence of Yao!
How much more so when it is as vast as the sky; one should simply allow the solitary cloud to fly at its own will.

On the twentieth day, [the Emperor] bestowed a silk fan upon him, inscribing Yuanji’s verse upon it. He had also once composed the "Verse on Cultivating the Mind," which says: "The First Patriarch sat in meditation at Shaolin;
he did not transmit scriptures or teachings, but transmitted only the mind. If later generations awaken to the nature of True Suchness, the secret intent..."
The profound principle of his coming was subtle and deep. In the spring of the following year, Bao-lian firmly declined [the appointment].
The Emperor followed his request and specially bestowed upon him one scroll of the Imperial Portrait to demonstrate His intention not to forget him.
At the beginning of Emperor Huizong’s reign, he applied his mind to the profound mysteries of Chan.
He issued an edict appointing Chan Master Fuyong Daokai to preside over Fayun Temple and inquired of him regarding the essentials of the school.

Two years later, in the fourth month of summer in the third year of the Zhenghe era, Chan Master Foguo Weibai submitted the thirty-fascicle *Zongmen Xudeng Lu* (Continued Lamp Record of the Chan School) which he had compiled; the Emperor bestowed a preface upon it.
In the month of Jia, there was a great tree by the roadside in Dazu (formerly known as Jiagzhou) that had been toppled by wind and thunder.

Within it sat a monk in meditative equipoise, his beard and hair covering his body and his fingernails encircling him. The local administration reported the matter in detail to the throne, and by imperial decree, he was invited to the capital to receive offerings.
At that time, the Indian master Dharmadhara (Zongchi) emerged him from his samādhi using a golden gong and asked, "In what era do you belong? The monk replied, "I..."
[He was] the younger brother of Dharma Master Huiyuan of Donglin. Because he traveled to Mount Emei, the era is not recorded. [The monk asked: "Is Dharma Master Huiyuan still alive?
Sengchi said, "Dharma Master Huiyuan was a person of the Jin dynasty; seven hundred years have passed since his passing. Thereupon, [the monk] ceased speaking further. Sengchi said:
The Master asked, "Where do you wish to return? He replied, "To Chenliu County. Thereupon, he entered meditative absorption once more.

The Emperor ordered his portrait to be painted and distributed throughout the realm, and also composed three verses for him. The first says: "The ancient adept of seven hundred years past— Who could know the news from within his samādhi?
How can this compare to departing westward in a single shoe? Birth and death are but vain labor; wood serves as his skin. The second says: "The Treasury..."
Mountains conceal themselves within the marshes; throughout the world, there is no path of concealment by which one may be approached. Send word to Zhuang Zhou: cease your deliberations.
It is not the person who carries the burden walking among the trees. Third: The sentient body is not insentient; for everyone, both here and there, it is the body within meditative concentration.
If you understand that Bodhi originally has no tree, there is no need to toil in asking Lu Neng.
Emperor Gaozong, having pacified the realm through his divine martial prowess, found the Three Teachings to be of one accord;

he especially took refuge in the Way of Shaolin. During his time as the Hidden Dragon (before ascending the throne), he dispatched his attendant Han Zhiyi to Tianning Monastery and commanded the presiding monk, Chan Master Foguo Keqin, to ascend the hall.
Keqin took his seat and recited two verses of gāthā, beginning with: "Virtuous causes..."
It summons virtuous fruits. Sowing grain does not produce beans; those of great merit practice it, and those of great merit receive it.
The eighty-four thousand *pāramitās* have already been perfected upon the tip of a single hair; they are realized beneath the staff and under the shout.
Treading with lofty steps upon the crown of Vairocana—this was on the twenty-fifth day of the third month in the first year of the Jingkang era. Three years later...
One day, he was again commanded to ascend the hall. Qín then raised [the theme]: "In India there was a king who once went to visit a patriarch and immediately requested him to preach the Dharma.
The patriarch said, 'Great King, when you came, you were like a good road; when you depart, you are like the coming of the Tathāgata. The king sighed in admiration and submission.
Qín took up [the point], saying: "The Buddha-dharma is worldly dharma; worldly dharma is the Buddha-dharma. Walk directly upon the path, and it will be as the wind blowing over the grass."

If you have not yet understood this in full detail, I shall speak it again in verse: It is most simple and most easy; Most honored and most noble. The coming and going of a thousand sages pass over its crown;
Inconceivable throughout the mundane and supramundane worlds. A single snap of the fingers perfects the eighty thousand gates;
Transcending all at once, one enters directly the stage of the Tathāgata. I respectfully submit these three verses to Your Majesty. At the end, he inscribed: "Jingkang."
The first day of the fourth month marked the change of the reign title. [He] beheld the sublime and profound verses on the *Tattvārtha* (The Meaning of Reality) by Chan Master Foguo.
Two years later, he ascended the imperial throne. Not long after, he traveled to Weiyang. In the eleventh month, he issued an edict summoning Qín to the temporary capital for an audience.
Upon his arrival at the palace gates, the Emperor dispatched eight palace attendants to escort him and granted him a seat. The Emperor—
The Emperor said, "I remember it all clearly. Yesterday I passed through Sizhou and saw the Elder Puzhao Foxin, who claimed to be your disciple.
I have long known that your Zen way is sublime and profound; may I hear it?

Qin replied, "Your Majesty governs the world with benevolence and filial piety, such that all living beings throughout the realm are bathed in your radiance. Even the grasses and trees, as well as insects and..."
"Each insect shall find its proper place; this is the mind transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Outside of this mind, there is no other mind.
If there were another mind, it would not be the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. The Emperor was greatly pleased and said, "I grant you the title of Chan Master Yuanwu.
After Qin had finished his thanks, the Emperor asked, "What do you think of your residence at Mount Jinshan? Qin replied, "Your servant is old and..."
"I am ill; I wish to retire to the forests. The Emperor said, "That will not do. Among the famous mountains under heaven, you alone shall choose where to dwell.
Qín resolutely declined. The Emperor asked, "Which mountain may I go to reside? Qín replied, "I wish to spend my final years at Yunju.
The Emperor granted his request. Qín further submitted, "Since Your Majesty has employed the Buddha-mind to nurture and transform all living beings, the myriad states pay homage..."

"Your Majesty, I too shall transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal to repay Your Majesty’s longevity. After the tea was served, an imperial decree was proclaimed for him to be escorted to the Five Ministries.
That night, by imperial command, the Five Ministries successively went to Yongxi Temple to request that he open the hall and expound the Dharma.
Emperor Xiaozong’s Way was born of innate knowledge, and his nature was bestowed by Heaven.
While he resided in the hidden state of Puan, upon hearing of the Way of Chan Master Furi Zonggao of Mount Jing, he dispatched an internal supervisor to inquire about its essential principles.
Zonggao presented a verse in response. Later, when the imperial residence was established, the Emperor again ordered an attendant to deliver bundles of silk and other gifts.

The Emperor commanded Wuxiaogao to go to the mountain to preach the Dharma for the assembly. He inscribed the three characters "Miaoxi An" (Wondrous Joy Hermitage) in large script and composed a eulogy to bestow upon him.
Gao composed four verses in response to present them. The Emperor was greatly pleased and filled with admiration. He then ascended the imperial throne.
The Emperor issued an edict summoning Daogao for an audience. Daogao pleaded with him that he was ill. Thereupon, the Emperor specially conferred upon him the title "Chan Master Dahui.
One day, because Huang Yanjie, the Gatekeeper, cited the verse of the twenty-second patriarch, Maṇḍarava, as recorded in the *Lamp Records of the Transmission of the Dharma*:
"The mind turns following the myriad objects; where it turns, it is truly profound. Following the flow and recognizing one's nature, there is neither joy nor sorrow."
The Emperor immediately realized its profound mystery. In the winter of the Gengyin year of the Qiandao era, the seat at Jingde Lingyin Chan Monastery was vacant;

by imperial decree, the monk Huiyuan was appointed as abbot. In the spring of the Xingmao year, he was summoned for an audience. The Emperor raised the question, "He who does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion"—what kind of person is this?
Huiyuan reported the story of Layman Pang (the full account is omitted here due to its length). In the autumn of the Renchen year.

He was summoned into the Eastern Pavilion. The Emperor said, "The other day, while sitting in quietude in this pavilion, I suddenly recalled the karmic conditions regarding the saying 'not being a companion to the myriad dharmas' that you previously cited. From this point, I have reached a certain realization. Yuan said:
"He does not consort with the myriad dharmas. How do you understand this, Your Majesty? The Emperor said, "The four seas are not too many.
Yuan said, "How about swallowing all the waters of the West River in a single gulp? The Emperor said, "There has never been any deficiency.
Subsequently, he was bestowed the title of Chan Master Fohai. In the spring of the Gui-si year, the Emperor visited his temple and personally composed [a verse].
The Emperor saw a portrait of Yuan and asked, "Who is this? Yuan replied, "It is my humble self; a student has painted it for me to seek a eulogy.
The Emperor said, "This is merely a painting; which one is the real you? Yuan bowed deeply and addressed him, saying, "The spring air is harmonious and melting;
we respectfully wish Your Majesty ten thousand blessings. The Emperor laughed heartily. They then proceeded to the eastern enclosure to view the paintings.

Next, at the wall, Yuan Zou said, "These are eminent monks of successive dynasties. The Emperor asked, "Are there any such today? Yuan replied, "The brushwork at the bottom of the western wall is even more skillful.
In the spring of the *Chunxi* cycle year *Bingshen*, the monk Deguang was appointed by imperial decree to reside at Lingyin Monastery.
In the eleventh month of winter, he was summoned for an audience in the private hall (*biandian*). Deguang recounted how Lingyun attained enlightenment upon seeing peach blossoms.
The verse says: "A swordsman seeking his blade for thirty years, How many times have the leaves fallen and the branches sprouted?
Since first beholding the peach blossoms, To this very day, he has had no further doubts. [The Master] asked: "Wherein lies the point where he has no doubts?"
The Emperor said, "Leading an iron ox with empty hands. The Emperor said, "If you were asked by an elder, how would you respond?
Guang said, "A thousand hearings are not equal to one seeing. Guang further cited an instance where Miaoshan asked Xiangyan, "Try to utter a single word before your parents were born.
Xiangyan had no reply. The Emperor said, "I have a saying. Guang said, "..."
"What is the one phrase prior to the birth of one's parents? The Master said: "Last night, this morning, and again tomorrow.
He then presented the verse on illumination: "The great heat melts metal and stone; the cold wind freezes the clouds. The fragrance of plum blossoms wafts afar."
There was naturally a branch of spring. Not long after, he was bestowed with the title of Chan Master Fozhao.
In the autumn of the Gengzi year, the Emperor invited Bao Yin, the abbot of Mount Jing, to Xuande Hall. The Emperor said, "The sages of the Three Teachings originally share this same principle.
Bao Yin replied, "It is like empty space; from east to west and north to south, it is fundamentally no different. The Emperor said, "But..."
The gateways established by the sages each differ. Confucius taught through the doctrine of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). [The Master] said:

"If it were not for the teaching of the Middle Way, how could the world be securely established? Therefore, even in the *Avataṃsaka*, worldly appearances are not destroyed in order to accomplish supramundane dharmas.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* states: "Worldly speech and the means of livelihood and production are all identical with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)."
[The two] were at odds. The Superior said: "Among the gentlemen of today, many study the teachings of Confucius, yet they merely attack the written words;
they do not perceive the Way of the Master, nor do they understand the mind of the Master.

Only Śākyamuni, the Old Man, does not teach people by means of written words, but points directly to the source of the mind to reveal it to sentient beings, causing each to awaken and enter [the truth]. This is what makes him truly superior. Thus he stamped [the seal].
He said: "It is not only the scholars of today who have not seen the Way of the Master. Even at that time, among the Ten Sages, Yanzi was considered the closest embodiment of it.
Yet, throughout his entire life, he could only say: 'At times he seems to be before me; suddenly he is behind me.
It is as if there were something standing there, distinct and eminent,' yet in the end he failed to grasp it. And yet, the Master’s Eight Characters were perfectly clear."
[The Master] opened [the door] and said to his disciples, "Do you, my disciples, think that I have anything hidden from you? I have nothing hidden from you.
There is no action of mine that I do not share with you; such is the person of Qiu. Judging by this, the Master never shied away from his disciples;
rather, it was the disciples themselves who missed the mark. Formerly, Chancellor Zhang Shangying...
Yun said, "Only after one has studied Buddhism can one truly understand Confucianism. The Emperor said, "My own view is also that this is so.
Yun replied, "Recently, Your Majesty granted an imperial edict to the Elder Deguang which stated:
'Nowadays, there are commoners who regard Chan as empty space and treat its words as mere sophistry; they do not know the Way. This struck the mark with great precision."

Today, the malady of popular custom is this: people generally regard the Buddha-dharma as a teaching of purity and quiescent extinction, and consequently cite the doctrines of Zhuangzi and Laozi to harmonize them with the Buddha’s intent.
As I observe it, the ground established by Zhuangzi and Laozi can at best only produce the insights of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* found within the sūtras and śāstras.
The Emperor asked, “How do you know this? Yuanzhen replied, “Because they fall into [the view of] emptiness.”

To discard the limbs, to cast out cleverness and intelligence—though the body may indeed be made like withered wood and the mind like extinguished ashes—this is precisely the state of those of the Two Vehicles, who extinguish their resolve and eliminate their wisdom.
They loathe the body as if it were shackles and abandon time as if it were a mixture of poisons;
thus, they remain far removed from those of the Mahāyāna. Those of the Mahāyāna do not realize Bodhi until all sentient beings have been saved. It is just like this...
Yin said, "If there were even one person who did not receive its bounty, it would be as if I had pushed him into a ditch myself.

He further said, "I am one among the people of Heaven who has first awakened; I shall use this Way to awaken these people. This is precisely the place where those of the Mahayana tread. The Emperor approved of this.
He once composed a eulogy for the Baguān Heshang (Baguān the Monk), which says: "The bag contains heaven and earth."
Carrying the sun and moon upon his staff, he is both rugged and coarse; a preeminent figure among the Sangha, he is both stubborn and deluded—a peerless being within the realm.
When he issues a command, one stroke leaves a scar; when he rouses the faculty of awakening, killing requires the sight of blood.
Distinctly and clearly, it is but a single drop of snow upon a red furnace. Furthermore, he once sported within the Great Luminous Treasury of Perfect Enlightenment. [End of excerpt].
Having perused the various sutras, he emerged from profound silence to comment upon their ultimate mysteries, awakening both humans and devas.
As in his commentary on the "Chapter on Pure Wisdom," regarding the passage "When all obstacles are present, that is ultimate enlightenment," he states:

"The initial arousal of the Bodhisattva's mind is called 'initial enlightenment' (shijue), while the perfection of Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue) is called 'ultimate enlightenment' (jiujing jue). Now, seeing all obstacles as they are, is itself ultimate enlightenment."

This refers to one who has already entered the stage of Buddhahood and possesses no mind of differentiation whatsoever. Regarding "attaining mindfulness" and "losing mindfulness," it is said that there is nothing that is not liberation:
attaining mindfulness is non-mindfulness, while losing mindfulness is having mindfulness. The Buddha knows that all thoughts are fundamentally empty and realizes there is neither gain nor loss;
therefore, all attain liberation. Regarding "establishing dharmas" and "destroying dharmas," both are termed *nirvāṇa*.

It is said: "To advance and cultivate is called 'accomplishment' (siddhi); to slander and destroy is called 'ruination' (bhaṅga). The Buddha knows that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and realizes there is neither accomplishment nor ruination;
therefore, he names them all Nirvāṇa. Regarding the distinction between wisdom and folly, they are both collectively termed *prajñā*. Thus it is said: "As for wisdom..."
The nature already realized by the wise and the nature not yet realized by the ignorant—when their fundamental source is investigated, they are identical in Buddha-nature.
Therefore, it is said that all are universally Prajñā. Regarding the dharmas accomplished by Bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists, they are likewise identical in Bodhi;
thus it is said: although the dharmas established by Bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists differ in being either heterodox or orthodox, they are all the awakening of Bodhi.

Regarding the nature [of phenomena]: when explaining that ignorance (*avidyā*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are not distinct realms, it is said: "Truth and delusion are of one essence; the nature is fundamentally liberated.

When explaining that all precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms, as well as lust, anger, and ignorance, are equally the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and that sentient beings and lands share the same dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), it is said:
"The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: 'With my Buddha-eye, I survey everywhere the sentient and non-sentient beings within the three realms.'"
All human dharmas are entirely ultimate; that which is ultimate is precisely the *dharmatā*.
To explain that the hells and celestial palaces are all pure lands, it is said: the Buddha knows that the two retributions of good and evil are both like flowers in the sky;

therefore, he says that the two realms of suffering and pleasure are both pure lands. To explain that those with nature and those without nature equally achieve the Buddha-way, it is said: "Those who have..."
"Nature" refers to the Three Vehicles. "Lack of nature" refers to the icchantika. When viewed through the Buddha-eye, all are entirely Buddhas.
To explain that all afflictions are ultimately liberated is to say: the Buddha taught that afflictions are fundamentally empty; therefore, they are called "ultimately liberated.
To explain the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm, which clearly perceives all phenomena as being like empty space—this is called the Tathāgata’s conformity [to reality].
Regarding the awakened nature, it is said: "The ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm" refers to the Buddha’s wisdom, which is as vast as the Dharma-realm and as profound as the great ocean.
The light of this wisdom illuminates all phenomena; like the great void, it is expansive and free from obstruction.
This is precisely what constitutes the Buddha’s awakening-nature in accordance with reality; it is like Confucius’s principle of "neither having a preference nor having no preference.
The worthy minister and Chancellor Wang Sui, a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), once visited Chan Master Shou-shan Xingnian and attained the meaning beyond words. From then on—
As his practice deepened further, he ultimately clarified the Great Dharma. On the day of his passing, he wrote a verse: "The lamp in the painted hall has already been extinguished;
Pointing my finger, to whom shall I speak? Coming and going are fundamentally ordinary; The spring breeze sweeps away the lingering snow."

The layman Li Chen of the Imperial Secretariat once visited Chan Master Fuyan Ya. While they were discussing the story of "The Spirit of the Bride Separated from Her Soul," before the conversation had even concluded, Ya said, "He follows him.
The layman asked, "What is your meaning, Master? Ya replied, "Be careful not to land yourself on the side of the bride.
The layman attained realization and said, "So it was all along right here! Ya smiled at him. The following day, they went together...
He entered the Library Hall (Zangyuan). At that time, Chan Master Xuedou Xian was serving as the Librarian (Zangzhu).

The Official said, "Is this the Librarian? Xian replied, "It is. The Official said, "Does the collection contain any mention of me? Xian replied, "It can be verified right before your eyes. The Official said:
"What is the matter with this testing? Xian said, "It does not require a single note. As the official hesitated, Xian said, "Please return to your quarters for tea, Warden.
While they were seated, a mist suddenly arose. Ya said, "The Warden was out on a mountain excursion; it is only fitting that he be hindered by this mist.
The official asked, "Why is there such a thing as this at the sacred site of Lingfeng? Xian said, "There is none below. The official—
Yanwei proposed a dialogue. Ya said, "The Abbot is a magnificent sight at Fuyan. Xian said, "Preceptor, do not open your eyes yet. Yanwei said, "A master! A master!
Xian said, "The Hall Director is highly esteemed. At that time, a Daoist and a scholar arrived at the monastery. Yanwei said:
"Among the three teachings, which is the most honored? Xianqi stood to one side. The Duke said, "If you have a mouth, why do you not speak?
Xianqi replied, "It is difficult to speak before the Son of Heaven. The Duke said, "Enough! Enough! and rose. Xianqi said, "Just now I was too hasty. The Duke shouted at him.
The scholar-official Wen Dinggong Zhang Fangping, whose courtesy name was Andao, while serving as the Prefect of Chuzhou, once visited Mount Langya.
As he paced along the corridors, he could not bear to leave. He then proceeded to the library hall, where he was so moved that his tears flowed.

Pointing to a scripture case between the beams, he said, "This is the record of my previous life. He ordered it to be brought out for inspection; it was the beginning of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* he had himself transcribed.

[The scroll] was continued by Qi Mu. It differs not in the slightest from the previous draft (the author of the former draft served as the Librarian of this temple; he passed away before the writing was finished, hence the vow to write it again).

Incense was burned as he opened and read the "Chapter on the Mind of the Buddha’s Words. Upon reaching the verse of praise, it said: "The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky;
wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet great compassion arises. Thereupon, his own views were thoroughly clarified, and he wrote this verse:

A single thought harbors birth and extinction; a thousand mechanisms bind one to existence and non-existence. Where the divine blade is lightly raised, it passes through like a pearl rolling off a platter.
In his later years, [the Master] produced this scripture and showed it to the Layman东坡 (Dongpo), and spoke of these matters to him. Dongpo inscribed a colophon at its end.
It was carved at Longyou Temple on Mount Fuyi.
The scholar-official Zeng Hui, a lay devotee, had lived as a fellow student with Chan Master Xuedou Chongxian during his youth; however, upon reaching adulthood, they followed different paths.

During the Tianxi era, he encountered [the Master] in the Huai region. The Master then cited the *Zhongyong* and the *Daxue*, supplementing them with passages from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the records of the Chan school to substantiate his point.
Xian said, "This [approach] does not even accord with the scriptural teachings, let alone the *Zhongyong* and the *Daxue*.
If you, Academician, wish to understand this matter through a direct and swift path," he snapped his fingers once and said, "Just realize it in this way."

He took it up. Under the Master’s words, the Official attained realization of the essential meaning. At the beginning of the Tiancheng era, while the Official was governing Siming, he sent letters and gifts to welcome the Master to serve as the abbot of Xuedou.
Once the Master had arrived, the Official said, "Recently, I discussed with Elder Qing the story of Zhaozhou interrogating the old woman."
"I do not yet know for certain whether there is a point where [the truth] has been thoroughly penetrated," [Wang] Gong asked. Xian said, "What did Elder Qing say?
[Gong] said, "He went off again like that. Xian said, "Let us grant Elder Qing one point for now.
Do you, Scholar, know that the monks of the world cannot escape this old woman’s trap? Gong said, "There is another way here."
At that place, Zhaozhou had not yet exposed the old woman’s deception, so for his entire life he suffered in silence. Xian said, “I have exposed her. The Duke laughed heartily.
Xian led the assembly into the city to seek alms and wished to see the Duke, but the gatekeeper informed him that audiences were forbidden.
The Master sent a verse to the Duke, saying: “Mist gathers in the azure sky as the snow clears; The sentiments of one dwelling on the mountain are sent to the capital city. My Lord Duke...”
"The Way exists before we have met; why do you vainly linger, walking within the shade of the sweet-tangerine tree? The Master replied: "Exhausted by worldly affairs, I was swept away in the flow;
yet my single nature is clear and bright, spanning past and present. When one meets the Way through direct perception, there is no obstruction;
why must one see the face before knowing the heart? He then invited the Master in and asked: "If the Way exists without obstruction, for what reason were you unable to enter? Xian...
[Zhaozhou] said, "The other day I saw an elder in another place; you did not ask me to mention [this matter] to him. The Official said, "What harm is there in mentioning it?
Xian said, "It would be my fault, Reverend Sir. The Official said, "Excellent! Excellent! Xian responded with two "Yeses."
When Layman Xu Shi, the Langzhong, was serving as Governor of Longxing, he received the Eye of the True Dharma from Chan Master Dongshan Cong (some say from Mount Zu Gong).
One day, while sitting with Lengtang Cheng and Shanglan Pu, Cheng asked: "I have heard that you, Langzhong, said..."
Sitting at night by the Stone of Linked Clouds, I planted spring pines amidst the rain. What was the conversation you had with Dongshan at that time?
The Master said, "Today the office has been dismissed early. Cheng said, "I heard you replied, 'The Great Sage of Sizhou appears in Yangzhou.
Is this true? The Master said, "Serve another cup of tea. Cheng said, "His reputation is not in vain. The Master said, "When will you return, Monk?"

Shan Cheng said, "Today you have been seen through by Shanglan. He then gave a shout. The Master said, "There is nothing that can be done about the boat; break the scoop! The Master went to Shanglan Monastery’s Sangha Hall and asked the Head Seat, "How many years old are you? The Seat replied, "Sixty-eight. The Master asked, "How many years of *śrāmaṇera* ordination (*bhikṣu-vaṃśa*) do you have? The Seat replied, "Forty-seven. The Master asked, "How many summer retreats has the Holy Monk attained? The Seat replied, "The same as [the Buddha]. The Master said, "So it is; so it is. He then struck the Seat once with his staff and departed. The Head Seat later reported this to the Master. The Master said, "He is a man of great capacity; he will surely become a teacher of people. Later, when the Master was traveling through Jiangxi, he met the Head Seat at Hongzhou Kaiyuansi. If one can transcend both the moon and the reflections, Then the Way is right before one’s eyes. If one still harbors thoughts of seeking, One is far removed from the source. The Honored Master Baozhang, a Sage of Manifestation who attained the age of one thousand years, was a native of Central India. He descended [to this world] in the twelfth year of the reign of Emperor Weile of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Dingmao.
The deity received his physical form with his left hand clenched in a fist. When he reached the age of seven, his hair was shaved and his hand was opened;
consequently, he was named Baozhang (Jewel-Palms). During the Wei and Jin dynasties, he traveled east to this land. He entered Shu to pay homage to Samantabhadra and stayed at Daci Temple.
He never ate, reciting over a thousand scrolls of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras daily. One who praised him said: "His weary jade teeth are cold, like a rushing mountain spring leaping forth."
Sometimes he would sit on the steps during the middle of the night, and spirits and ghosts would weep. One day, he said to the assembly: "I have a vow to remain in this world for a thousand years.
This year marks six hundred and twenty-six; thus I am known as 'The One of a Thousand Years. Subsequently, I traveled to Mount Wutai."
He moved his residence to Huayan on Mount Zhurong, Shuangfeng on Mount Huangmei, and Donglin on Mount Lu.

Eventually, he arrived at Jianye, where he encountered Bodhidharma’s arrival in the Liang dynasty. The Master approached him to inquire about the essential meaning and attained awakening. Emperor Wu, admiring his years of practice and spiritual maturity, invited him into the inner court.
Not long after, he traveled to Wu, where he composed a verse: "In the city of Liang, I met the Teacher; through Zen meditation, I realized the ground of the mind."
Wandering aimlessly through Xi and Yi, I exhausted all the finest mountains and waters.
Flowing downstream to the east, I traveled from Qianyan to Tiantong, proceeded to Mount Mao, ascended Mount Taibai, and passed through Yanwang.
I stayed at the seventy-two hermitages of Cui Feng, returned to Chicheng, and rested at Yunmen, Fahua, Lipu in Zhujia, Chifu, Dayan, and other locations, before finally returning to Feilai Peak.
In the stone grotto there was an inscription that read: "Having traveled to the ends of the four hundred prefectures of China, it is here that the recluse most delights to wander.
This was during the fifteenth year of the Zhenguan era. Later, he resided at Baoyan Monastery in Pujiang, where he formed a close friendship with Chan Master Lang.
Whenever he sent a message, he would dispatch a white dog to gallop there; Hui-lang likewise employed a green monkey as his messenger.
Thus, he inscribed upon Lang’s wall: "The white dog arrives bearing a letter; the green monkey returns with the bowl washed. All the places the Master passed through later became monasteries.

On the first day of the New Year in the second year of the Xianqing era, he fashioned a statue with his own hands. By the ninth day, the statue was completed. He asked his disciple Huiyun, "To whom does this resemble?
Yun replied, "It is no different from the Master himself. Thereupon, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the lotus posture.
Addressing Yun, he said, "I have remained in this world for one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years. Now I am about to depart this life. Listen to my verse: *The Fundamental...*

"In coming, there is no birth-and-death; now, I likewise manifest birth-and-death. I have attained the mind that comes and goes; having been born elsewhere, I shall return here again. He then gave this instruction:
"Sixty years after my passing, there will be a monk who comes to take my bones; do not refuse him. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
Fifty-four years after his entry into *nirvāṇa*, the Elder Dafu arrived at the site of the stupa from Yunmen and paid his respects, saying:
He hoped that the stupa would open of its own accord. After a short while, the door of the stupa indeed opened; his bones were found linked together like golden rings.
He immediately took them to Mount Qinwang and erected a *stūpa* to enshrine them.

Calculating from the *dingmao* year of the reign of King Weili of the Zhou dynasty to the *dingyi* year of the Xianqing era of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang, it is exactly one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years. From that time until this present age, four hundred years have elapsed.
The rest has been lost from the monastic histories. During the Kaiyuan era, a disciple of Huiyun named Zongyi once had it engraved upon stone to commemorate it.
Koubing Zao was a descendant of the Weng family of Xinfeng in Jian'ning; his mother dreamed of a bhikṣu with a radiant and majestic spirit.

However, she once carried her mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) and sought lodging; people pointed at her and said, "This is a *pratyekabuddha. Subsequently, she became pregnant and gave birth in the fourth year of the Huichang era of Emperor Wuzong.
A fragrant mist filled the room and did not dissipate for many days. At the age of thirteen, she requested to leave the household life, and her parents granted her permission.
She followed Master Haeng-jeon of Heungbok-sa on Mount O as her teacher. In the *wuyou* year of the Xiantong era, she shaved her head and received full ordination.
At first, he was sought out by the assembly for his lectures. Later, he went to visit Chan Master Zhenjue of Xuefeng, carrying a bundle of *fu-ci* (water chestnuts) and a jar of sauce.
Xuefeng asked, "What is in that bundle? He replied, "Water chestnuts. Xuefeng asked, "Where did you get them?
He replied, "From the mud. Xuefeng asked, "How deep is the mud? He replied, "It is several zhang deep. Xuefeng asked, "Is there anything else besides this? He replied, "Yes."
"Deeper and deeper, more and more existent. He asked again, "What is in the vessel? He replied, "Sauce. [Feng] said, "Where did you get it?
He replied, "I made it myself. [Feng] said, "Is it cooked yet? He replied, "It is not far from being done. Feng marveled at this and said, "In the future, you will surely become a teacher to a king.
Later, he returned from Ehu to Mount Wenling to build a hermitage (which is now Yongfeng Temple) and subsequently resided at General’s Rock. (2)
A tiger attended at his side. A divine being offered him land, which became Ruiyan Monastery. Students gathered there in great numbers.
He once said to the assembly, "The practice of the ancient sages must rely upon rigorous austerity. Now, in summer I wear paper clothing, and in winter I bathe by striking the ice.

For this reason, the people of the world called him the "Ancient Buddha Who Strikes the Ice. When the Grand Tutor Zhang Gongzi Jun heard of the Master’s reputation for the Way, he went in person to welcome him.

He paid his respects. Before long, he relinquished his residence to establish a monastery. When Lady Lian asked him about the rank of his descendants, he replied that they would hold it for ten generations (which later came to pass as he had said).
While residing at Lingyuan Monastery, he ascended the hall and said: "The fourfold assembly has gathered like clouds;
what can this old monk say to you? He then descended from the seat. A monk piled charcoal to form a fire-shrine and said, "I request the Master to enter here and practice."

[The Master] said: "True jade does not change with the flowing water; lapis lazuli vies with the multitude of stars for their brilliance. [The student] asked: "Is it simply this that is so? [The Master] said:
"Do not mistake the servant for the master. [The student] asked: "Ultimately, what is it? [The Master] said: "The plum blossoms open in the twelfth month."
The Provincial Governor, Lord Chen Huì, commissioned three great iron Buddhas at the western bank of the stream at Xiǎnqīn Monastery in Jiān'ān.
Once they were completed, he provided a meal for the monks and addressed the assembly, saying, "Whoever is able to compose a eulogy for these shall be granted them. The assembly remained silent.
The Master was seated at the end of the row. Rising, he replied, "A hundred-year-old piece of cast iron becomes a Buddha in a single morning.

[Wang] Hui was greatly pleased; he immediately knelt and escorted him back home (Chen-Tie was Wang Hui’s childhood name). In the *wuzi* year of the Tiānchéng era, the Master responded to the summons of the ruler of Fǔmǐn, who invited him to reside in the inner hall.
Bowing with reverence, the ruler said, "Thank you for descending from afar. During the serving of tea, the Master lifted up his cloth bag and asked, "Does Your Majesty understand? He replied:
"No," he replied. "The King of Men and the King of Dharma each have their own illumination. He remained for ten days, then declined on the grounds of illness.

On the second day of the twelfth month, he bathed, ascended the hall, and passed away after addressing the assembly. The king, along with the monastics and laypeople, prepared fragrant wood, ghee, oil, and tea to perform the cremation.
A radiant auspicious glow filled the mountains, and five-colored *śarīra* (relics) were obtained. He was interred in a stupa at the main chamber of Ruiyan Monastery. His age was eighty.

He was fifteen years old [when he entered the order] and sixty-three *laba* (years of seniority). His posthumous title was Miaoying Fawei Ciji (Wondrous Response, Dharma Majesty, Compassionate Rescue).
The Master’s austere integrity and extraordinary conduct, as well as his supernormal knowledge of others' minds and his wisdom-eye, are fully recorded in the *Benlu* (Original Record).

Jiuxian (Wine Immortal) met Master Xian; he was the son of the Lin family of Changzhou in Gusu. His mother conceived after dreaming of swallowing a large pearl. From birth, many extraordinary omens attended him.
His appearance was grand and strange; his mouth could hold both fists. At the age of seven, he once submerged himself in a deep abyss, yet his clothes remained dry.

He subsequently left the household life and took refuge with Master Kai of Yong’an in Jiahe. At thirty, he shaved his head, received the precepts, and attained full ordination. He then went to visit Master Qian.
Chan Master Tanglong Cezhu realized the Mind-Seal (xinyin). He returned to reside at Mingjue Monastery, where he devoted himself solely to drinking wine.

When intoxicated, he would compose songs and verses to admonish both monastics and laypeople; consequently, he was known as the "Wine Immortal" (jiuxian). Initially, upon returning from Qiantang, he carried an iron hammer;

whenever he saw tiles or bricks on the road, he would strike them. When someone asked him the reason for this, he replied, "The paths of the world are uneven, so I am breaking them apart. (Jianlong era)
In the interim, he renovated the temple buildings at a cost of several million coins, yet no one knew the source from which these funds were obtained.

Later, when he was rebuilding the triple gate, he dispatched craftsmen to retrieve stone pillars from Lake Dongting; though they worked for a long time, they could not find them. The Master immediately climbed the mountain to summon the Wine Immortal (Jiubai Xianren).

After a short while, the stones appeared, floating down the river on the wind. As the boat was about to capsize, the boatmen were struck with great terror. The Master untied his *kāṣāya* robe and used it as a sail.
The wind immediately shifted. A tiger entered the city and saw the Master prostrating himself; the Master stroked it, and the tiger then departed.

County Governor Mei, who had previously not known the Master, dreamed of conversing with him; when he saw the Master in person, he found him exactly as he had seen in his dream, and he consequently increased his reverence and respect.

Whenever the Master passed by a wine shop, the guests would invariably fill the seats upon his departure. For this reason, people would daily wait for his arrival, listening for whatever he might require. The Master...
Zhāngshùn went to his home and said, "In the past, when you drank my wine, you never paid for it. Now I shall repay you; this will enrich you for three generations.
Seeing a stone mortar, he vomited into it and covered it, saying, "Open it after three days have passed. When the seal was opened after three days, there was a mass like a chicken egg;
this was yellow wine. That year, the epidemic was rampant; those who sprinkled this wine [on the afflicted] and took it had no [illness].
He did not recover. Consequently, his family became wealthy. Whenever a person in the commandery fell ill, he would not provide a talisman to those who sought one; such individuals were not saved.

Later, two characters—“Chen” (陳) and “Seng” (僧)—were written upon the talisman. In the second year of the Xiangfu era, at dawn on the night of the Yuanxiao festival, after bathing and retiring to his chamber, he joined his palms and raised his right hand.
He opened his mouth to the left and passed away. For twenty-one days, his body did not slouch and the color of his lips remained as it was.

The monks of the temple wished to lacquer it, but his disciple said, "This is not the Master's intention. They subsequently performed cremation, collected the bones, and fashioned a statue of him. He lived to the age of eighty-eight.
He was fifty-eight years old at the time of his passing.
Venerable Ziyen of Nanan Rock was a native of Tong’an. His clan was Zheng, and it was traditionally said that his family were emanations of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.
At the age of eleven, he left home and became a novice under Master Qiye at Woxiang Temple in Jianxing.

At the age of seventeen, Yuanfan went to Luling to pay his respects to Chan Master Yunhuo of Xifeng, whereupon he immediately realized the Dharma of the Mind and attained the power of knowing past lives.
He took leave of the master and resided at Huangshi Rock and Mount Panggu; both were dens of snakes and tigers, yet when the Master arrived, they became his servants.

Whenever people prayed for rain or fine weather, or for male or female offspring, their requests were invariably answered. Consequently, every household enshrined an image of him and worshipped it. There was also a novice monk...
He was without worldly gain. He prostrated and requested a verse. The Master wrote for him: "The Great Wisdom arises within the mind; where in the mind can it be sought? It accomplishes all meanings;
there is neither past nor present. He had him recite this. Before a month had passed, he could recite it from memory after a single reading.
Whenever the Master composed a work containing cryptic language, he would append the four characters "Zhongzhi" (Among the Sages) as a postscript. The Master’s attire was... [text ends]
He was pure white in appearance; his head was covered with cloth. Once his [final] traces were manifest, his community reported this to the court.
An imperial edict highly praised him, and officials from Prime Minister Wang Qinruo and Vice President Zhao Anren downward presented poems. The Master set them aside and did not look at them.

On the sixth day of the first month of the Yimao year of the Chunhua era, he gathered the assembly and said: "You all should know that the wondrous nature is vast and empty; fundamentally, there is no birth."
He entered extinction. Having demonstrated that there is coming and going, what further could be doubted? On this day of his birth, now was precisely the time; he thus passed away in auspiciousness.
He had traversed eighty-two years of the world and sat through sixty-five summer retreats. His posthumous title was bestowed as Chan Master Dingguang Yuanying.
Fahua Zhi was the son of the Xu family of Shouchun. Having reached the age of twenty, he traveled to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) and subsequently received full ordination.

He remained for a long time at the Qijuzhi Monastery, where he engaged in lecture assemblies. One day, while reading the *Record of Yunmen*, he suddenly attained awakening. Before long, his past lives became fully manifest;
he would speak and laugh alone, his lips moving and murmuring incessantly every day. The world transmitted his recitations of the Dharma.

He named himself after the *Huayan jing* (Avataṃsaka Sūtra). Whenever he entered a marketplace, he would hasten forward with his robes lifted, sometimes raising his hand to trace patterns in the air and standing motionless for a long while.
At other times, he would follow butchers and wine-sellers, partaking of food and drink without discrimination. Nevertheless, his prophecies regarding calamities and blessings invariably came to pass.

Consequently, his fame spread throughout both the court and the common people. In the third year of the Zhihe era, Emperor Renzong, as the imperial succession had not yet been established, burned incense one night.
The Emperor prayed silently, saying: "Tomorrow, at Hwachongjeon Hall, I shall prepare a vegetarian feast and reverently invite the Great Being of the Lotus Sūtra (Dharma Flower Bodhisattva).
I pray that he will deign to grace us with his presence and not decline. At dawn, the Emperor donned his ceremonial robes and stood solemnly waiting. Suddenly, a report was brought:

"There is a monk named Dharma Flower who is coming straight from the Right Eupaceok Gate; as he approaches the inner palace, no one has been able to stop him. The Emperor smiled and said, "This is I."
He was invited to come, and after a short while he arrived. He ascended the imperial couch, sat in the full lotus posture, and accepted the offerings.

As he was about to depart, the Emperor said, "Because my heir has not yet been established, the high ministers all speak of this. As I have entered the twilight of my years, I wonder whether I shall have any offspring."
"The *Lotus Sūtra* is its singular resolution. The Master then took up his brush and wrote thirteen characters, repeating this thirteen times, totaling several dozen lines.

He then cast down his brush without further words, and none could fathom his intent. Later, when Emperor Yingzong ascended the throne, [the Master] was among the princes at the Prince of Pu’s residence;

he was indeed the thirteenth. Thus, it first accorded with the previous prophecy. When Prime Minister Lü Xugong questioned the Buddha about this, [the Master replied: [Note: The final sentence fragment "丞相呂許公問佛" indicates that the narrative concludes with the inquiry of Prime Minister Lü Xugong regarding the Buddha.]
Fada said: "Originally there is not a single thing; in one flavor, all is truly real. When Jixian Wang asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
he replied: "A surge of azure rises within the shadows of the green mountains; a precious pagoda chants aloud, shaking the morning breeze.
He also said: "Please invite Fahua to burn incense," and added: "Do not seek it through fasting and precepts; do not seek it from the Buddha."
Xu Yue, Assistant Instructor at the National Academy, asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

He replied, "The one on the eastern side of the street. Xu Yue said, "I do not understand. He replied, "Three kinds of people cannot understand it. A monk asked, "Does a Buddha exist in this world? He replied, "Mañjuśrī in the temple.
Someone asked, "Are you an ordinary person or a sage? He raised his hand and said, "I do not dwell here. (Qingli era)
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month in the year Wuzi, he was about to pass away.

He said to his followers, "Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have accomplished the transformation of the Jetavana land and manifested my body to spread the teaching. Now I am returning south. Having finished speaking, he passed into stillness while lying on his right side.

Zhizu Zhihua Dao was a native of Kaifeng (his family name is lost in the records). His family had been engaged in agriculture for generations. When his mother was two years pregnant, she went to deliver food to her husband in the fields;
he was born beneath a tree and washed in the river. The child said, "Do not freeze me. At that time, a crimson light illuminated the heavens.

The Grand Astrologer reported that a person of extraordinary character had been born, and the Emperor ordered him to search for the child. When the Master was found, he was raised in the household of a high-ranking official.
While still in swaddling clothes, he could speak of past events. At the age of three, he began sitting in the full-lotus posture (paryaṅka), knowing himself to be a bhikṣu.

Upon reaching adulthood, he met Yuanfan; his body was entirely covered by a single robe (saṃghāṭī). Neither bitter cold nor intense heat could affect him. On days when he ate more than twenty people, he remained unsatiated.
Liquids never entered his mouth; for two or three months he did not hunger. He would remain in one position—whether reclining or sitting—for as long as three years.
It was so. He had never recited the scriptures, yet his eloquence was unimpeded; he had never practiced the Way of cultivation, yet white light emerged from the crown of his head.

Suddenly, he would open his eyes wide and shout, not out of anger; all day long he would speak and laugh, not out of joy. Whenever he foretold to people matters of good or ill fortune, there was not even a hair’s breadth of error.
During his time in the capital, the five provincial governors vied with one another to invite him. On occasion, he said to others:
"Tianping White Clouds is my place of return. At the beginning of the Chongning era, he emerged from Yimen holding a whisk and singing with laughter;
though they tried to detain him, they could not turn him back. He came east to Baiyun Temple on Mount Tianping in Gusu. Monastics and laypeople followed him in admiration.

When anyone asked him about the Buddha-dharma, he did not answer; however, when someone requested it in verse, he would write this out in large characters and show it to them. During the Zhenghe era, he suddenly passed away.
He passed away. Upon cremation, his stomach and intestines were as translucent as lapis lazuli; his bones were green like jade, while those that were yellow were like gold.
There were countless *śarīra* relics. The monastics and laypeople erected a stupa at the site where he had converted others to enshrine them, excavating a burial pit three feet deep.

A purple stone casket was discovered, its lid inscribed with the words "Dharma Hall of Contentment" (Jizu Daochang), which further amazed the assembly. On the day he was interred in the stupa, the earth shook.

The Prefect reported these matters to the throne, who bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya* robe with golden threads and posthumously conferred the title of Great Master of Pure Conduct (Jingxing Dashi).
His stupa was named Mingyin (Illuminating Cause).
Feng Fahua (his name is lost), a native of the Zhang family in Dongjing, received ordination at Kaibosi Temple.

He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* without ceasing and had no fixed dwelling place; thus, the world called him Feng Fahua. When people asked him about good or bad fortune, his responses were like prophecies, and when time passed, they were invariably verified.
At the time of his passing, he sang this song: "Return, go back! Return, go back! Do not go to Si."
The prefecture is not Wutai. One takes off the old shoes and puts on new ones; the old shoes immediately wear away to nothing. The new shoes refuse to tread upon the dust.
The new shoes are just like the pattern of the old ones; do not guess who it is that replaces the new for the old.
When going, one goes upon the path of radiance; when returning, one comes along the level road. How many old acquaintances are there in this present life?
"How many people like me will return? Having finished this song, he passed away.
The elder Li Tongxuan was a man of unknown origins; some say he was a scion of the Tang imperial house. He was likely a manifestation of Mañjuśrī or Samantabhadra.
In the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era (one source says the seventeenth), he lived in seclusion on Mount Fang in Shouyang, Taiyuan.

In an earthen grotto, upon his initial arrival, a tiger carried his scriptures for him; divine dragons transformed into springs; and celestial maidens attended upon him. At night, the light from his teeth served as a lamp.
Occasionally, he consumed dates and cypress wood, whereupon he was titled the "Dazibo Dashi" (Great Being of Dates and Cypress).

He once expounded the profound mysteries and revealed the hidden depths of the *Avataṃsaka* Great Teaching, elucidating it through discourse. His arguments unfolded with ten thousand turns, like water rushing toward the sea, synthesizing the ten gates of interpretation with marvelous skill.
Exhausting the purport of the entire scripture, it comprises forty fascicles and is titled the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka).
Its introductory preface states: "The root of sentient beings relies upon the ocean of wisdom as its source; the stream of conscious beings takes the Dharma-body as its substance.

It is only because emotions arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because conceptualization changes that the substance becomes distinct. When one realizes the root, emotions vanish; when one knows the mind, the substance merges. Now, this Mahāvaipulya..."
The *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra* elucidates the primordial limit of sentient beings and reveals the fountainhead of the fruition of all Buddhas.
As for its being the "basis," it cannot be accomplished through effort; as for its being the "fountainhead," it cannot be attained through practice. When effort ceases, the basis is revealed;

when practice is exhausted, the fountainhead is perfected. Since the fountainhead and the basis are devoid of effort, he who is able to act with sovereign freedom in accordance with conditions is none other than this Vairocana.
Taking the fundamental nature as primary, wisdom accords with the faculties [of beings], and great compassion rescues all things; it is for this reason that he is so named.

Relying upon this foundation, he establishes the moisture of his teachings, which flow profusely throughout the Dharma-realm to nourish all living beings. Thereupon, he takes up residence in the four heavens and manifests the eight phases of his life.
Within the Bodhimanda, he manifests an araṇya (hermitage) to initiate the completion of the Hall of Universal Radiance, wherein he abides in his saṃbhogakāya (reward body).

In this great mansion, Samantabhadra, the eldest son, attained the power of the "concealed body" (kāyaguhya) by realizing the fruit; Mañjuśrī, the youngest son, first received his initial enlightenment at the Golden Mountain.

Through the *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*, he manifests his spirit throughout the entire Dharma-realm; by means of the "Universal Eye" (*Samantanetra*) dharma-gate, he beholds oceans of lands within a single mote of dust.
The two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—interpenetrate body and land; the two gates of cause and effect are such that essence and function are mutually identical.

Penetratingly, he employs the celestial jewel-net of the Tathāgata to manifest the ten lands in their manifold layers; he takes up the stainless maṇi-jewel to illuminate the ten bodies in their profound resonance.
Within the boundless realms of the lands, self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth; throughout the ten ages of past and present...
From beginning to end, it never deviates (one version reads "leaves") from the present thought. In its vastness, it takes empty space as its measure;
in its minuteness, it dwells within the most subtle atom without leaving a trace. The ten directions do not contract, yet there is no deficiency within the smallest of characteristics;
not a speck of dust expands, yet it contains the ten directions without obstruction. This is the fruit-virtue of the ocean of wisdom, which is uniquely distinguished across the five stages.
The gate constantly abides in the Dharma Hall, demonstrating the advancement of cultivation atop the Nine Heavens. It is thus in this realm; so it is in all ten lands.
The assembly of sages is like clouds, merging within the oceanic gathering. Holy and ordinary beings are not equal, appearing like many mirrors reflecting myriad forms.

There is no mutual hindrance between them. Were a thousand lamps placed together in a single room, this sutra—comprising forty chapters of sublime scriptures—mutually opens the gates of wisdom that lead back to the fruition.
Its hundreds of millions of wondrous words collectively extol the ocean-like conduct of the Buddha-flower.

Through the ten bodies and ten assemblies, it expounds the dharma-gates of "ten times ten"; through the ten locations and one hundred thousand [verses], it reveals the penetrations of "ten times ten."
In the "Chapter on the Ten Manifestations" (*Daśābhimukha-parivarta*), he demonstrates cause and effect to conclude the beginning and end;

within the Jetavana Garden, he benefits humans and devas to clarify the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). While Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra were separated from him by sight and hearing despite being face-to-face, six thousand bhikṣus received the "Ten Clarifications" (*daśa-prakāśa*) upon the road.
At the eastern edge of the City of Enlightenment (*Bodhimaṇḍa*), the five assemblies all arrived before the temple of the Ancient Buddha.
Together they ascended to the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*). Śāriputra illuminated the path as the guiding leader, thereby manifesting that the assembled multitude were of one mind.

Furthermore, he established the Dharma-gate of the five stages (*pañcāvasthā-dharmamukha*), possessing virtuous conduct. His exemplary model caused the unenlightened to be inspired; it was easy to comprehend, and through understanding and practice, there was no further doubt.

Returning to the presence of Mañjuśrī, the foremost of teachers, he attained direct realization at the summit of Mount Miaofeng. Having passed through the five assemblies, he completed one hundred and ten [stages].

This Dharma-gate reaches the garden of Maitreya, where the Buddha-fruit of a single lifetime is finalized; one looks back upon Mañjuśrī, the original companion, clarifying that the fruit is identical to the cause.
Subsequently, one enters the wondrous body of Samantabhadra, manifesting the perfect consummation of essence and function.

As for the title of this scripture, *The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "Great" (*mahā*) takes non-directionality as its meaning; "Direction" (*vaipulya*) takes wisdom and principle as its meaning.
This constitutes the merit. In its vastness, even a single hair and a *kṣetra* (world-system) can contain one another. The Buddha is thus the non-action of both essence and function;

the "flowers" metaphorize the delightful gates of practice (*caryā-mukha*), capable of unfolding the merit of both principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma*). "Adornment" (*vyūha*) refers to the adornment of the environment and the inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna-vyūha*). "Sūtra" (*sūtra*) means that which threads together and sews.

As for the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World Rulers," it classifies and assembles the various streams of Dharma-gates, demarcating them into chapters. This sūtra contains forty chapters in total.
This is the most excellent scripture among all categories. Since this chapter establishes the beginning, it is called the "First.

Therefore, it is titled: *The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Chapter One: The Sublime Array of the World Rulers*. To explain this one sūtra as a whole, it is analyzed through ten general sections:
First, clarifying the classification of schools based on the teachings; Second, clarifying the classification of teachings based on the schools; Third, clarifying the meaning of the teachings.

1. Differentiation; 2. Clarifying the similarities and differences in attaining Buddhahood; 3. Clarifying the differences in perceiving the Buddha; 4. Clarifying the periods for expounding the teachings; 5.
Clarifying the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Pure Land; 6. Clarifying the realms of those gathered and transformed; 7. Clarifying the duration of cause and effect; 8.
Clarifying the beginning and end of the assembly’s teachings, and so forth. [This was composed] over eighteen years (or twenty-eight years).
The treatise was completed on the twenty-eighth day of the third month, and he subsequently entered nirvana. On that day, birds and beasts cried out in grief, and a white rainbow pierced the sky;
the fourfold assembly gathered to witness this, exclaiming at such an unprecedented event. He was interred in a stone cairn to the north of Qianshan.

During the Qingtai era, villagers cleared away the stones and discovered his golden bones linked together; when struck, they produced a sound like a reed organ. In the third year of the Tianfu era, a stone pagoda was rebuilt over the site.
He was interred seven *li* to the east of the mountain, where a temple was first established and named Zhao-hua Monastery.
At the beginning of the Imperial Dynasty, the Min monk Zhi-ning compiled his treatises on doctrine from throughout the scriptures; this became known as the *He-lun*.

In the year Wushen of the Yuan-hou era, the Layman Zhang Shangying, known as Wu-jin, while serving as the Fiscal Commissioner for Jiang-zuo, traveled by imperial decree to Shouyang. He then observed the fasts and went to pay his respects at the monastery.

Beneath a dilapidated house, amidst a scattered collection of volumes, he discovered the *Huayan Xingxiu Jueyi Lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Practice of the Avataṃsaka) in four fascicles.
