Huineng replied, "I do not know. What kind of principle is this? The Second Patriarch prostrated himself and stood in his place.
Mozhao said, "You have attained my marrow. [The monk] asked, "Can it be called two different things? One day, the Sixth Patriarch said, "All of you, quickly prepare the boats;
I wish to return to Xinzhou. A monk asked, "After the Master has departed, when will you return?
The Patriarch replied, "When the leaves fall, they return to the root; when one comes, there are no words. Is this not also a distinct principle? It is just like this...
When Master Mazu gave a single shout, Baizhang was deaf for three days. Can one still find some underlying principle or logic in this?

As for the staff of Deshan, the shout of Linji, Xuefeng rolling the ball, Jueyan pointing his finger, Daowu performing a dance, Bimoye holding up a pitchfork, Danxia burning the wooden Buddha, and Zhaozhou interrogating the old woman—these various and manifold instances of comparison and evaluation.

In the future, this will accord perfectly with what the Old Śākyamuni did—pointing one finger to heaven and one finger to earth—fitting like the two halves of a tally, without the slightest discrepancy.
When some people hear such talk, they immediately say, "One need only clarify the causal conditions of the Eye of the Path;
as for other subtle and minute matters, once you have understood them, that is enough. Little do they realize that it is actually they themselves who are muddled and indistinct. It is simply...
This matter of the "Eye of the Path" (Dao-yan) is already a thousand errors and ten thousand mistakes. Some say:

"If it is like this, then such things as Dongshan’s Five Ranks of Sovereign and臣 (Minister), the Three Leaks, Linji’s Four Means of Selection, the recent Fusang’s Nine Strands, and Jianfu’s Two Kinds—though they cannot be one's own self—are nonetheless all the same. For what reason did the ancients [distinguish them]?"

Many have compiled these into categories, yet they do not realize that it is precisely because they are one and the same. It is for this very reason of oneness that the ancients compiled them into such collections.
To those who have attained awakening, when they observe these, there is not the slightest difference;

yet to those who follow the stream of intellectual understanding, there appear ten thousand distinctions and a thousand variations. Therefore, the ancients said: "Melt a vase, a plate, a hairpin, and an armlet into a single piece of gold," and "churn the butter."
Curd and clarified butter (*ghṛta*) are of one single flavor. If one is a person of subtle penetration, it is not necessary to proceed in this way.
A bottle, a plate, a hairpin, and a bracelet are fundamentally one gold; curd, milk, and clarified butter are originally one flavor. Why must they be melted and stirred?
Furthermore, I see certain brothers who, having recognized that which is "bright and lucid" as it moves and acts, immediately claim they have understood. Everywhere...

One requires the certification of a person of realization. A raised brow, a blink of the eye, palms joined, fists raised, a single blow of the staff, or a single shout—all are the total manifestation of my own mind.
To come forth in this manner, opening one’s mouth, is it right or not?
One might say that one abandons hundreds of thousands of great oceans and recognizes only a single bubble as the essence, taking it for the entire tide. This matter is immeasurable. It is not...
This is an inconceivable matter. How could it ever be reached by the deliberations and measurements of the limited consciousness of those who engage in conditioned thought?
Have you not seen what is taught in the scriptures: that it would be like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s glow, even if one were to continue for aeons as numerous as motes of dust?
In the end, they could not penetrate it. Furthermore, he said: "There is the cultivation of thought, which arises from the state of having a mind;

all such things are merely the illusory conditions of the six sense-objects and are not the true essence of the mind. He also said: "The empty and false, floating mind abounds in various clever views, yet it cannot accomplish the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment.
This is precisely what he meant. Thus, truth and falsehood share the same source, and falsehood is established because of truth; how can one help it?
Few are those who exhaustively penetrate the root source; most follow the branches and pursue the leaves, turning instead into men who merely dally with shadows.

If one were indeed to exhaustively penetrate the source of the Dharma, then movement and stillness, coming and going, would all be the Tathāgatagarbha. If this is not yet the case, it is simply to mistake a thief for one’s own son;
thus, the family’s wealth and treasures will never be realized, and one will instead be obstructed by the dust of emotions and the consciousness of karma, [obscuring] the spiritual source.
The light of wondrous wisdom cannot be manifested, and its great function fails to appear before one.

A true man of great character naturally possesses a spirit that fills the heavens and a majestic presence that encompasses the earth. The era of Vimalacitra is not distant; Maitreya is not yet to come.

Suddenly, if the eye of the Way opens at once, you will sit firmly atop the crown of Vairocana, seeing no Buddhas or patriarchs appearing in the world, while the old monks throughout the land look up [in awe].
To speak in such a manner before those who are true practitioners is much like flaunting one's own knowledge;
it is an offense against their pure hearing. Yet, those whose minds are enlightened perceive the meaning beyond the words, while those of deluded sentiments cannot help but laugh it off lightly.
The Record of the Founding Patriarch of Tiantzhu, Chan Master Chonghui, says: "The Patriarch’s coming from the West was like a fortune-teller.
Seeing that you did not understand, he drilled through the lines of the divination for you. Once good and bad fortune had arisen, you were to observe them for yourself at once.
At that time, a monk asked, "What is the person who sells fortunes? He replied, "As soon as one steps out the door, it is no longer accurate. If...

I, this mountain monk, am not like that. The Patriarch’s intent in coming from the West was like the sound of a crow calling; it was as if signs of good or ill fortune were about to manifest, informing people beforehand.
The people of the world did not understand this, yet they claimed the crow’s cry was an omen of calamity sent to them, and so they reviled and drove it away.

Had the crow not cried out, the matter of good or ill fortune would have remained undetermined. Although its original intention was to be helpful, it could not avoid receiving a wicked response. Suddenly—
Suppose someone were to come forward and say: "Just now you spoke of causes and conditions throughout the past and present, yet there were not so many different matters;
how is it that you are now speaking in such a manner? Is this not a contradiction in your own words? You should simply say to him: "There is another good place here;
wait until you have become an old crow, and then I will speak to you. [He would then] stand for a long time.
The Essential Teachings of Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin of Tianning. He showed them to Zangzhong Long, saying:

"Since the time of the Patriarchs, we have focused solely on the direct transmission of the single path, taking no pleasure in 'carrying water and dragging mud' or issuing proclamations that establish sectarian strongholds to leave people at a standstill.

Indeed, throughout the more than three hundred assemblies of Śākyamuni Buddha, he established teachings according to the capacities of his audience and set forth models for the world; for the most part,"
It is thoroughly pervasive. Therefore, this final direct and swift path is concise and essential, engaging those of the highest capacity.

Although from the time of Kāśyapa through twenty-eight generations there was little demonstration of external mechanisms and much revelation of principle and wisdom, at the moment of transmission, there were none who did not provide face-to-face guidance.
This was like overturning a *khaṭvāṅga* staff, casting a needle into a bowl of water, displaying the mark of the circular light, holding up a red banner, or grasping a bright mirror.

The transmission of the Dharma verses, likened to an iron stake, and Bodhidharma’s refutation of the six schools— his establishing of propositions against the non-Buddhists, his making the world peaceful,
and his turning "my heaven" upside down to become "your dog"— all demonstrate a divine mechanism so swift that it cannot be fathomed by deliberation or thought.
Upon arriving in the Liang dynasty and traveling through the Wei, he spoke even more openly of the "separate transmission outside the teachings" and the "single transmission of the mind-seal.

The succession of the robe through six generations was clearly indicated; this continued until Caoxi Dajian, who provided a detailed exposition of both the doctrinal and the essential transmissions. Having passed through these periods for a long time, [the tradition] became firmly established.

The Great Master of the School of Right Vision and Great Liberation revolutionized the common path so that one would not be stalled by names and forms, nor fall into the verbal expressions of rationality.
He released a vital, vivid state—unfettered and free—wherein the wondrous pivot was revealed.
Through the wielding of staffs and shouts, he used words to dispel words, mechanisms to seize mechanisms, poison to counteract poison, and function to shatter function; thus did the [Dharma] flow.
For over seven hundred years, it has been transmitted through various branches and lineages, each excelling in its own particular style. Vast and resonant, its influence is beyond measure.
Yet, when one investigates its ultimate essence, it does not transcend the direct pointing to the human mind. Once the ground of the mind is clarified, there is not the slightest obstruction;
one sheds all notions of victory and defeat, self and other, right and wrong, as well as intellectual views and conceptual understandings, penetrating to the state of great rest and great peace.
In the field of stability, how could there be two different approaches? As it is said, "The hundred rivers flow in different directions, yet all return to the sea.
One must possess this superior capacity for enlightenment, endowed with lofty discernment and far-reaching vision, and have the resolve to perpetuate the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
only then can one enter deeply into the inner sanctum, gain thorough conviction, and directly maintain the Dharma. Only then may one receive certification and be fit to serve as...
Planting weeds. You should discard this and treasure these words with extreme care; do not treat them lightly or let them pass.
The late Master Wuzu was throughout his life solitary and austere, rarely granting approval. Standing firm and dry like a sheer cliff, he relied solely upon this one point.
He often said of himself, "It is like leaning against Mount Sumeru. How could he allow his words to fall into emptiness or be used as mere slick-headed deception to hoodwink others? Taking this—
This "Tasteless Iron Sour [Jian]" verse on splitting the jaw is presented to students to be chewed upon;

one must wait until their "bottom of the bucket" falls out, until they have lost such evil knowledge and views, until not even a thread hangs in their breast, and they have penetrated through to utter purity.

Only then may one begin to apply the training; only then can one restrain the fists and kicks. Thereafter, the Vajra King’s Precious Sword is shown to test whether they are truly able to practice and bear the burden.

When everything is utterly pure and non-existent—where mountains are simply mountains and waters are simply waters—one must further turn toward that realm where even the thousand sages cannot entangle or confine; therein, one realizes the realization attained by all the patriarchs since antiquity.
To uphold the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and apply it for the sake of sentient beings, one must still drive the plowman’s ox and seize the hungry man’s food;
when this is verified and perfected without leakage, one is a true practitioner of the ancestral house.

In the kingdom of Magadha, [the Buddha] personally enacted this command, and at Shaolin, [Bodhidharma] faced the wall to fully uphold the orthodox lineage. Yet, the people of the time misunderstood, and consequently...

To remain silent and think that this constitutes being "seamless" and "beyond intellectual grasp," standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high—this is not yet to know the matter of one's own fundamental nature.
To indulge in the calculations of conceptual consciousness and take this for a "lofty view" is a grave illness. The matter transmitted from of old was never like this.
Yantou said: "It is merely a tiny bit revealed before one's eyes, like the spark struck from flint or a flash of lightning. If you try to deliberate upon it..."
It cannot be attained. Do not harbor doubts or attachments; this is the sphere of practice for those who have transcended. Unless one knows that there *is* [this reality], no one can know it.

Zhaozhou’s “Go drink tea,” Bimozhe holding up his staff, Xuefeng rolling the ball, Heshan beating the drum, Zhizhi’s single finger, Guizong dragging the stone, Xuansha’s “not yet thorough,” Deshan’s staff, and Linji’s shout—all of these are means of penetrating through.

To the very bottom. To cut through the entanglements directly. Great capacity and great function; though there be a thousand variations and ten thousand distinctions, they all return to a single source.
This can be used to untangle the sticky and remove the bonds for others. If one interprets according to the words, then one must be given the fodder appropriate to one's own portion.
It is like ten *hu* of donkey’s milk: with but a single drop of lion’s milk, it is all dispersed. This is what must be transmitted from foot to foot.
Maintain this. Let it continue in succession for a long time; you must simply not yield to human sentiment and not allow it to become easy, for only then will it be authentic.
"The final phrase is where one first reaches the secure gate"—truly, these are the words! To transcend birth and death and to grasp the seal of the true Dharma entirely depends upon this very moment.
Only those who step upon the pivotal bolt at the highest level will truly understand. Master Long.

Zhizang attained enlightenment in Huxiang and spent over ten years traveling between Beishan and other places. He was a true seeker who had thoroughly investigated the profound mysteries and was a monk of genuine caliber.
Consequently, he was appointed to share the teaching seat and instruct disciples for three years.

Having received the Imperial Decree to move to Tianning in the capital, I desired to obtain his Dharma words to manifest our spiritual affinity; thus, I have transcribed these several passages for him. The tenth month of the sixth year of Xuanhe.
On the middle day of the second month, the old monk Foguo wrote this.
Zen Master Foyan Yuan of Longmen addressed the assembly, saying: "If one can now directly believe that 'it is so,' one is already called an inferior person;
how much more so if one cannot even directly believe it—what use is such a person? One must directly believe."
"What is this so-called 'not being mediocre'? Where have you been all this time?
You must know that you have already lost a piece [of the truth]. Thus, what was previously unresolved becomes an extraneous view.

I observe that among the ancients of old, there were those who attained enlightenment from delusion; everything that has been circulated is precisely [the teaching] of attaining enlightenment from delusion."
There are those who awaken and thereby understand delusion; all that is propagated for them consists of dharma-gates for awakening and understanding delusion.
There are those for whom there is neither delusion nor awakening; all that is propagated for them consists of dharma-gates of neither delusion nor awakening.

Furthermore, those who come later and attain awakening after having been deluded are also very numerous, yet they are truly not worth mentioning; how much less so those who neither know awakening nor [delusion].
To be "awakened to delusion"—this is precisely the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Only those from the past such as Nanquan and Guizong could truly call this the "view of neither delusion nor awakening. Nowadays, students merely parrot the talk of "neither delusion nor awakening," yet how have they ever actually arrived at it?
You must not speak lightly; it is because you still harbor doubts. I shall now ask you one thing.
Regarding this matter: when you first entered your mother’s womb, what did you bring with you? When you came, there was not a single thing;

there was only this mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*), which is neither form nor appearance. When the time comes for death, you cast off this burden of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and again there is not a single thing—there is only this mind-consciousness.
For those who now travel as mendicants and enter into the assembly, this very thing is the sovereign master.

Furthermore, I ask you now: this body, which is sustained by the vital breath and the essence-blood of your parents and grasped as "my body," begins at birth and gradually grows into its present form—all of this is said to belong to you. But tell me, does it belong to you or not?
If you say it belongs to you, consider that when you first entered the womb, you brought nothing with you; this body is merely the essence-blood of your parents.
At that time, it belonged to you; yet, even though you were meant to live for a hundred years, you still cast off this corpse. How could it have ever belonged to you?
If you say it does not belong to you, look at how you cannot do without it for even a single step. When scolded, it allows you to quell your anger;
when in pain, it enables you to endure. How can you say it does not belong to you? Try to examine it closely and determine whether it exists or not; you will surely be able to distinguish it.
It is not that [the Way] does not descend; it is simply because the root of doubt has not been severed.
When one says the Way "comes," from the time of birth, as one gradually grows to three years, five years, and even up to twenty years, it remains fixed and unchanging.

By forty or fifty years, while this body is shifting and decaying moment by moment—moment by moment impermanent—it can certainly not be called "existent. When one says the Way "comes" in various ways, it functions...
If one attempts to resolve this through understanding, one will not yet attain the Way. Long ago, there was a man who lost his way while traveling and stayed overnight in an empty house.
At night, a ghost arrived carrying a corpse on its back. Shortly thereafter, another ghost came and said, "This corpse is mine.
The first ghost replied, "I brought it here from that place. The second ghost then forcibly seized it. The first ghost said, "This..."
Among them was a traveling guest who could serve as a witness. The two ghosts drew near and asked, "Whose corpse is this that has been brought here?

The guest reflected to himself, "Both ghosts are malevolent; surely one of them will harm me. I have heard that those who do not speak falsely at the moment of death will certainly be reborn in heaven.
He then pointed to the first ghost and said, "This ghost brought it. The second ghost flew into a great rage and tore the guest away.
The front ghost apologized in shame, saying, "Because you provided testimony for my sake, I have caused your limbs to be incomplete.
He then restored each part of the corpse one by one. However, the head, the torso, and the internal organs had already been taken by the rear ghost;
the front ghost restored these as well, one by one from the corpse. The two ghosts then contended on the ground over the flesh until it was completely consumed.
He departed. Then, before the eyes of the traveler, he saw that his parents' bodies had already been devoured by two ghosts.
He looked back at the body he had exchanged and wondered: what is this? Is it me? Is it not me? Does it exist? Does it not exist?
Thereupon, his mind became utterly distraught. He ran to a monastery and saw a bhikṣu, to whom he recounted all that had occurred. The bhikṣu—
He said, "This man is easily transformed and delivered; he already knows that this body is not real.

Thereupon, [the Master] briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma, and the man immediately attained the fruit of the Path. You people merely speak of investigating Zen and citing kōans, and you call this the Buddha-dharma.
This is the marrow of Zen. Why do you not investigate it with such doubt? Do you understand? Your body is not non-existent;
its existence is due to the mind. Yet, as for the body, it has never existed. Nor is it that the mind is non-existent; yet, as for the body, it has never been non-existent. Do you understand?
Furthermore, to say that the mind is neither existent nor non-existent—after all, this is not what you originally possessed. Now...
There is nothing. That which was originally non-existent now exists. Such views of permanence and annihilation have long been established.
Chan Master Chanti Zhao of Letan addressed the assembly, saying: "Gentlemen, how hot it is! Having reached the height of heat, one then encounters the height of cold.
This constant cycle of cold and heat oppresses people far too much. If you have already clarified the matter of your own life, then even in the cold..."
When it is cold for others, it is cold for you; when it is hot for others, it is hot for you. If one has not yet clarified this matter for oneself, then in the cold, the cold kills one;
in the heat, the heat kills one. But tell me: at the time when it is neither cold nor hot, where is the person?
Where is the Buddha? There is neither Buddha nor sentient beings. "Buddha" is simply the meaning of awakening—what is called self-awakening and awakening others. Awakening...
"The perfection of conduct—do you understand this? It is just like when you are bitten by a louse; that is self-awakening (*sva-bodha*).

To know that others are being bitten in the same way is called awakening others (*para-bodha*). Furthermore, to know that oneself and all sentient beings are fundamentally equal is called the perfection of awakening-conduct (*bodhi-caryā-paripūri*).
Where else could a Buddha come from? Your current practice of Chan is merely a matter of learning."
To study the Buddha as a phenomenon external to the mind is called being a non-Buddhist (tīrthika); this is termed a false view. Have you not seen what the Tathāgata Śākyamuni said:
"In a past life, I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, yet in reality, there was not a single dharma to be obtained"?
And what Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said: "In a past life, I saw the Ancient Avalokiteśvara; how could there have been another Buddha coming? You—
Fellows, you need not seek anything else now; you simply look upon the ancient Zhang as Zhang, and upon the ancient Li as Li.
Then no one will be able to do anything with you, and throughout the twelve hours of the day, you will never find freedom.
It is simply because you love learning about the Buddha that this corpse—the four great elements and five aggregates—obstructs and kills you.
Therefore, Baofeng earnestly instructed you: "If you act as one who has died the Great Death, then you will not expend much mental effort.

If you can be like one who has died the Great Death, you will no longer perceive the four great elements; even the seven great elements will naturally extinguish themselves. As for these seven great elements:
These are earth, water, fire, wind, space, consciousness, and awakening. As for the great element of space: you, son of the Chan school, sit until not a single thought arises;
the past and future limits are severed; subject and object are both forgotten; and you see only emptiness and nothingness.
Enveloped by this nature of emptiness, you no longer perceive the four [elements]. Yet, emptiness has no self-nature; it is established as "emptiness" because of that very nature. Sit further still.
It has been a long time. There is no such thing as a "great emptiness"; there is only the person who understands the matter, whom one calls the "great consciousness.
When people of today practice their cultivation and reach this point, they call it the "original face" and rely upon the Dharma-body.
This is precisely to mistake a thief for one's own son. If you encounter Baofeng, he will teach you to let go all at once; if you can let go all at once—
Let go. Even if you wait from birth until old age, you will only end up as a worn-out Chan practitioner. This too is merely practicing according to the teachings, principles, practice, and fruition;
it is certainly not the separate transmission outside the teachings. As for what are called the teachings, principles, practice, and fruition:
The names and phrases spoken by the various sages of antiquity are called "teaching" (dharma). To proceed toward the goal by means of these names and phrases is called "principle" (tattva).

To practice according to these names and phrases is called "conduct" (caryā). To realize the goal through these names and phrases is called "fruit" (phala). Nevertheless, one has not yet escaped the experience of birth.
When one relies solely on the Jewel Peak [Samādhi], like a great dead person, one no longer perceives a body moistened by saliva, tears, pus, or blood;
thus, there is no water element (*āpas*). Furthermore, one no longer perceives warmth or the capacity for movement and activity; thus, there is no fire element (*tejas*) or wind element (*vāyu*).
Moreover, one no longer perceives the boundaries of past or future; with both object and self forgotten, there is no space element (*ākāśa*). Furthermore...

When one sees those who are proficient in worldly affairs, there is no "greatness of knowledge. Furthermore, when one does not see those who possess self-awakening and awakening others, whose awakening and practice are perfected, there is no "greatness of awakening.
Since these seven greatnesses are empty, how could the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics—the purple-golden hue—possibly be attained?
Therefore it is said: "Fundamental awakening is wondrously luminous; the nature of awakening is luminously wondrous. This is also called the Dharma.
The body is signless, like empty space. If you know the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it belongs to the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*);

if there is wearing of robes and eating of food, along with the excretion of feces and urine, it belongs to the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). As the Great Master Yongjia said: "The three bodies and four wisdoms are the mystery within the essence;
the eight liberations and six supernormal powers are the seal of the mind-ground. He also said: "Clearly seeing, there is not a single thing. Furthermore—
There is no person, nor is there a Buddha. The great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning.
If it were Bao Feng, he would have said to you: "To see clearly is like being a great dead man—neither joy nor anger."
Truly, the entire body acts as a different species; meeting him everywhere, he is real everywhere. [The Master] stood for a long time.

Chan Master Miaokuan Qian of Kaishan, at the conclusion of the summer retreat, addressed the assembly, saying: "The ancient sages established this 'closing of the summer' (jie-xia), calling it 'protecting life.

They observed the three-month summer retreat with their feet restrained. For those of late learning and beginners, this is the means to cultivate practice, discern the Way, and purify the three karmas."
Among the four modes of deportment, do not allow for any transgression. I venture to ask the great assembly:
how, then, should one cultivate? How should one practice? If you say there is a dharma to be cultivated or practiced, you fall into deception.
If you say there is not a single dharma to be cultivated or practiced, how can one attain peace and security? Have you not seen that in the past, a monk asked an elder: "How [should one act]?"
"This is cultivation. Xu宿 said, "Seeing the nature is cultivation. One often encounters such talk in the monasteries and takes it for granted;

yet one does not realize that these ancients had truly realized and awakened to the ultimate point, responding from their own fundamental ground without such flowery artifice. They did not strike with the staff, nor did they shout, nor...
The Way is like a frog leaping up to the Brahma Heaven; it is like an earthworm crossing over the Eastern Sea. It is not at all like this. Simply speak to them plainly:
"Seeing one's nature is the practice of cultivation. This is also truly so. But tell me, what is the nature of you all?
And how do you see this matter? It is truly laughable. Before you have seen it, for a thousand...
It is difficult beyond measure. Yet, once it is seen, there is nothing easier than this ease.

I recall that in the past, there was a fellow practitioner who had long studied Chan under the old master. He reached the very limit where all skillful means are exhausted, yet he simply could not penetrate through.
Every day when I entered the room to question him, he would only reply, "I do not understand. There was a later...
He laughed at others. Having practiced Chan for many years, he could only say, "I do not understand. When his fellow practitioners heard this, they could not bear it and said, "You little devil!
Before you were even born into this world, I already went three times to the Heshan Temple to extract your teeth.
Let me teach you something! Later, after he had attained realization through Chan, they gathered together at the hermitage. One—
One day, while discussing an ancient case (gū) with a verse by Master Yong, I, this mountain monk, cited his verse on the story of the Five-Supernatural-Powers Seer, saying:
"Throughout immeasurable kalpas, one has never encountered it; how can one reach its center without moving? Do not say that the Buddha-dharma is but a trifle;
what about that one supernormal power of Gautama? I, this mountain monk, cherish his words: "How can one reach its center without moving? Since he already...
Movement. How can you reach it? Hūṃ. Hūṃ. This very place is the point of intersection; there is no space between them even for a hair’s breadth.
The difficulty lies right here; the ease also lies right here. One must be a person of immeasurable capacity to succeed.
A fellow practitioner then asked, "Why do you say that Gautama’s single penetration is the most bitter? I, the mountain monk, replied to him, "You have not yet..."
"When I appeared in the world, I already withdrew my tusks three times within the temple of Mount Huo. Facing one another, we could not help but burst into loud laughter;
naturally, this strikes the south and moves the north. Only in this way can it be called 'seeing one's nature.'"
The Buddhas of the three periods of time saw that you had deluded this very nature and were thus pointlessly subjected to saṃsāra.

Therefore, they gave rise to compassion and exercised pity, extensively expounding the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. It was as if they were exchanging bitter gourds for honeyed fruits to wash away the karmic roots of you all.
Originally there is no substantial reality; it is because you possess the view of a "sentient being" that they bring forth a Buddha to cleanse you.
Because you possess the view of ignorance, I bring forth bodhi to wash it away from you.
Because you possess the view of birth and death, I bring forth nirvana to wash it away from you. If you did not have these various views, then the Buddha would not have appeared in the world;
he would not have taught the Dharma; he would not have spoken of seeing one's nature; nor would he have spoken of cultivation.
Indeed, within this nature, there has fundamentally been no Buddha, nor any sentient beings; fundamentally no bodhi, nor any afflictions; fundamentally no nirvana, nor any birth-and-death.
Therefore, the ancients said: "There are no three realms from which to escape; there is no bodhi to be sought; there are no Buddhas or patriarchs to be realized;
there are no sentient beings to be saved. It is pure and naked, and also free and easy—there is nothing to be grasped.
It can be grasped; yet, though there is nothing to grasp, it can manifest Buddhas, manifest sentient beings, manifest bodhi, manifest afflictions, manifest nirvana, and manifest birth-and-death.
Do not look at what it manifests. What is it before it manifests? Therefore, Master Linji said:
"A student of the Way must attain a truly authentic understanding. If one attains a truly authentic understanding..."
Unstuck in birth and death, free in going and staying, there is no need to seek excellence from another; excellence arrives of its own accord.

Only in this way can it be called "cultivation. It is not some other dharma being taught to you as cultivation. If there were any other dharma, it would entirely belong to the sequential causes and effects of the Three Vehicles, rather than being the primordial Buddha.

He spoke of his return to escort the remains of Cijue for cremation. Then, proceeding by stages, he accepted the invitation from Kaishan;
he entered the monastery and ascended the hall, exchanging greetings with guests and seeing them off—busily occupied until this very day. Now tell me: is this the Buddha-dharma or the worldly dharma?
Is it the realization of nature or the non-realization of nature? Is it cultivation or the lack of cultivation? When one arrives here, how is it?
It is certain. Often, out of ten people, five or six will certainly not emerge [from their delusion]. This brings to mind when Master Geyu was ascending the hall and said:
"Do not say that only those who have not yet attained are in a state of frantic agitation.
Even those who have attained and clearly understand that there is a place to go are still in a state of frantic agitation. Yunmen later brought up this story and questioned his head monk:
The Seat (the Chief Monk) said, "How is it? The Gatekeeper (Muzhou) said, "The Head Seat has lived here for a long time;
his head is white and his teeth are yellow, yet he speaks such words. The Seat asked, "I wonder, how about you, Senior Monk? The Gatekeeper said:
"The essential path is attained immediately; upon seeing it, one sees it. If you do not see it, do not confuse the Way.
Zhaozuo asked, "As for what the Abbot said—that 'it is floating and pressing'—what about that? Yunmen replied, "A cangue on the head and shackles on the feet.
Zhaozuo said, "In that case, there is no Buddha-dharma. Yunmen said, "This is the realm of the great beings Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra."
The Master said: "Great and small Yunmen—beforehand he was enough to terrify people to death; afterwards he was enough to make people laugh to death.
Had I been there at that time, I would have said to him: 'Do not speak such foul words.
You all, hearing this being said, must not go about trying to calculate it here; you must truly reach this state before you will succeed. If you truly reach this state..."
Once you know Yunmen’s point of arrival, you will know Guoqingshan’s point of arrival; once you know Guoqingshan’s point of arrival, you will know Kaishan’s point of arrival;
once you know Kaishan’s point of arrival, you will know the point of arrival of one's own original nature.
Once you have known where the person’s own nature falls, you must not yet stop; you must further practice for thirty years until you have attained a separate livelihood.
Why is this so? Have you not heard it said: "The head of a snake still requires a heavy scratching?"

Even if one’s faculty were as swift as a flash of lightning and one’s eloquence like a cascading river—such that one could analyze the path and reach the destination—it would still not equal returning to me the "First Head. This morning, within the room, there was nothing extraordinary at all.

The nostrils are in my hands; I certainly do not intend for you to turn back a phrase or employ some clever artifice, only to say that you have "hit the mark."

It is so. Do not say you have exhausted the understanding of past and present, that you have mastered all distinctions, or that you have fully realized the great capacity and great function—like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning, the relationship between father and son, ruler and subject, and the arts of seizing and releasing, killing and enlivening. If there is even a single point here that is not clear, then all of this is irrelevant;
what more can be said of such grand talk? Have you not seen the Old Man with the Yellow Face say: "The pine tree is straight..."
The thorns are curved; the crane is white, the crow is black—all of these are understood through their fundamental causes.
I venture to ask the great assembly: Why are the pines straight? Why are the thorns curved? Why is the crane white? Why is the crow black?

There is a certain kind of arbitrary person who says, "Differences arise because one receives differential retribution. I shall ask you this: what cause did the pine create, and what retribution did the thorn receive?
What kind of retribution? It has nothing to do with your ability to analyze or discern. Furthermore, there is another class who says:

"Pines are naturally straight, thorns are naturally curved, cranes are naturally white, and crows are naturally black. This is the view of the "Naturally-Existent" (Svabhāvavāda) heretics among the ninety-six types of non-Buddhist schools in India.
Again, there is another class who calls this "Mind-Only," and they cite the teaching that "the three realms are mind-only."
"Taking 'all phenomena are but consciousness' as the evidence, let me ask you this:

since it is but a single mind, why are there the curved and the straight, the dark and the white? Furthermore, these distinctions cannot be fully resolved. Again, some say: 'All phenomena are originally still;
it is only people who create their own clamor. Why do they give rise to such manifold discrimination? Let me ask you: call the curved..."
Can you call the direct the indirect? Can you call the white the profound? Furthermore, it cannot be analyzed or categorized.
Brothers, such evil knowledge and evil views are all due to failing to understand the fundamental source; they are merely beating around the bush and seeking complications for themselves.
You have never reached the place that is simple, direct, and straightforward, nor the place that is vast, expansive, and clear. Have you not seen Baoyun suddenly extend his hand?
He said: "For what reason is it called 'the hand'? Tell me, where does Baiyun’s intention lie? And how would you respond?
Within the Gate of the Patriarchs, there is no dharma that is not attended to, and no matter that is not penetrated.

Regarding this fundamental matter: do not say that one must utter a shout or strike a blow; you have already missed it. It is right here and now.
You merely continue to roar from your lips, while within your belly it remains a vast, dark void. For the time being, there is no connection at all.

The student said, "I do not understand. Yun said, "Three stalks, four stalks, all bent. The ancients were unimpeded in their directness and unimpeded in their subtlety.

When Master Huichang first came from Nanxiong, he carried within him a belly full of literary talent and eloquence; he relied upon Chan Master Yue of Yunfeng.

While reading the *Chuan Deng Lu*, he reached the kōan concerning the monk who asked about the "bush of bamboo" at Duofu; suddenly, he attained sudden enlightenment. Personally...
Seeing that the two masters were in harmony with one another, he went straight back to Huangbo. As soon as he spread out his sitting mat, Nan said, "You have entered my room.

Excerpts from Two Cases of Master Fohui Quan of Jiangshan.
Case: Ba Ling addressed the assembly: "The Patriarch said, 'It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving.
Since it is neither wind nor banner, where does one place it? If anyone can act as the Patriarch’s advocate, come forth and meet with Ba Ling.
Xuedou said: "The wind moves; the banner moves. Since it is both wind and banner, where does one place it? If anyone..."
Acting as the master for Ba’ling, he comes forth to meet Xuedou. The Master said: "Do you wish to know where these two venerable seniors have ended up?
Jiangshan will tell you a parable for you. It is like a family whose ancestors have long possessed immense wealth and property.
There were two brothers who each competed in their expenditures; the elder spent five hundred, while the younger..."
This person caused them to be linked together; day after day and month after month, they fought without ceasing, until the ancestral estate and livelihood were suddenly squandered all at once.
Consequently, their descendants were left with no place to find security or establish their lives.
Suddenly, a close friend, seeing that the descendants were destitute and exposed, lent them his own ancestral house, and they took up residence therein.
Descendants must reflect upon their ancestral estate of old; how could it now belong to another?

You must employ skillful means to recover the original deed, for only then will you have reached the ultimate goal. If you merely follow along with the present day by day, accepting whatever comes your way, you will inevitably remain living under the roof of another.
O Great Assembly, Jiangshan has finished speaking this parable for you. Now, [consider this:]...
He questioned the assembly: "By what means can one recover the original contract from that time?
He then cited the story of a monk asking Jia Shan about the "realm" (jing), and Fa Yan’s response [as follows]. The Master said:
"All you Zen adepts, even Master Fayan did not realize he had fallen into a trap. If it is not called 'the realm,' what would you call it? Since he could not cut it off..."
To sever both ends and cause descendants in later generations to bite and chew one another, saying: "Heaven and earth share the same root;
the myriad things are one body; there is no dharma outside the mind, and no mind outside dharma"—such various calculations are just like dreaming within a dream.
How could they know that the Mother of Ghosts has lost her beloved child and has nowhere to seek its traces? *Sēn*.
The Sandalwood Spirit was overturned and entwined by snakes; blood flowed from his eyes.

"Clouds atop trees. Do you still know of one who, without traversing the rungs of the various sages' ladder, alone transcends the mundane world?
The Master then laughed heartily.
He brought up the story of Deshan’s alms-bowl and said, "Yantou and Deshan have both been judged by the same verdict; Xuefeng has passed down fifteen hundred blows."
"The ground where a hundred teachers of goodness reside.

The question lies within the answer; the answer lies within the question. If you hesitate or deliberate, I, the old monk, will be beneath your feet. The Master said: "Baoying..."
One should simply understand how to hold fast. Cuiyan, however, was not like this: Hanshan fell to the ground, Shide helped him up, and Fenggan prostrated himself;
yet he did not see Mañjuśrī. Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva frequented wine shops like a fish;
moreover, he did not recognize his own master. Then, he struck the ground once with his staff.

I simply say: 'The walls have ears.

"Feeding the donkey, feeding the horse. Master Langya Jue said, "Quickly, bring the food!
The Master said, "Although Langya has this 'order of non-transgression,' if it were Baiyun, it would not be so. It is like feeding a donkey or feeding a horse;
simply say: 'May the practitioner always remain as they are today.'"
The Case: Longya’s verse says: "I traveled to every famous mountain on foot, Toiling for many years until my feet were worn through with socks.

Now that I am old, I can no longer walk; In my hand, I hold this broken wooden ladle. The Master said: "The old man Longya may truly be said to find it difficult to forget what he is most familiar with."
Two cases concerning Chan Master Baoning Yong.
Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: "On South Mountain there is a turtle-nosed snake; you all must look at it very carefully. Changqing said [as follows].

Understood. Case cited:
When Wuzhuo met Mañjuśrī while they were drinking tea, Mañjuśrī lifted up a glass cup and asked, "Is there such a thing as this in the South?
The Master (Zhaozhou) answered on his behalf by pointing to his own mouth.
Two cases concerning Chan Master Huanglong Huichang Xin:
The World-Honored One held up a flower; Kāśyapa smiled. The Master said: "To pierce straight through the skull is already to have exchanged one's eyes.

[The Master] raised the case. Emperor Zhuangzong said, "I have recovered the Central Plains and acquired a treasure, yet there is no one to appraise its value.
Xinghua [responded as follows]. The Master said: "Xinghua acted according to the situation at that moment; however, he failed to realize that he was burying an Emperor of the Day.
At that time, had he simply said, 'It is a pearl from a clam or oyster,' even if it were acquired, it would have been of no use."
I teach him that hereafter there shall be a separate way of life, so as to avoid mutual neglect.
Now, if someone were to ask you, Elder, how would you appraise it?
Three cases concerning Chan Master Wenzhen Yun’an of Letan.

Linji’s little bit of livelihood—each has divided their own territory and established their boundaries, their vital energy piercing the universe, causing even clear-eyed monks to do nothing but laugh.

Case: One day the World-Honored One saw Mañjuśrī standing outside the gate and said, "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī, why do you not come inside?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I do not see a single dharma outside the gate; why do you instruct me to enter?"
The Master spoke on their behalf, saying: "I am not your equal.

"The head is sold at a high price. Have you all heard it yet? If you have not, give me back my ears!

The monk said, "It is. Yunmen said, "The talk has fallen. The Master asked, "Where is the point where the talk has fallen?

Here are two cases cited by Chan Master Zhikai Zhengjue Yi.
Master Jia Shan’s verse says: "Clearly there is no dharma of awakening; the dharma of awakening is what deludes people. Stretching out both legs, I sleep."
"Neither false nor true. The Master said, "O virtuous practitioners of Zen! This is the wondrous medicine for curing the malady of those who have long been attached to the precious city.

Until you have reached the land of the transformed city, you must strictly avoid taking it by mistake. Should you take it, Jīvaka will fold his hands in helplessness and the King of Physicians will knit his brows in dismay."
Case: Zhaozhou addressed the assembly, saying, "Sometimes I take a blade of grass and make it into a sixteen-foot golden body;
sometimes I take a sixteen-foot golden body and make it into a blade of grass. Wufeng said, "I sometimes take my staff and make it into the Buddhas of the three periods;

Rest for the evening. Drifting with the waves and following the current, all is in vain. How many practitioners of meditation beneath the forest trees can reach the ultimate goal with a mind free from artifice?
He then gave a shout and said: "Do not judge others by your own standard."

To speak thus, you fail to realize that Yunmen has fallen within the circle and sleeve of the Yellow-Faced Old Man;
even until now, he cannot leap out. If you can see through this point, not only will you recognize Śākyamuni, but you will also pierce the heels of Yunmen.

A footnote: "To covet one more cup of wine, he lost the fish in his entire boat.

In monastic discourse, one must not simply stop; otherwise, one merely stirs up the vapors of rice gruel and meals to pass for one's entire life.
It is said: Xuedou addressed the assembly, saying, "The Great Gate of Generosity is open, with no obstructions. Suppose a monk were suddenly to come forth."

"Do you all understand? After a long silence, he said: "Wait for empty space to fall to the ground."

Are not these very lanterns and pillars, the great earth and mountains and rivers before you right now, your fellow practitioners whom you strike and bump into?

Case: Master Zhenjing addressed the assembly, saying: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things share the same substance as I.
From head to toe, they are arranged horizontally and vertically. When a fire breaks out on the continent of Uttarakuru, it burns away the eyebrows of Śakra;
the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea cannot bear the pain and lets out a roar of thunder, such that the oceans are overturned and the mountains are uprooted."
Yue: The clouds darken the vast sky. At the crossroads, Old Zhao, son of Liáo, awakens from his drunken stupor and rises up.
Clapping his hands, he laughs heartily and says, "In the city of Yún-yáng, there have been few thieves lately. He then picks up his staff and says:
"Thief! Thief! The Master said, "That was quite a performance of self-display. But alas, the nostrils and eyes each have their own master. Why?

At that moment, a dog happened to bark from the east corridor; the Master called to an attendant to investigate the gate.

Five Cases from the Record of Chan Master Tiantong Ying’an Hua.
Master Dayu Zhi addressed the assembly: "Everyone has gathered here to eat some radish soup. If you call it 'a bowl of radish soup,' you will enter hell as fast as a shooting arrow.
The Master [Ying’an] said: "Excellent words! Yet, for all their excellence, they have no source. Is there anyone who can discern this?"
[The monk] said, "I have obtained it. I will give you one *liang* of gold. He raised [the matter].
The Sixth Patriarch said, "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. It is your mind moving, O worthy one.
The Master said, "One blind man leading a crowd of blind men, pulling each other into a pit of fire."

He said, "Strike the one in the center. The monk bowed; Xinghua said, "The assembly, yesterday I went to a village meal.
On my way back, midway, I encountered a sudden storm of wind and rain, so I took refuge in an old temple and got through safely. The Master said, "I see the lamp shining."
The Buddha’s original radiance and auspicious signs were like this.
[The Master] raised a case: A monk asked Yunmen, "If one does not give rise to a single thought, is there still any transgression?
Yunmen said, "Mount Sumeru. The Master said: "Yunmen’s answer was indeed accurate and appropriate, yet it nonetheless fell into the 'second head. Mingguo, however—"

"Please bring forth that question. It is said:

the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. The Master said, "The hundred birds do not come and spring has already grown old;
I know not who is the person who reaches the hermitage."
Ciming raised his hand and said to the assembly, "All worthy sages and saints are distinguished by means of the dharma of non-action (wuwei).
That mountain in front is the attendant mountain; that mountain behind is the main mountain. But tell me, where does the dharma of non-action reside? After a long silence, he said:
The subsequent text is extensive; let it be reserved for another day. The Master said: "Tiantong also wears a single eye.

A Case from Master Bian of the Main Hall at Daochang Monastery:
When Bodhidharma first met Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the Emperor asked, "What is the primary meaning of the holy truth? He replied, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage.
The Emperor said, "Who is it that stands before me? He replied, "I do not know. The Emperor was not in accord with him, so he subsequently crossed the river and went to the Wei.
After Bodhidharma had departed, Master Zhigong asked, "Your Majesty, do you recognize this man? The Emperor replied, "I do not.
Zhigong said, "This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara; he transmits the Buddha’s Mind-Seal. The Emperor felt remorse and dispatched a messenger to go and retrieve him.
Master Zhigong said, "Do not say that because Your Majesty sent an envoy to fetch him, he would not return even if the people of the entire nation went. He simply would not come back.
The Master said, "Later, there were some who said, 'If one examines it by the calendar, fourteen years have already passed since Master Zhigong entered parinirvāṇa.
How could there have been such an event beforehand? At that time, Xuedou did not examine the matter at all. The Master laughed."
He said: "From antiquity to the present, not a single person has ever attained clear realization. How bitter it is for the Buddha!
Little do they know that Xuedou, at the very beginning of his *Gong'an* verses, established this great causal nexus to see those ancients who had realized the true pulse of the Dharma.
He spread a vast net across the heavens to await the fish of his own choosing. As the years and months have deepened, [the net] has become even more..."
Seeing shrimp, fish, and small crabs—how many clear-eyed monks have had their skulls pierced through by these things!

This mountain monk cannot restrain his impatience; for your sakes, I shall reveal a bit of news: A sharp blade may cut the flesh, yet the wound eventually heals; But malicious words wound a person, and the resentment never fades.
One sees only that at Guoqing Temple, the "talented" are honored; Who knows that in a wealthy household, even a young child is esteemed?
Jiao. Regarding the one case concerning Chan Master Guanzhong Huiahuai’s citation of Xuefeng attaining enlightenment at Mount Ao:
the Master said, "As for Yantou’s words, 'Each and every thing arises from oneself'..."
It flows forth from one’s own breast. Now tell me: when Xuefeng attained enlightenment three times previously, did it also flow forth from his own breast?
If it flowed forth from his own breast, then why is it said that he was still not yet settled?
If it did not flow forth from his own breast, then from where did it come? Is there anyone who can cut through this?
"Ma! If you can cut it off, not only will Xuefeng’s Ao Mountain be where enlightenment was attained, but all sentient beings throughout the entire world will simultaneously achieve perfect awakening.
If you cannot cut it off, then what is this talk of attaining enlightenment at Ao Mountain?
Even if one were to transmit the mind at Shaoshi, one would still not have seen it in a dream."
Master Dongchan Meng’an Yue presents one ancient case concerning "Cold Spring in the Deep Ravine.

"From within and without, he has deceived me into coming here. Even so, it is not yet known that Huo Shan has already died three thousand *li* away beneath the Secret Demon’s Fork. Let those with the eye of discernment distinguish this!

The Master said, "Dongshan relies on his position to deceive people; Zhenru turns with the wind to apply his teaching. Tonight, if suddenly there were...

Why? When going downhill, one does not run; a swift opportunity is difficult to encounter.

The Master said: "Are you making offerings to your family members today, Monk?

Not only did he cut off Yunmen’s heels, but he also gave vent to the indignation of all the monks in the world. Even so, it is just like when Yunmen spoke these words: [the dialogue continues].

within each and every speck of dust, who else could there be?

"I do not yet understand the meaning of this. To him, he further said: "The business of the donkey has not yet departed, and the business of the horse has already arrived."
Case: There was once a monk on Mount Xuefeng who went to a hermitage. His hair was long and he did not shave it; he used a wooden ladle to scoop water.
Whenever anyone asked him, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? he would say, "The stream is deep and the handle of the ladle is long.
When Xuefeng heard of this, he remarked, "How extraordinary! One day, he secretly took a razor and went there with his attendant.
[The Master] saw him. Feng said, "If you can speak the Way, I will not shave your head. The monk then washed his head with water, and Feng immediately shaved it off.
The Master said, "This monk is much like Zhuge Liang hiding in his thatched cottage;
only after the Prime Minister visited three times did he arise. But tell me, once he had arisen, what kind of business did he accomplish? A sharp sword sweeps open the heavens."
The earth is still; as soon as the frost-sword moves, the Ox and Cow constellations shiver with cold.

**Seven Poems by Chan Master Fachang Yu** The Dharma-body snail swallows a great elephant;
A stone tiger bites a foreign horse. Startling the dragon of the Duans, It tramples down the roof tiles of the cloud-houses.
The price of rice in Luling:
a three-eyed tortoise; A pronged horn on a rare qilin. Rising clouds bring evening rain; The mountain stream moon brightens the curtain at night.
The wind and the banner.
It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. A black-and-white cat with a speckled face.
The traveler at night, greedily seeking the bright moon, does not realize he is crossing through water in his clothes, shivering from the cold.
Three catties of hemp—how shall the fire-hemp fibers be divided? Boiling wax-snow tea to dispel your intoxication, there is yet a path where travelers have not reached;
wild flowers smile with joy upon the old branches of spring.
The Mystery within the Body of the Three Mysteries: A solitary-horned clay ox sleeps upon the water; turning his body, he strikes through the moon in the clear pool;
atop the peaks of Mount Wu, the waves surge to the heavens.

○ Chan Master Foyuan of Longmen, Eleven Verses on Pointing at the Finger (V): The Original Reality of the Cessation of Delusion The original reality is the cessation of delusion; the finger is merely a pointer. If you grasp the finger, you lose the moon; if you seek the moon, you must let go of the finger. When the mind is empty, all phenomena are empty; when the nature is revealed, the myriad things are revealed. Do not seek truth outside of delusion; do not abandon the false to pursue the real. Delusion and truth are originally one; where can they be found apart? If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, look directly at your own face. The ten thousand dharmas are all within the mind; the three realms are entirely the self. If you can recognize this in an instant, you will transcend birth and death. Do not rely on words and phrases; do not dwell in conceptualization. When the mind is suddenly awakened, it is like the sun breaking through the clouds. The ancient Buddhas have already spoken; they have pointed it out for you. If you do not understand this now, you will wander in the cycle of birth and death. The Way is not far from you; it is right here before your eyes. If you can see it clearly, you will attain liberation. Do not seek it in scriptures or treatises; do not look for it in the mountains or forests. It is simply the ordinary mind; it is the very place where you stand. If you can realize this, you are a Buddha; if you doubt it, you are a sentient being. In a single thought-moment, you may ascend or descend; in a single moment, you may be enlightened or lost. Therefore, do not waste your time; do not delay your practice. If you truly wish to see your own nature, you must cut off all deluded thoughts. This is the pointing at the finger; this is the direct transmission. If you can grasp it, you are free; if you miss it, you are bound. Thus ends the fifth verse of "Pointing at the Finger."

○ Master Jing Chan Shengyin Xiuyu’s Twenty-two Poems in the Style of Hanshan:
An Autobiographical Account.
I have often seen people composing in the style of Hanshan, yet others do so in the style of Shide. Each has their own ambition to soar toward the heavens; what benefit would it be to imitate them?

Dwelling in the mountains, the mountain colors are emerald; facing the waters, the sound of the streams is long. Amidst the seasonal splendor of wind and flowers, and the snow and moon, I sing and celebrate from time to time.

I recall quite well when I had not yet studied Chan, listening to the teachings for ten years; day and night I counted the treasures of others, yet how could I have ever gained so much as half a coin?
I resolved to set out on foot, seeking everywhere for medicine to cure my ailment. When I finally reached a place of rest, I found myself still without shoes to wear.

While traveling, I relied solely on my feet; wherever I arrived, that became my home. My midday meal was as simple or elaborate as it might be, and my three robes were haphazardly draped over me for cover.
Empty fame is but water in the ears; trivial profit is sand in the eyes. With one awakening from the sleep of twilight, the golden bird emerges from the ocean’s edge.
This self-elevated verse is my own lofty chant; this loftiness is not arrogance. My noble mind refuses to follow worldly movement; the chirping of petty birds is but a vain clamor.
Where there is no water, there is surely no source; where there is smoke, there must be a hearth. Heaven and hell are both created by oneself and then returned as one's own retribution.
Recently I have seen an ordinary person, dignified and majestic like a Buddha or a Patriarch, who enters a room seeking a teacher of wisdom to clarify the matter of birth and death.
I asked him, "Are you not a thief? At that moment, his face turned as pale as ash. I told him, "Do not give rise to anger; this very thing is birth and death.
Practice Zen to escape birth and death; do not be led astray by demons at will. Let the eight winds blow as they may, yet the six dusts shall never defile you."
Not like tangled words that confuse the mind—this is the phrase that cuts off all streams. Looking up at the blue sky, standing upon the earth, one transcends Buddhas and patriarchs.
A bowl of congee at the fifth watch, a meal at the hour of the dragon; two sleeps throughout day and night, and the affairs of a day are all settled.
To disparage others is to disparage oneself; to praise others is to praise oneself. As for right and wrong, honor and disgrace—these are like gold in a furnace or pellets of metal.
Plow diligently upon the fertile field; it benefits both yourself and others. Do not plant thorny brambles, lest your descendants find no way out.
The benevolent person loves and cherishes benevolence; the crafty and sycophantic give rise to jealousy. I urge you to turn back your head early and look at what lies before you.

Do not mock my own account, for these coarse words lack refined principles. They are certainly not intended to display literary skill; rather, I have committed my aspirations to writing by means of the brush.
Within the span of a hundred years’ breath, what use is there in bitter calculation? I exhort you not to harbor the poison of delusion;

impermanence arrives all too suddenly. A single melody celebrates peace and prosperity; it has nothing to do with "la-li-leng. Mountains and rivers both belong to the Song; clouds and waters shall henceforth be granted to the monks.
At that time, the wind-chimes of the pines strike; the moon-lamps of the ravine burn long. May the King be like Mount Nanyue, with ten thousand generations of emerald peaks layer upon layer.

At the hour of Midnight, the twelfth watch, when both mind and objects are forgotten in a vast, primordial chaos, one turns the pivot of heaven and the myriad phenomena shift; the earthen ox enters [the water].
Who among the ocean has personally witnessed this?
At the hour of the Cock (2–4 a.m.), a single cry announces itself without before or after. Startled awake, one’s dream-body surges upward;
the Old Man Śākyamuni runs crosswise.
At dawn, at the hour of Yin (5–7 AM): Green bamboos and yellow flowers brush the eyes with clarity; spiritual birds and strange beasts vie in their clamorous calls.
All are able to turn their heads and roll their eyes.

At sunrise, at the hour of Mao (7–9 AM): Purple mists and red clouds rise from the islands; countless seekers of profit and fame jostle one another, yet as they step out their doors, they forget [the Way].
If one discards the treasure within one's robes,
then at the hour of eating, holding an alms bowl and toiling in vain as one wanders through the market is pointless; yet if one were to receive the donor’s food with the mind,
it would be like a person who consumes a stipend without merit.
At the hour of Youzhong (Yi): Choosing the brothels and wine shops—turning one’s head reveals the one who has transcended the dust.
One laughs at Mañjuśrī leading Ānanda. At the hour of Renwu (Wu):
Standing tall and shining alone, without beginning or end. Upon a heap of refuse, the jade horse neighs; in the crystal palace...
The Supreme Vajra Dance.
Before noon has passed, the shadows of ten thousand trees and a thousand peaks slant downward. One searches the market for rabbit horns and tortoise hair;
though sold at a high price, one still thinks of the value it held when purchased.
The hour of *bùshí* (the seventh watch). Two-thirds of the day have passed. Even if you should recognize the path by which you came, by the time you reach home, it will already be dusk.
The hour of *rìrù* (the eighth watch).
Residual clouds reflect back upon the willows before the gate; a silent melody accompanies the cowherd’s return, with the ox mounted upon his back.

The child’s lion’s roar at dusk in the hour of the Dog (7–9 p.m.): the tones of the gongs and horns reach far and near as one. When one understands this essential point, hearing is restored and the cataracts of the senses are removed;
seek Maitreya upon Mount Potalaka.
The hour of Ren-ding is Hai (9–11 p.m.). In every thought-moment, impermanence is swift as a *kṣaṇa*. Turn the light back to examine the unmoving mind;
sitting in illumination, who is there to face the ten voids?
By Chan Master Long of Huqiu, two poems.
The alms-bowl of the wandering mendicant gathers the grains of the great earth; within a single hair-tip, the universe appears. Dwelling at home is not separate from the affairs of the road;
one is always on the road without ever leaving the gate.

Master Dharma of Lan-gu was difficult to detain; he took his single shoe westward and returned home. It was solely because of the moon over Xiong’er that its cold radiance has shone brightly for a thousand ages.
One verse for Chan Master Chang’an Chong of Jianfu Temple:
Reading the *Zhuangzi*, one realizes that once a form is received, it is never forgotten as one awaits the end;
human life is entirely like this. Who awakens to the mystery within? The white sun shines without partiality; the green mountains sleep at will.
The pine wind comes without ceasing; the springs and rocks naturally accord with one another. The path leads out above a thousand peaks; the clouds return to the side of the bamboo trail.
[Five Poems by Chan Master Baohua Focijian of the Five Schools]
Linji’s copper head and iron beak are the grievance of a hundred schools; with one shout, he divides the two while illumination and function are both complete.
With a three-foot "blow-off" blade, he settles the realm, yet at the moment of departure, he hurls it toward a blind donkey.
Yunmen’s three phrases are all strung together on a single thread; casually hung before the imperial palace. How many passing travelers have their eyes startled?
A carp from the Eastern Sea flies up into the sky.
The purple court and yellow gate of Cao-Dong bear the warmth of spring; who now attends the Sovereign in the sleeping palace?
I long cherish the place where the hundred officials divide their duties, as the jade whip strikes the stirrups and one emerges from the Golden Gate.

One from the lineage of Shitou and Yangshan scatters forth ten thousand; the winnowing fan explains the discourse on non-arising. When the Master of Caotang rises from sleep, his mouth is full of chatter;

Walking Beyond: A Water-and-Ink Guanyin Who Knows How to Push the Millstone. ○ Two Poems by Chan Master Guangfu Shang on Departing from Huanglong. [Poem 1] The mountain peaks are high and steep; The path is long and winding. I have come from afar, Seeking the Way within this vast expanse. [Poem 2] The clouds and mist obscure the distant mountains; The river flows through the deep valley. Leaving behind the old traces, I now head toward the green fields. The moon is bright upon the water; The wind rustles through the pines. Though my journey is far, My heart remains steadfast. The dawn light breaks over the eastern peak; The morning dew falls upon the western ridge. I bid farewell to the Yellow Dragon Temple, And set out upon the road ahead. The birds sing in the ancient forest; The flowers bloom by the spring stream. Though I am alone, I am not lonely; For the Dharma-body is everywhere. The great earth is vast and boundless; The blue sky is high and clear. With a single step, I transcend all; Where is there any place to go? The sun sets behind the western hills; The moon rises over the eastern sea. I have finished my travels; Now I return to my source. The autumn wind blows through the pine trees; The winter snow covers the bamboo grove. In the midst of these changes, My mind remains unmoved. The myriad phenomena are like a dream; All things are but an illusion. If one can awaken to this truth, Then birth and death are no more. The ancient buddhas have already passed away; The patriarchs are likewise gone. Only this empty space remains; It is neither coming nor going. The sound of the bell rings out clearly; The fragrance of incense drifts afar. Within this silent stillness, One attains liberation. The mountain crags are steep and rugged; The valley streams flow deep and clear. I have seen through the illusions; Now I dwell in peace. The clouds gather and disperse; The rain falls and ceases. In the midst of these transformations, I find the eternal stillness. The bright moon shines in the sky; The pure wind blows through the air. This is the true reality; Beyond all words and thought. The great ocean is vast and deep; The towering mountains reach the heavens. Within this boundless expanse, I have found my home. The morning mist rises from the valley; The evening clouds settle upon the peaks. As I gaze into the distance, I see the world as it truly is. The ancient mirror reflects all forms; The great earth supports all beings. In this state of non-duality, There is neither self nor other. The thousand sages have already departed; The ten thousand phenomena are now still. In this moment of silence, I realize the ultimate truth. The mountain flowers bloom in spring; The autumn leaves fall in gold. Through these changing seasons, I witness the eternal nature. The great Way is simple and plain; The true teaching is profound and vast. If one can let go of all attachments, Then one enters the realm of liberation. The ancient buddhas have all returned to their source; The patriarchs have likewise entered the void. Only this empty space remains; It is neither coming nor going. Master Chan Zhenxie Li of Changlu offers three verses for the assembly:

The meaning and phrasing are difficult to distinguish; seek them beyond the paths of poetry and elegance. Raising one’s blade, one gazes empty into the four directions; Pausing one’s steps, the whole ox is lost.
The emotional dust of the eyes falls away; returning to the root, the scene is profound and mysterious. Ten thousand conditions reach it not; even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot repay its debt.

The path is severed and there is no place for attachment; like an empty boat carrying the moon back home, when strength is exhausted, the single color is forgotten, and when merit is spent, the total mechanism is lost.

Secretly congealing where the currents flow, melting through as it faces with or against the tide; on a night when the wind is still upon the ancient sail, one moves spontaneously according to high and low.
Not violating the phrase of the clear waves, the limpid river drenches a single hook. At the prow, the weather is calm; beneath the awning, the autumn night is bright.
The geese’ shadows sink into the cold waters; the white ox hides amidst the reeds. You must know that beyond plowing and fishing, a profound stillness is difficult to contain.
One verse by Master Lingfeng on the postscript to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fojian.
Flowing water and lofty mountains do not reside in the strings; casually they form melodies and verses. Rows of coral trees, branch after branch, are beautiful;
scattered silver beads, grain by grain, are round. Striking down the gates of Chan without the slightest obstruction, he adds several layers of grievance for the patch-robed monks.
If one attempts to clarify the essential point on paper, how can it compare to creating the profound mystery for oneself at the moment of encounter?

The Purple Microcosm’s imperial tent is sealed with green moss; silent and deserted are the heavy chambers of the sleeping palace. Through the night, the jade water-clock transmits the noble voices of the court;
not even the six palaces are permitted to strike the golden bell.
Heshang Hongzhi’s Verses on Yangshan’s Words (3):
When the thread of the spiritual mechanism is not established, true emptiness is revealed; If it were a state of annihilation, there would be nothing with which to compare it.
A bottomless moon-boat sails across the night; A boltless lock passes through both ends.
A glance back illuminates the scene like spring rain; when will the letting go be like the clear morning breeze? A white-haired child rides a snow horse;
turning to approach his father—how could this be the same as ordinary merit?
Now that you have recognized it as it truly is, you ascend the precious chariot, parting the clouds beneath the moon.
Who can discern its departure at dusk and arrival at dawn? Wherever one opens the door, one encounters it.

**Deshan Fuxing Tai Chan Master, Five Poems** **Spring:** The days grow warm and the winds harmonious; heaven and earth are in spring. Wild flowers and fragrant grasses are all renewed at once. The sublime beauty of Vulture Peak remains as it was.

**Summer:** The sun blazes high, the world is vast and open. The myriad phenomena are all equally bright. The cool breeze rises from the deep mountains; the moon shines upon the clear lake. **Autumn:** The autumn wind is crisp, the sky is pure and vast. The waters are clear, the mountains are green. The golden chrysanthemums bloom in profusion; the red maples turn brilliant crimson. **Winter:** The snow falls thickly, the cold is intense. The ten directions are silent and still. The plum blossoms on the branch begin to bud; the heart of man is naturally tranquil. **On the Day of Prajñā:** The four seasons turn, the wheel of time revolves. The nature of reality is ever-present. When one realizes this, there is no distinction between past and present; the Dharma-body is eternally manifest.
Present! Who was the person who smiled back then?
Ten thousand trees spread wide as the summer days lengthen; in the gardens, plum and apricot chew on their crimson fragrance. Do you know that the wheat has ripened before the mountains?
Each and every one is brought forth at the opportune moment.
Fluttering yellow leaves fall in the secluded courtyard; ten thousand *li* of cloudless sky, the universe is clear. A brisk, cool breeze arises outside the door;
the three phrases of Śākyamuni become increasingly distinct.
The forest trees wither away, returning to their original roots; Frigid frost and freezing snow lock the pine gate. In the earthen hearth, embers are smoldering, warming the whole body;
When cold and heat arrive, there is no need for further discussion.

Zan: The Dharma Master boarded his ship and arrived in Liang during the Putong era; with a single blow of the hammer, he shattered all conditioned effort. Who would say that sitting facing the wall meant there was nothing to be said?
Yet, alas, the teeth at the gate still reveal the wind.
