If you open your mouth, I know your words have fallen into error. The fragrant food of the *Upariṣṭha* Heaven is not eaten; one must submit to this with sweet compliance.
Eating human mucus and spittle—Yunmen raises up his bamboo whisk.
Zen practitioners must strictly avoid the needle and the awl; phoenixes do not perch upon thorny brambles, while [the *gan*]-birds guard their empty ponds in solitude.
Yunmen raises his bamboo whisk—his entire being drenched in water and trailing through mud. He announces to those of the highest caliber who seek the mystery:
let go with a full release from the precipice; do not delay.
Yunmen raises his bamboo whisk—if you hesitate to deliberate, I know you have lost your way. Even if you could save your own eyesight, at that very moment...
They have lost their nostrils.
Yunmen raises his bamboo whisk, exposing his heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys. How pitiable are these dead-end Chan practitioners;
even now, their souls flee and their gall bladders fail.
To the Chan practitioner Dingxu, I show the eye of Mahesvara, set vertically upon the crown of his head; behind his elbow, he slings the talisman that seizes life. Blind the eyes, untie the talisman:
Zhaozhou hangs a gourd from the eastern wall.
The Elder Fusheng of Jiji relied upon the Primordial Void of the Eighteen Realms. Thirty-one people shared the same surname Lü;
they dispersed to travel the mountains, each occupying a peak, yet these thirty-one people remained together in one place.
Master Puyong demonstrated the mark of non-action;
he struck the poison-dripping drum and practiced unconditioned compassion. He "slaughtered the Buddhas and slaughtered the patriarchs"—thus one may perceive Puyong.
Although Miaoxi did not yet dare to grant him full approval, he came straight down. Like a dragon or a tiger, he was shattered by a single blow.
The great void remains to this day with a single gap that no one has filled.
Chancellor Li Hanlao painted the portrait of the Master’s crown-protrusion and requested a eulogy;
this fellow committed an immeasurable transgression in unnecessarily provoking me. This scholar has been killed by him, who hides a blade within his smile.
"Our ancestor Bodhidharma did not know what kind of grievance or enmity existed; he has been constantly inciting calamities and creating misfortunes.
"Venerable Gaomo, acknowledge this! Stay alert; do not let the words fall away."
The Daoist of the Tang dynasty requested a eulogy for this Compassionate One.
There is nothing to grasp; suddenly there is joy, and suddenly there is wrath. When joyful, the harmonious breath is like spring, and a hundred flowers open their buds.
When wrathful, thunder, lightning, wind, and clouds arise all at once. If one acts in such a manner, it would not be [the work of] anyone other than the Buddha.
The Asura King is none other than the Great Awakening of the Golden Immortal. You practitioners of the Tang should pull it in tight; do not unfurl it when meeting people.
Roll it up and put it away in the corner by the wall.
This Chan practitioner from the ancestral lineage requests a eulogy:

His coarse appearance resembles that of a monk from Sichuan; his carefree elegance is just like a traveler from Zhejiang. He specifically points toward the time before emotions have arisen, bringing forth the "one barrier" of Baoci.
His venerable nature is not fixed and cannot be fathomed. When seen at a small scale, one finds the eyes of the gnat too large.
"Kuan! When you see the Great, you think the vast void is too narrow. How can a master such as this receive the offerings of devas and humans?
He deserves a slap across the face!"
Three Verses by Chan Master Xuedang Xing of Wugu, Presented to a Zen Practitioner:
When the words issue forth, all obstacles vanish; A turn of the body reveals the coldness of the ancient sword. To clarify the matters mentioned above, One must first ensure the skull is dry.
Xue Dongpo’s Verse on Staying at Donglin Temple:
"The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue; The color of the mountains is the pure body. The eighty-four thousand verses— Clearly and vividly presented to people."
In praise of Master Foyan:
"Because of me, you receive my prostrations. Xuansha has emerged from the nest. After Longmen gave him the lamp-offering, he said:
"Tsk! *Huguo Cigan Yuan Chan Master, two poems:*
Answer: Chan Master Huqiu Long’s *Weighing the Buddhas and Patriarchs* is truly sublime and peerless.
A single phrase penetrates all, and myriad functions are thoroughly realized. Transverse and vertical movement is like a rolling pearl on a tray;
every thought is perfectly integrated in great rest. One must require that every drop be as rotten as pus; do not emulate the "half-[measures]" of the South.
Arising and ceasing—suddenly, the waves of the four seas overturn the void; they shake Mount Sumeru until its rocky cliffs split asunder.

Within the flash of lightning and the reflection of fire, one distinguishes the black from the white; amidst a mass of blazing flames, one scoops up flying snow. From the eight facets of its translucent clarity, a pure breeze arises;
it is the bright, solitary moon of a frosty night. The "Unranked True Man" is a dry dung-puck; within the purple pearl curtain, patterns of fine silk are knotted. Grasp it!
A blade that cuts hair as it blows makes the gallbladder shiver with cold; it provokes the stone man to gasp and spit out his tongue. Fully raised or half-raised, its wind is chillingly fierce;
seizing the food and driving the plow, its wondrousness is inexhaustible. Blows fall like raindrops and sounds like thunder; a single stroke at the critical moment brings immediate transcendence.
Do you not see that the true spirit and correct command of the Linji school should be like this? Bare bones laid upon the ground constitute one’s living legacy.

To offer words of recommendation before the speech of the *huashishi* (funeral envoy) is to create complications; to take responsibility after the sentence is spoken is likewise not yet authentic. Cut off both ends and the idle paths.
Pu. [I] do not know who is the one who has passed through the barrier.
○ Five Poems by Chan Master Bian of the Main Hall at Daochang, Sent to the Street Alms-collectors.
A virtuous woman does not wear the clothes of her natal home; how could a husband borrow wealth from his allotted portion? From where could ten cups or five goblets have come?
He merely brandished his two fists as he pursued them back.
When the Zen practitioner arrives, the horse-faced yakṣa merely bows his head; the ox-head jailer immediately raises his fists. Dongbin sings a verse on the principle of the potter’s kiln:
the shell-shedding turtle flies up into the heavens.
Self-Appraisal (3):
Elder Tubaofa’s place of awakening is like a slippery head that surpasses water-mallow; his pliancy and stubbornness are no less than sticky glue.
He was once kicked by a three-legged donkey until his nostrils were split into four.
A blind wife blowing fire at midnight; a deaf man hearing singing at noon. Having painted such a mark of excellence, he enters birth and death to subdue demons.
Sometimes he stirs up the waves of the Dragon Gate; even the Dragon King Sāgara cannot do anything about it.
This decrepit abbot does not speak of rules and regulations; he gathers three hundred monks to discourse on meaningless talk.
Throughout his life, he has sought only personal advantage, even seeking dry ground when falling into the water.
Chan Master Qingshan Fang:
Four Verses on the Four Modes of Deportment Walking in the Mountains Step by step, treading upon the unborn; Holding a staff that overtops my head, I do not dispute over its weight.
Dwelling in the mountains, there is no path at all to birth and death. Hell and heaven are both merely idle furnishings.
Sitting in the mountains, the pines and bamboos are truly grand; from time to time they stir up a pure breeze, singing themselves and harmonizing with themselves.
Sleeping in the mountains—Patriarchs and Buddhas stand shoulder to shoulder; spiritual powers and wondrous functions are all right there by one’s pillow.
Five Verses by Chan Master Fohai Yuan of Lingyin, shown to the practitioner Wuzhu.
Xiatang has one thing that is not right: he sweeps away the very core of the monks' understanding, startles the iron ox of Shanzhou, and swallows up the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
Sent to Senior Seat Holder Tishou of Baishi Peak.
Many monks dwell upon the peaks of White Stone; the Iron Ox has sucked dry the waves of the well.
When the Cloth Bag opens its mouth again in years to come, even Buddhas and Patriarchs will remain as helpless as before.
Entrusted to the Reverend Wuan of Daochang:
With a snowy summit like Mount Kunlun, you strain your mind to guess; The ten-headed rākṣasa breaks into a smile. Enter first into the cold cauldron of boiling water;
When the eyes of the Xu River are crossed, wait for me to come.
Master Shidao taught that in the study of Buddhism, awakening should be the standard. Empty words do not enter the gates of the public; look at Yi’s cursive calligraphy:
a single dot penetrates the stone by three fen.
Self-praising, my entire body is one with the great earth; the void is devoid of the four quarters. Not recognizing the "pine tree," I call it "three pounds of hemp.
At times of excellence, I am ten parts elegant; at times of adversity, I am one flavor of rusticity. Casually pulling a plow up into the Buddha hall, I mount...
Riding a horse inside a begging bowl; urinating and defecating on level ground. Who knows whether this is real or false?
Zen practitioners have come here to paint a portrait of it—a torch atop the head of a tiger.
Four Poems by Chan Master Xueting Jing of Huqiu,
with a Preface by Wang Yining of Longtu on the Four Oxen Diagrams.

Fundamentally there are no ranks or positions; how could one allow for the horizontal establishment of steps? The essence is cut off from names and words; how can one permit the forced creation of knots and joints?

Having leaped out through the profound gate, what does it matter if one has dusty feet and a head of ash? Only when the golden lock is shattered by a shout does one finally understand how to don fur and wear horns.

He gathers and transforms beings at random, manifesting forms according to the needs of sentient beings. This single, firm, and dense body blends into all sensory objects, appearing throughout past and present.
The drawing of the cowherd is merely one auspicious sign among his various skillful means; whether black or white, existent or non-existent, none of them have yet reached ultimate perfection.
Now, the practitioner Xueting uses four oxen, all of a single color—white—with the space between them...

The two positions: when awakened, one rides against the current; when deluded, one rides with the current. That the two positions, front and back, represent the ox symbolizes the time before the parents were born and at the moment of nirvana.
That all four are white symbolizes that even in delusion nothing is lost, and even in awakening nothing is gained.
Birth does not come; death does not go. The open ground is level and vast; the Dharmakāya is manifest. First:
Before parents were born, beyond the void kalpa, before the world was formed, this nature was already complete.
It is level, clear, and bright; its fundamental substance is pure and true. Sentient beings arise through delusion; the sages...
From compassion, one gives rise to wisdom. The verse says:
In the state where chaos is undifferentiated, when the three conditions have not yet converged, its spiritual powers are difficult to fathom, and even the Buddha-eye cannot peer into it.

Vast and open, the entire body is pure white; sleeping peacefully on the bare ground, it is plump and full. Yet, because of its attachment to the beauty of spring colors, it is once again blown away by the winds of karma.
When two or three conditions coincide, the six thieves arise in concert. Abandoning one’s father, one flees; deluded, one pursues external objects.
Entering and exiting through the same gate, each remains unaware of the other. Racing outward in pursuit, one naturally falls into decline.
To be thus constrained is called delusion. The verse says:
Having changed its feathered coat, it is from now on no longer free; knowing only the affairs of today, it has forgotten the ox of old.
Though every step follows the same track, he stands tall and does not turn his head. The four mountains grow ever more distant; though they pursue one another, there is no time when it ceases.
3. Suddenly turning his head, he sees him; face-to-face, they meet. Throughout the twelve hours of the day, he is entirely sustained by his power.
King and minister, their ways harmonize; father and son, they are in perfect accord. Benefiting self and others alike, he continues the Buddha’s wisdom.
Because it is one's own life-force, it is called "awakening. The verse says:
In a fleeting moment within the courtyard of one's home, turning the head, one recognizes Him. There is no need for constant guarding; at any time, mount Him sideways or upright as you please.
Like a traveler returning home; like a child finding its mother. Amidst the wild weeds of the level fields, one blows and chants "Li-lo li.
(4) From beginning to end, it is a single thread; arising and ceasing are simultaneous.
All day long it is born, yet not born; all day long it dies, yet not dead. Vast and traceless, profound, clear, and empty—like gold being refined.
Gold returns to water as water; without severing afflictions, one enters nirvana.
Not abiding at the profound pass, nor dwelling in the position of correctness, one dons fur and wears horns to walk among the ranks of other species.
This is the Dharma-gate of sudden realization of all Buddhas; it is not a realm for sentient beings to see or hear. The verse says:

Cast off the garments of birth; return to the Immovable Honored One (Acala). All myriad conditions are suddenly brought to rest; this is the single path to the gate of Nirvana. The waves of the great ocean subside;
the blue sky is cleared of a single speck of cloud. Clad in fur, you share the same nature as other species; there is no land where your body is not manifested.
○ Four Poems by Chan Master Ying’an Hua of Tiantong, Written Spontaneously Before the Hall of Huangbo, he issues the true command;
Today at Tiantong, he tests the distant and the near. In his old age, he contemplates the parting of the staff.
Entrusted. I have not yet seen the man who received the staff that year.
Praising Linji—Linji is bald and lacks eyesight. Seeking advantage, he knows no contentment; hanging up a sheep's head, he sells dog meat.
He cherishes every ounce and grain like jade; yet within his breast lies another kind of poison. Heaven lightly brushes it away.
Zanchan has depicted this with tenfold likeness, save for one point of confusion that neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs can detect. Let it be as it is.
Arms and shields lie leveled upon the ground.
This Chan practitioner has painted the portrait of the Master’s crown-protrusion and seeks a eulogy:
"Body and mind are as one; there is nothing beyond the body. He does not wish to become a Buddha, nor is he an ordinary person; he is content to be a prisoner in the highest dungeon."
A lacquered bucket. No calculating of even a *zhi* or a *zhou*. Ten thousand ages of silver mountains and iron walls, with not another word of "this" or "that.
If this is so, bury the old monk alive; if it is not, beat Tanhui to death. Darkly penetrating two layers of formidable barriers, the blazing flames leave no room for even a mosquito.
Master Boshan Ben’s Two Poems on Bathing the Buddha:
Today marks the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth. This very day of that year—how could it be otherwise? If one says he returned at eighty, [it is but a conventional expression].
Extinction. Though his eyes were clear and distinct, he was suddenly blind.
He dispatched a monk with a letter of succession and shot the great tiger of the South Mountain. From this path, travelers have passed through; yet for years, the hunting dogs have been utterly gone.
Using it: Lying down facing a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks.
○ Seven Verses by Chan Master Yan of Wan’an at Donglin, Explaining the Way.
The mind is like a wall, the eyes like eyebrows; with moonlight for bait, smoke for a cloak, he lowers his line at the fishing weir. A profound, cold radiance coalesces as a single expanse;
without disturbing the waves, he takes the fish and returns.
Together with Chan practitioner Dongzhao,
he pulls out Zhaozhou’s tongue, clears away the thorns before the gate, returns home to lie down and sleep across the bed,
and coldly laughs at those rushing south and north.
Addressing the Assembly (2):
Do not take useless, stubborn hide and make it into a leather ball; who can kick it up to the high tower? Now I am decrepit and utterly without strength;
when I can no longer roll it along, I shall simply rest.
We dwell together upon the Pan-t'o Rock; water is far, mountains high—there is nothing else.
Only the moon atop the peak, full of sentiment, shifts its shadow onto the steps deep into the night.

Zan [Dongshan] stood before the Five Milk Peaks of the Dharma, sitting in cold stillness for nine years. His solitary style was beyond peer, and his name dared not be sullied. To inherit the fragrance, he severed his arm;
like selling off stagnant goods, the moth larvae have offspring whom the wasp carries away. He then spoke this incantation: "Be like me! Be like me!"
Self-Appraisal (1):

Coming from the Three Rivers, I have responded to conditions in the Two Zhe regions. On my shoulders I carry the heavy burden of the fragrant papaya; around my waist I bind the three strips of bamboo from a horse winnowing fan.
For rice I chew iron nails; for soup I boil wooden shavings. I am truly a descendant of Yuanwu, yet I have lost Yangqi.
The family tradition: the crafty man harbors many doubts; the clever boy misses the essential point.
It is real yet not real; it possesses form yet is not form. A whisk made of tortoise hair, a staff carved from rabbit horns—singing and dancing all alone.
Blowing alone and singing alone: "Recognize the nun as your own daughter; Master Zhigong was no ordinary monk.
*Two Poems by Chan Master Jiantang Ji of Guoqing to See Off a Monk Building a Universal Stupa*
Her jade-like bones are naturally elegant and translucent; like a wild sheep hanging from a cliff, her traces are nowhere to be seen. Why have you built this pavilion in vain?
It is out of a longing for the pines and bamboos to draw in the pure breeze.

Sending off the Venerable Yuyi, Guest Vinaya Master Ke—One word enters the official gate; though there is reason, it is difficult to stretch forth, enough to make one laugh to death. He did not follow Xinghua’s command while at Yinjing;
who will say in years to come that he was intimate with the staff?
Six Poems by Chan Master An-ti of Jiaoshan, Composed While Encountering [Him] at Baishi Hermitage.
The man who dwells at Baishi does not abide in the *nāga-samādhi*; His staff has worn its branch bare, and his alms bowl is mounted upside down.
People search through grass for an enemy; the void hangs the mirror of karma. Under a shout, the sword’s light is cold; let go, and the decree of Mahākāla is issued.

Forgetting artifice and severing illumination, he rouses the eye that veils the heavens. The ancient tale of the Empty King is complete: the air-ball is as hard as iron, yet the stone mortar is as soft as cotton.
In the sea of suffering, there are no startling waves; in the red furnace, the fire and smoke have been severed. As for Zhuang Zhou’s dream of a butterfly, how could the whole world be its origin?

To the assembly: (3) Stepping forth upon the solitary and perilous ground where no grass grows, one wanders at ease where there is no place to rest. Facing the wind, one expands the vastness and devours the void.
Mouth! You have sent your entire family into the fire pit.
Your fierce appearance is of a truly rustic sort. You judge the sages of old while slighting your own descendants. Casting yourself off onto a solitary peak—how fitting for one who would kill!
Within the staff there is an eye that covers heaven and earth.
The feet of a man-child pierce through to Chang’an; having attained his seat and donned his robe, he refuses to deceive himself. Three feet of cold light radiate through the night moon;
a single blade of autumn water strikes one with chilling intensity.
Praise to the Dharma:
Ten Thousand Blessings! An old staff-bearer comes from the West; he does not follow conventional conduct as he crosses the shifting sands. Struck by another, his front teeth are knocked out;
yet like a mute man before, he continues to eat bitter melons.
A single verse in praise of the old fellow from Moon Hermitage, Chan Master Liai of Yùquán Qiónggǔ:
He is entirely without seams or cracks; he turns iron into gold and points to a deer as a horse—truly a man of extraordinary brilliance! Zhang Zhuoxiu.
A mere talkative fellow! This many-mouthed master can capture and release at will; he rides upon a three-legged donkey and points out the teachings of all quarters to establish his own hegemony.
When he encounters the lowly, the true eye of the Buddhas of the three ages is difficult to perceive; when he encounters the noble, even the Eight Great Dragon Kings find it hard to offer a price.
Aha ha! How very mistaken! It was simply because he lost his eyesight in the Spring Garden that from then on he became so wicked.

It is called "Tāotāo" (Flowing Onward). Its current spreads throughout the world. Suspended high in the empty hall like a lion displaying its full majesty, it leaves all manner of monsters and demons to marvel in secret from the shadows.
Lamp-Zen! Lamp-Zen! First of all, you must not treat it with levity. To provide them with this transformative instruction—*Duḥ!* (Aha!)
Two Poems by Chan Master Zhuan’an Zhu of Gong’an on the Portrait of Leaving the Mountain:
At midnight he scaled the city walls to head for the Snowy Mountains; The dragon towers and phoenix halls were beyond his reach. Now he has rolled right out from amidst the weeds.
Inside. A single idle man within heaven and earth.
Self-praising:
Moonlight shines upon the secluded valley; the sound of a spring falls over the precipice. Amidst the colors of water and mountain, he is but a piece of withered, rotten firewood.
○ Seven Poems on Miscellaneous Verses by Chan Master Fen of Jianmen Although it is said that practicing Chan involves applying effort,
The moment one stirs even a hair’s breadth [of conceptualization], one incurs execution. How many times have I seen you inquire deeply?
Question: The intent of raising chickens lies at the very beginning of the fifth watch.

Having long been accustomed to walking upon the tip of the staff, one sits still, holding back the golden sun so it does not rise in the east. A single current of the celestial river flows on without end;
peaches fill the eyes as they chase the spring’s crimson.
In the open field, the white ox must be slaughtered; at the red furnace, the surging waves are taught to be dried up.
Having transcended and emerged freely in all directions, one still lacks the lifelong "sickness-free pill."
Spreading the bowl and opening the mat, the assembly is dismissed; coming crosswise or going straight, let people harbor their doubts as they will.
When a child meets his own mother after a night’s separation, how could he wait for others to speak of right and wrong?
Level ground of pure gold becomes dung and soil; conversely, dung and soil become pure gold.
Even if one were to employ them as if they were identical, how could a painted tiger ever know how to bite a person?
Following custom, I cast my hook across the Five Lakes; his boat is full of fish, so he laughs at my lack of success.
Little does he know that the bait on my hook is aimed at the Azure Dragon, not at the common fish.

Soaring through the present and shining through antiquity, this impartial phrase is not a fabrication forged by a thieving mind. It is a place where the ocean of learning and the sky of meaning find no foothold;
I now pick it up and present it to you, O practitioners of Zen.
○ Ten Miscellaneous Verses by the Monk Jusun Green waters and red peach blossoms;
I have wandered through the streets and alleys more than a hundred times. Zhang San knows me; Li Si...
"You recognize me; you recognize me yet do not recognize me. Between these two fists, which one is larger? Of the two, one is large.
It once split open the void with a single strike; now it is rubbed and made to be just so. Take up Mount Sumeru as a pillow and lie down.
Awake, he wanders the streets; drunk, he wanders the streets. Having no money to buy wine, he begs for it to drink.
In a state of dazed confusion, he forgets what comes before and what follows. Opening his two eyes, he sees the Big Dipper; grasping its handle, he draws up the waters of the sea.
He pours them directly into his mouth from the sky; by mistake, he swallows the Fire Dragon, which returns to the five viscera. At midnight, he lets out a great roar.
Follow me, follow me. I shall give you the Dharma for settling yourself: climbing the pole and performing somersaults.
At the head of the Yangtze River, the waves are deepest; when travelers reach this point, they all hesitate.
When you arrive at a place where there are no waves in the future, you must still apply your mind as you did when the waves were present.
Once again, I hear the golden goblets being filled; the Jade Mountain has once more reported its collapse. Do not let the night-watchmen hasten the hours; seize the moonlight to return home.
One-six, two-six—the matter is already complete. One-nine, two-nine—I want to drink wine.
Stretching out my two legs to sleep, when I wake up and rise, heaven and earth remain as they were before.
Stupefied by delusion; delusion, stupor. Fallen blossoms drift with the current, naturally lingering. Satiated by wine, I rub my belly.
My very self is originally the son of Master Lin.
Expensively purchasing cinnabar to paint the moon—when calculated, it is a waste of effort. Reclining drunk beneath the shade of green willows, one rises to forcefully discourse on *tathatā*.
The clay figure repeatedly exhorts: do not let the jewel within your robes be lost.
Green trees before the gate hold no singing birds; beneath the courtyard’s blue-green moss lie fallen blossoms. I shall discuss this matter with the eastern breeze:
to whose house does the fullness of spring’s colors belong?

Autumn arrives and the mountains grow cold, the waters turn frigid; spring comes and the willows turn green, the peach blossoms turn red. A single point of movement follows ten thousand transformations; in the river village, the mist and rain hang thick.
Is it existent? Is it non-existent? Is it empty? Is it not empty? With a colander, one scoops up the northwest wind.
Born in this Jambudvīpa world, human beings possess much affection and aversion; they simply desire to drink wine, which is why they fall prostrate in the streets and lie along the roads.
After death, they are reborn in this Sahā world, having no wish to be reborn in the Pure Land. Why is this?
Because in the Western Pure Land, there is no selling of wine.
Eight Verses by the Grand Historian Huang Shan-gu Dao-ren, titled "Placing a Head upon a Head at the Hall of Rest.
How can one attain rest? Only by slaying the Buddhas and Patriarchs can one find peace and stability. Northern Uttarakuru.

In Aparagoyānī, matters are as one family: eating rice and wearing clothes. As for the single path leading upward, where a thousand sages blink their eyes—there Han Xin struck the pass and Zhang Liang burned the granaries.
Presented to Chief Seat Yong by Brother Sizhi.

On the day you depart, you leave with hands cast loose; when you return, there is no step to ascend. If you expect to meet [the truth] in the future, it will be just as if you had never practiced at all.
Presented to Chief Seat Yong.
Having seized the Hu boy’s horse, one should simply let it be. Cease lamenting that Li Guang was not enfeoffed as a marquis.
It was clearly a tiger of the South Mountain he shot; upon closer inspection, it was but a stone.
Incense Offering for Chan Master Chong of Huilin (3):
Last night at the third watch, the dogs barked amidst the snow; the eastern neighbor closed his gate and pushed out the moon. This is the nature of that ocean of awakening, clear and perfect;
if a patch-robed monk would kill a person, he must see blood.
Tattered robes worn for many years cannot bear a needle; a single melody of the Hu flute, timeless through all ages. In the past, hearing the Shao music, one alone forgot its flavor;
the man who waits by the stump remains as the moon sinks in the west.
In Aparagoyānī they open the period of quietude; in Uttarakuru they receive the morning gruel. Hui-lin sings the Yunmen melody:
"Last year, on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month."
Master Zhēnrú Zàn said: "To take the heterodox as the orthodox;
to take the medicine as the disease. To point to the well when asked for water; to give the steamer when asked for rice. To kill people as numerous as hemp stalks."
Emerging from the samādhi of wrong livelihood, the precepts (*śīla*) are pure, and eighty-four thousand [precepts] are likewise pure.
This is called the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye of Vairocana. It is sealed with the seal of equanimity and covered by the *saṃghāṭī* robe.

When one who is mindless arrives, the door opens at a snap of the fingers. Where the holy and the profane are exhausted, golden locks grow moss; red and green hues intermingle, such that north and south can no longer be distinguished.
The dew. Its reflection falls upon a thousand rivers; who knows where the moon resides?
To say "it is Lu Zhi" is acceptable; to say "it is not Lu Zhi" is also acceptable. Setting aside for a moment whether it is or is not—let us proceed.
The Master called out, "Who is this Lu-zhi? If it were a phrase that cuts through like a chisel striking iron: "The head of the hidden is white;
the head of the sea is black. *Jia-tai Pu-deng-lu*, Volume 29.

Pronounced zhōu (幬). Mì (汨): Pronounced mì. Mǐ (洣): Pronounced mò (莫禮切). Shěng (眚): Pronounced suǒ (所景切). Jī (擠): Pronounced zāi (賷).

○ Chan Master Fohui Quan of Jiangshan’s “Song of Mo’an” (with Preface) In the spring of the ninth year of the Xining era,
I moved from Qianqing in Hangzhou to reside in this monastery. As the abbot’s quarters were vacant, I took up residence there.
Thereupon, he cleared half of his studio and constructed a thatched hut beneath the rocky crags to serve as a place for repose.

In the twelfth month of that year, the hut was completed; he named it "Silence" (Mo), taking its meaning from the closing of the room by Mahākāśyapa at Rājagṛha and the sealing of the mouth by Vimalakīrti at Vaiśālī.
Not long after, a guest came to visit me and said, "The Master’s hut is finished; the significance of the hut has been established."
Yet the Master is currently busily gathering his disciples and attracting scholars; he distributes the lamp to dispel darkness and deepens the source to guide those in the abyss.
To say that he arouses compassion to rescue all beings and opens the ignorant to remove their obscurations is indeed the height of praise, yet he is named "The Silent One."
"Is that not also delusory? I said to the guest, "You know silence, but you do not know the reason for that silence.
Stay here, and I shall tell you: silence is the true path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and the fundamental nature of all sentient beings.

If this fundamental nature is correct, one remains constantly tranquil even amidst clamor; if it is erroneous, one seeks principle while loathing the dust of the world. Thus, as for clamor and silence..."
Right and wrong are thus resolved. Although the categories and enumerations are numerous, they all do not depart from my ultimate silence.

Therefore, when the Sage of Western India, the Buddha, responded to conditions and moved things, his golden texts and jade-like phrases were indeed beyond counting; yet, in the end, he is said to have taught nothing.
This is precisely what is being clarified here. People of later generations have been muddled regarding this Way; they take speech to be merely speech and silence to be merely silence.

Even if they claim that speech and silence are one and the same, they do not know what that essence is. They merely harbor indignation in their hearts and mouths, treading upon it without thorough understanding and employing it without discernment.
Boasting and self-satisfied, they consider themselves to have attained it, and further say: "That [other person] is silent."
Those who transmit [the teaching] merely speak of a void that cuts off all words. How could the Way of our Buddha be like that? Alas!
How could such people understand the Way of our Buddha? I am one who studies silence; regarding this silence, how could I possibly exhaust its depths?

The stench of worldly ambition lingers; the road back to my hometown is cut off, alas, as thorns pierce the sky. Empty flowers fall too easily; I grieve that this brief life cannot be prolonged.

When thoughts arise and thoughts perish, there is no need for suppression or cessation. Flowing on spontaneously and boundlessly, when have they ever arisen or perished? This very arising and perishing is itself quiescent extinction—this manifests as Mahākāśyapa.

After a long time, one becomes tranquil and serene; the six sense-gates become empty and still. As the six gates gradually subside, discrimination arises within them. As soon as discrimination is born, it has already undergone arising and ceasing.
This arising, ceasing, and transformation are manifested from one's own mind and are used by one's own mind. One should then turn back and contemplate this process once over.
A single reversal, never again; a halo crowns the head, and spiritual flames soar in brilliance. Mind after mind is unimpeded, encompassing horizontally and penetrating vertically.

*The True Return to Unborn Permanence: A Memorial Address by Chan Master Lingyuan Qing of Huanglong Fushou.*

Wei Qing, the forty-eighth descendant in direct descent from Śākyamuni Buddha, the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa, was born through the manifestation of fundamental enlightenment in response to conditions;
yet he realized that conditions are themselves empty and possess no inherent nature from the outset.

His clan, lineage, and kin cannot be fully detailed, for he takes the single thought of the true cause as his primary object of veneration. Thus, he is reckoned among the distant descendants of Śākyamuni.

His style name was Linyuan Sǒu (The Elder of the Spiritual Source). Relying upon the "self-enlightening cause" (*svayambhūhetu*) and the wondrous nature that it reveals, he manifested these appellations within that which is beyond names and words.

He is akin to Linji’s “True Person of No Rank” or the “Mind-King” of Master Fu Dashi; he is indeed the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana—something known only through personal realization, which none others can fathom.

In the thirty-two sections of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one cannot speak of emptiness without first establishing that which is not the Dharma, nor can one preach the Dharma without first convening an assembly. The myriad phenomena flourishing in all their variety are called "causes" (*hetu*);

the single mind responding to conditions is called the "source" (*yīn*). Therefore, the sūtra begins with the section on the "Causes and Sources of the Dharma Assembly. From emptiness arises wisdom; thus, the questions and answers proceed in tandem.

This being so, it is followed by the Section on Subhūti’s Request. When the fundamental principle transcends the distinction between the correct and the heterodox, and the vehicle is without the categories of great or small, one transforms and delivers beings according to their three capacities;
thus, setting aside divergent doctrines, this alone is honored as supreme. Therefore, it is followed by the Section on the True Principle of the Mahāyāna.
Having attained the principle, one acts without dwelling upon appearances. Therefore, it is followed by the Section on Wondrous Practice and Non-abiding. Every practice is thusness.

This is called "seeing reality. Therefore, it is followed by the section on "Seeing Reality According to Principle. Having seen it, one believes it; thus the roots of goodness become firm and deep. Therefore, it is followed by the section on "Right Faith in the Rare.
To attain that which cannot be attained is called true attainment; to speak that which cannot be spoken is called true speaking.

Therefore, it is followed by the section on "Neither Attainment nor Speaking. [The fear of] neither attainment nor speaking— (Note: The final character "怖" appears to be an incomplete fragment or an error in the source text, as it stands alone without a clear object. It is translated here as a standalone term for completeness.)
Regarding the sinking into emptiness: all Buddhas emerge from this; therefore, it is followed by the section on "Arising in Accordance with the Dharma.
Although there are four fruits, their characteristics are fundamentally non-dual; therefore, it is followed by the section on "The Single Characteristic and the Characterless.
When the pure mind arises, this is called the Pure Land; the adornment of various marks is itself non-adornment; therefore, it is followed by the section on "Adorning the Pure."
The Section on the Divisions of the Earth: The merit of the conditioned has limits and an end; the merit of the unconditioned is peerless and supreme.
Therefore, it is followed by the "Section on the Superiority of Unconditioned Merit. Wherever this sutra resides, devas and nāgas pay it respectful service;
therefore, it is followed by the "Section on Honoring the True Teaching. The Ultimate Way is nameless, yet through skillful means, practitioners receive and uphold it by means of these names.

Therefore, it is followed by the section on receiving and upholding according to the Dharma. Having heard the sutra and understood its meaning, one deeply awakens to the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*);
therefore, it is followed by the section on detachment from signs and quiescent extinction. By receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting [the sutra], one benefits both oneself and others;

the merit is boundless and immeasurable. Therefore, it is followed by the section on the merit of upholding the sutra. The karmic offenses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are eliminated in a single thought-moment. As for the fruit...
Retribution is never in vain; how could it require many kalpas? Therefore, this is followed by the section on "The Ability to Purify Karmic Obstructions.

Since there is fundamentally no self, how can there be a person? Yet, in order to deliver those persons, a provisional self is established. Therefore, this is followed by the section on "Ultimate Non-Self.
One eye encompasses the five eyes; one grain of sand encompasses the sands of the Ganges; one world encompasses many worlds; one...

Because the mind encompasses various states of mind, it is followed by the section on "Contemplating the Unity of the Single Body. Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, this single transformation is universally applicable;
how could the field of merit consisting of the seven treasures be like the four propositions? Therefore, it is followed by the section on "The Universal Transformation of the Dharma-realm.

With the three bodies fully complete and all marks perfectly realized, both person and phenomena are forgotten; thus, even this "full completion" is not truly complete. Therefore, it is followed by the section on "Detachment."

The section on the "Characteristics of Detachment from Form" discusses emptiness throughout the day without speaking a single word. To claim that there is anything spoken would be to slander the Tathāgata;

therefore, it is followed by the section on "That Which Is Not Spoken Yet Is Spoken. Supreme right knowledge truly has not even the slightest dharma; dharmas are non-apprehendable, and this perfect penetration is vividly clear;
therefore, it is followed by the section on "The Non-existence of Any Dharma to Be Attained. If even a single dharma remains in the mind, afflictive emotions arise.
High and low; purifying the mind and cultivating goodness—how can the dharmas ever be exhausted? Therefore, this is followed by the section on "Purifying the Mind and Practicing Goodness.

Though one may bestow treasures as vast as mountains, the mountains themselves are not inexhaustible; yet the Great Body and Wondrous Wisdom are the true mountain of jewels. Therefore, this is followed by the section on "Incomparable Merit and Wisdom.
The establishment of the gates of transformation has not yet transcended the trap and snare; to speak of the essential point, in reality there is nothing to be transformed.
Therefore, it is followed by the section "Transformation has no Object of Transformation. To perceive forms or seek sounds is to walk a deviant path;
herein lies the wondrous accord, where the true and eternal is uniquely revealed. Therefore, it is followed by the section "The Dharmakāya is Without Characteristics.

Having characteristics yet being without characteristics, empty yet not empty, spanning from antiquity to the present—whom would one call subject to annihilation? Therefore, it is followed by the section "Neither Annihilation nor Extinction. Great!
The mind achieves patience; it is inherently free from greed. Worldly blessings are already vast; how could there be further reception?

Therefore, this is followed by the section on "Receiving through Non-Reception and Non-Greed. Whether going, coming, sitting, or reclining, everything is in accordance with Suchness (tathatā). Therefore, this is followed by the section on "Tranquility of Dignified Conduct" (īryāpatha).

When the mind of faith is uninterrupted, this is itself a subtle atom (paramāṇu); when the jewel of faith is universally pervasive, this is called a world-system (lokadhātu). A single atom of a world-system—

It is so; it is the natural law (*dharmatā*). Therefore, this is followed by the section on "The Characteristics of Unity, Union, and Separation. The four views are all non-existent; these are called the "four views.
Therefore, this is followed by the section on "The Non-arising of Knowledge and Views. A single thought-moment of generating the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) yields merit in the same way.

Manifesting in response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to transform sentient beings—how could one help but do so? When the True Buddha’s transmission is circulated, his capable task is complete. Therefore, this is followed by the section on "Response."

The Transformation is Not a True Part; This Concludes [the Section]. (This is the tenth part of this sutra: "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. The original text of the Great Emperor says: "One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.

The thirty-second part: "No dharma can be obtained. The original text of the King of Equality says: "The Part on the Profound Faith of Sentient Beings. Although the wording differs slightly, the meaning is largely the same; there is no necessity to change it.)
Record of the Shàn-fǎ Hall at Dōng-lín.
On the eighth day of the seventh month in the second year of Yuán-yòu, the Shàn-fǎ Hall of Cān Monastery at Dōng-lín, Lú-shān, was completed.
It consists of seven bays; its height is five *zhàng*, and its depth is ninety *chí*. Its width is eleven [bays].
In the third month of the sixth year, Layman Wu-jin came from north of the River. Seven hundred disciples from Donglin followed him, with Bi-en-du as their leader;

they had all personally attended upon and made offerings to the current elder, Chan Master Zhaojue, whereby they deeply grasped the essentials of the Dharma, discerned the heterodox from the orthodox, dissolved away intellectual understanding, and practiced with single-minded diligence to uphold the teachings.
Regarding religion, Bi and the others then bowed their heads in prostration and addressed the layman, saying:

"This Hall of Good Dharma of ours has indeed traveled to the four quarters, seeking scholars and officials to record its construction for the edification of future generations; yet, in the end, not a single person was able to undertake the task.
Why is this? It is because this hall is so magnificent that it is difficult to capture in a likeness. Our Master’s preaching of the Dharma—"

"Because it is difficult for anyone to reach this place, it has been three years since the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans of our mountain have guarded it, awaiting your arrival, O householder.
Householder, please enter. The householder said, "The Dharma you preach differs from that of the Buddhas of the past;
it is not something that can be measured by my names, words, or consciousness. I have none—"
I have obtained and recorded this. Why is that? The Buddha Vairocana taught the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" atop Mount Sumeru;
Śakra, within his palace, prepared the Lion Throne of Universal Radiance Treasury for him. He taught the "Chapter on the Ten Practices" in the palace of the Yāma Heaven;
at that time, the Heavenly King of the Time-Portion manifested a precious lotus throne above his own palace.
Regarding your seat: while preaching the "Chapter on the Ten Dedications" in the Tuṣita Heaven, the King of the Suyāma Heaven spread a lion-throne of maṇi-treasury upon his palace.

Because the gods abide where the Buddha abides without departing from that state, he preached the Dharma in the "Heaven among the Earths," which is the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. That throne was then set in place, yet—
As for those who have attained transformation (*nirmāṇa*): their every action is true and they transcend the mundane world.
Thus, they preach the Dharma in the heavens amidst the void; this refers to the Yāma heaven. Their seats are transformations, yet they do not yet reach the level of "spreading" [the Dharma].
Transformation relies upon the void, yet it is not the means for entering into existence (*bhava*). Truth is for self-benefit, yet it is not... [the means for benefiting others].
It also benefits others. The mind returns to the Truth yet enters the mundane; it employs wisdom while practicing compassion.
Above, it causes one to transcend, such that one may emerge from the summit of desire; below, it causes one to descend, such that one may become one with the myriad things.
Therefore, preaching the Dharma in the Heaven among Heavens—Tuṣita—is precisely this. When its seat is spread and laid out, the Transformer is installed therein.
Indeed, there is much that need not be further discussed. When the Buddhas of antiquity preached the Dharma, they observed the faculties of their listeners;
thus, they established doctrines according to the specific conditions of the soil, which could be categorized and explained. Now, your teacher has constructed a vast hall and a towering throne.
The Dharma drum is on the left; the staff and whisk are on the right. From the perspective of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, non-abiding is abiding.
From the perspective of the Yāma Heaven, non-action is action. From the perspective of the Tuṣita Heaven, there has been no movement from the beginning, and now there is no returning.
Nevertheless, allow me to attempt to discuss its boundaries for you: that wondrous, profound, numinous clarity.
Vast, empty, and quintessential essence—nothing accompanies it as it departs, nothing welcomes it as it arrives. There has never been dreaming, yet there has never been waking;
there has never been purity, yet there has never been dilution; there has never been decay, yet there has never been formation;
there has never been defilement, yet there has never been purification. Through clinging they are born; through profusion they take shape.
The transformations of birth, death, suffering, and joy circulate through coming and going. For this reason, the Buddhas employ various parables and skillful means;

they preach the Three Vehicles for them and expound the Five Teachings for them. Yet, even with verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, these are insufficient to overcome their emotional attachments and seize their consciousness.
In the ultimate sense, it is through the pure Dharma-eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvana, which is formless.

The true mark, the treasury of the eye of the True Dharma—stripping away words and letters, this separate transmission outside the teachings was entrusted to Kāśyapa and has been handed down through successive generations until this day.
When the Dharma hall had not yet been built and the Dharma seat had not yet been ascended, even a flash of lightning presented as a kōan would still have been considered secondary;
what use, then, would there have been for students to come forward? Nevertheless, this hall has now been established, and this seat has been ascended.
Furthermore, can the ultimate nature of phenomena (dharmas) be described? Or is the ultimate nature of phenomena indescribable?

Now, when one knows that the hall is upright, one knows that its position is upright; knowing that its position is upright, one knows that its windows are upright; knowing that its windows are upright, one knows that its foundation is upright;
knowing that its foundation is upright, one knows that its consciousness is upright; and knowing that its consciousness is upright, one knows that its sensory objects are upright. Knowing...
If one knows that the dust is correct, then one knows that the ear is correct. Knowing that the ear is correct, then one knows that the nose is correct.

Knowing that the nose is correct, then one knows that the tongue is correct. Knowing that the tongue is correct, then one knows that the body is correct. Knowing that the body is correct, then one knows that the mind is correct.
In this manner, it extends even to the empty space of the ten directions and the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates.
There is nothing that is not made upright. That which the ancients called "this place being most auspicious" had its meaning in this very point;
is it not so? Yet, since the time of Shaoshi and from the era of Caoxi onwards, [the Dharma] has spread to the four quarters and divided into five schools.
Teachers offer different instructions; people have diverse habits. The Way of the Patriarchs is subtle; let me speak of it briefly. A qilin within the moon; stone shoots by the brook.
Cold pines and courtyard cypresses; gazing at mountains in the sun. The sound of rain and the cry of the cuckoo; meeting Bodhidharma while lost.
Dusting away the clouds to see the Buddha; the fisherman nesting in his hut; extending the tongue and withdrawing the body; raising the eyes for a single glance; lifting a fist or pointing a finger;
striking with a whisk or knocking on the meditation seat; placing hands together at the chest or opening both palms wide.
Some call this the "Eye of the Way," some call it "Roots and Objects," some call it "The Ultimate," and some call it "The Final Word. All of these are merely following the wind.
He scatters ashes upon the field of galloping conflict; he deepens the channels to drain the foul from the dilapidated well.
The Chan Master, therein, enters the great *mahā-vikrānta-samādhi* (Samādhi of Great Agility) and mounts the unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-prajñā*).

Through the dialogue of host and guest, employing methods of granting and revoking, or taking and giving, he hopes that those who are deluded may attain understanding, those who cling to views may have them shattered, those who are defiled may be cleansed, and those who are afflicted may find healing. Thus it is said:
Where there is a matter, there must be its underlying principle; where there is its substance, there must be its name.

That which is magnificently adorned and excellently good, and which cannot but be established, is the hall. That which employs skillful means to guide and instruct, and which cannot but be explained, is the teaching.

This is the Dharma. To transmit faith and demonstrate it to posterity, such that one cannot but act upon it, is the purpose of this record. It would not be right for me to refuse the request of the assembly at Donglin to compose this record.
The circumstances regarding the conversion of Donglin into a *śīla-vihāra* (monastery of discipline) open to the ten directions are fully detailed in the preface to my *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings);
here, they may be mentioned briefly. Recorded on the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month of the year.

There is no one who has not transmitted [the teachings] to others through written characters and spoken language. The present verse of the Seven Buddhas is one such instance.

As for the Central Lands (China), more than three hundred thousand years ago, when the Lord Baoxi (Fuxi) appeared, he drew the eight trigrams and created writing and seals, establishing the beginning of written characters.
This was no different from the rise of Śākyamuni; today, the Great Canon of Teachings may be called truly vast.
Yet, at the very end, he alone brought forth the flower to show it to his foremost disciple, Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa smiled with joy. It did not rely on written words nor take form in speech; it was called the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
Yet the Master held up a flower and transmitted it to his disciple, who received it with a single smile.

Since this was recorded upon wooden leaves and circulated among the people, it has never been seen to differ from that of the ancient sages. How could it be said that what is called "text" is not text? It is called...
Is it speech that is beyond speech? In the past, there was the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) in thirty fascicles;
this was indeed the non-textual text and the non-verbal speech. Once the lamp had been transmitted, from one it multiplied to ten thousand and a million—how could there be an end to it?
Thus, it was expanded during the Tiānshèng era and continued during the Jìngguó era. However, the works produced by these two houses were both hastily drafted and incomplete. All...
The examples were not established; the details were too sparse and missed the mark. Although it was a work by a sage-like worthy official, there were things incomplete;

one could only find glimpses scattered throughout the chapters of the various patriarchs, which those who understood the matter regarded as a regret. The *Sengzheng* (Director of Monks) of Wu, Shou, finally composed the *Pudeng* (Universal Lamp).
Over the course of seventeen years, he produced thirty fascicles. The regret of former days has been eliminated without leaving so much as a hair’s breadth. Especially...
As for those who have gloriously manifested the light [of the Dharma]:

the brilliant edicts and sagely compositions of my imperial ancestors—even a single phrase or half a verse—have all been collected and recorded with authoritative basis, sufficient to be transmitted to ten thousand generations and treasured as a great instruction.
Their contribution to the Śākya school is truly the greatest; I shall now present them to the Emperor.

The Imperial Library has a copy preserved in a famous mountain monastery. Furthermore, [the Emperor] presented a separate manuscript to me, You, so that you might record its general outline for future generations.
Since the Longxing era until the JiaTai era, I have served as a court historian for five reigns; though I have now retired on account of old age, I await my end among the mountains and marshes.
Regarding the legacy of my ancestors, I have sought— with my own meager contributions like dust and dew— to supplement the vastness of mountains and seas,
unaware that my strength falls short of the task. On the day of Yibyou,
the forty-third month of the Jiatai era, [I], Taizhong Dafu, serving as Director of the Baomuge Library and retired from office...
